en: {The Section on Brahman} [1,i] Bliss, one, immortal, unborn, consciousness, and imperishable.
We pay homage to Prajāpati, who is both the non-universal and the universal, and who is free from fear.
[1,ii] Regarding the Vedāntas, the learned hold conflicting views:

some consider them to lack authority; for if the Self is established by other means of knowledge, the Vedāntas would be merely repetitive (anuvādaka); if it is not so established, there can be no apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning]; or, if it were not the meaning of a word, it could not be the object of the sentence; and since they do not teach engagement or desistance, they would lack human purpose (apuruṣārtha).
Others, however, under the pretext that the authority [of scripture] lies only in the necessity of practical application (*pratipatti-kartavyatā*), declare it to be non-authoritative.

Still others, because of the contradiction with ritual injunctions (*karma-vidhi*) and the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, consider the literal meaning to be figurative when the scriptural sense is accepted.
To refute that, it is said: "Bliss" (*ānanda*).
And he honors the Supreme Deity with praise characterized by the expression of [His] qualities and with prostration characterized by the bowing of body, speech, and mind;

and he introduces the subject matter of the treatise: namely, that by means of refuting misconceptions, the validity of the Vedāntas with respect to such a reality is established, and therefore this too is the purpose of the treatise.
[1,iii] On this point, some [object]:
if Brahman consists of bliss (*ānanda*), then the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) would engage [in practice] out of passion for bliss (*ānanda-rāga*).
Furthermore, activity rooted in passion is the seed of saṃsāra; thus, it would not lead to liberation.
It is said that the vision of the Self belongs to one who is tranquil and self-controlled;
and one who acts out of attachment to bliss does not become tranquil.

Therefore, one who is agitated by sufferings and free from passion for pleasures, proceeding toward the reality of Brahman which transcends all suffering, is liberated. And the scriptural passages concerning bliss (*ānanda*) refer precisely to the transcendence of all suffering;
for the word "bliss" is observed to be used when the suffering of hunger and so forth has ceased.
And others say that this very [pleasure] is bliss (*sukha*).
Nor does this over-extend to stones and the like, because it is pleasure when experienced as an inward-turning state, or because it is the experience of the Self characterized by that [pleasure].
To those [who hold such views], he says: "Bliss" (*ānanda*).

The mere cessation of suffering is not itself happiness, because we observe pleasure and pain simultaneously in one who is tormented by heat when half of his body is submerged in a cool lake. Now, if you argue that there is happiness because the other [pleasure] is absent despite the presence of suffering from the half-body not submerged, then it would follow that one being cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell is happy due to the absence of suffering from other hells; and likewise, one suffering through the medium of a single sense organ would be happy due to the absence of suffering through the medium of the other sense organs.
Furthermore, even in the case of that which is not suffering, there arises a pleasurable sensation through contact with specific objects.
Even where there is the cessation of suffering, pleasure is not merely that cessation itself, because one takes up specific foods and drinks;
for the cessation of suffering is accomplished by various such foods and drinks.
And that [pleasure] does not possess any specific distinction such that a specific means for it would have to be required in order to produce that distinction;
however, since pleasure possesses degrees of excellence, its dependence on a superior means is logical.
As for what some think:
even if no other suffering is to be removed, nevertheless, since desire is of the nature of suffering, happiness consists in its eradication.
Even in that case, one who is free from desire would not experience happiness in the enjoyment of specific sense objects.
Moreover, even one who is neutral becomes possessed of joy upon contact with a pleasant object.
This might be argued:
only that object for which there is desire brings pleasure, and no other.
Therefore, objects become sources of pleasure only through the cessation of desire;
otherwise, that which is pleasant for one person would have to be pleasant for everyone.
But if pleasure arises from the cessation of desire, then it is logical that whatever a person desires or finds agreeable is pleasant for them alone.
In that regard, [it is argued] that even for one who is without desire, when desire is manifested through the enjoyment of specific objects, there is happiness upon its cessation.
This too is unsubstantial, because the enjoyment of objects does not necessarily extinguish desire;
for it has been said: "Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desired things."
Likewise, it is said: "Passions increase in accordance with the practice of enjoyments, as do the skillfulness of the sense organs.
Furthermore, the cessation of desire arises from seeing the defects in sense objects; in that case, there would be a pleasure equal to that of actual enjoyment.
And if the attainment of the desired object were the same [in both cases], there would be no difference in the degree of joy, because the cessation of desire would be indistinguishable.
It might be argued:
"In the case of excessive desire, there is the conceit of an excellence of pleasure upon its cessation, whereas in other cases it is otherwise.
But that is not so.

An object attained through excessive effort does not please as much as one that was sought after but arrived without exertion. For instance, one does not rejoice so much because "this was obtained with difficulty" as one does because it arrived unexpectedly, contrary to what was hoped for.

Furthermore, if pleasure consisted merely in the absence of desire for the enjoyment of desired objects, then the preceding and succeeding states of the state of enjoyment would not differ from one another;
or, if it consisted in the destruction of desire, the subsequent state would not differ [from the preceding].

If you argue that in the state of enjoyment one is simply someone whose desire has been awakened and subsequently destroyed, then it would follow—contrary to experience—that one is happy in both the preceding and succeeding states, while being miserable elsewhere.

Furthermore, an object that has not been attained but revolves in memory is an arouser of desire, whereas one that has been attained is its cessation. If an attained object were an arouser, there would be no cessation of desire because of it.
Moreover, pleasure does not reside where there is desire, for we observe that even one who has sought an object through hundreds of mental longings may still suffer upon its enjoyment.
Desire, however, is preceded by pleasure, because it is seen to arise when that [pleasure] has been previously experienced.
Even that occurrence of desire among those possessing a particular species of birth, even with respect to something never before experienced, is based on experience from a previous life.

And just as for someone, desire arises toward something due to causes such as the distinction of species and so forth, so too does some pleasure belong to someone; thus, there is no lack of systematic order.
Furthermore, some are even distressed by the cessation of desire, because in its absence, there is an incapacity to enjoy sense objects. Therefore, they are not seekers of cessation.
They desire to turn away from the object because it has become unenjoyable due to some cause.
Why, then, do they suffer? Because they fail to obtain the pleasure characteristic of that birth which was previously experienced.
Just as those whose senses are impaired by bile or other humors desire to turn away from excellent food and drink, so too they are tormented by the cessation of their desires.
In this regard, there is no cause for it other than the interruption of the joy experienced in that birth;
therefore, the rejection of pleasure that is to be personally realized is improper.
We see, however, that it was described by your honors merely to entice those who are attached to pleasure.
Thus, happiness is nothing other than the cessation of suffering;
and this is the primary meaning of the word "bliss" (ānanda).
Furthermore, when verbal testimony is the means of valid cognition, it is proper to understand things exactly as they are expressed by the words.
[3,ii] Furthermore, activity therein is not bound by passion;
for passion is not merely desire.

They declare that passion (*rāga*) is an attachment to unreal qualities projected by ignorance (*avidyā*). However, the clarity, inclination toward, and desire for reality (*tattva*) arising from the purity of the mind through the vision of reality is not established as belonging to the category of passion; just as the lack of agitation produced by the vision of the unreality of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is not established as belonging to the category of hatred (*dveṣa*). Otherwise, even though reality transcends all suffering, activity rooted in hatred toward it would result in the continued bondage of cyclic existence.

Moreover, even for those who are attached to the excellence of others they have seen, mastery over the senses is taught as a means consisting in the renunciation of desire and so forth; likewise, it shall be so here as well.
And how is there a prohibition against attachment to objects other than the desired one in that case? Because, when everything is prohibited, no activity is observed.
Likewise, there is desisting from attachment to other things, even from that which has arrived, due to attachment to the highest pleasure.
And so it has been said:
"Selfishness is not praised, nor indeed is desirelessness found here.
[3,iii]
This might be argued:
if bliss were to be experienced within Brahman, it would follow that there is duality, since the object of action is other than the agent;
and the relationship between agent and object does not exist without an action and an instrument.

Consequently, the statement "Brahman is bliss" would not be possible; if it were designated as such merely by possessing that quality, the claim that it is "without a second" would be untenable. Furthermore, if it were unperceived, it would be equivalent to non-existence even if it existed; thus, its mention would be futile.
For its mention is for the sake of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*); yet how can that which is not cognizable be a human purpose? It is said:
this should be understood as being like [the mention of] a result and like [the mention of] an agent. For instance:
All investigators maintain and recognize that the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is either distinct from it or non-distinct;
yet it cannot be imperceptible, for if it were imperceptible, it would follow that everything is imperceptible, since the perceptibility of entities depends upon that [fruit].
Nor can it be perceptible, because no further fruit would be perceived, which would lead to an infinite regress.
Therefore, it is cognizable because it is self-luminous;

yet it is also non-cognizable because, unlike an object, it lacks the status of being an object of action. Furthermore, if the agent—the Self—were not cognizable, consciousness itself would not exist.
For at that time, it does not occur to one thus: "This has been known by me."

For the self cannot be perceived by another when it comes to the fruit [of an action] or the object, nor can it be connected [to them]. And if there is no such connection, what distinction is there between that which is perceived by oneself and that which is perceived by another? Furthermore, it is not something to be perceived as an object, because if it were an object (*karman*), it would follow that it is distinct from the agent (*kartṛ*), and it would follow that it is not the self.
Therefore, its very state of being perceived consists solely in its self-luminosity.
Likewise, the nature of bliss belonging to Brahman, which is the light of its own self, is not an object of cognition, because it lacks the status of being an object (*karmatva*).
Nor is it non-cognizable, because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).
Even the negation in the passage, "By what means could one see whom? refers specifically to an object of action.
For it is said that he is characterized precisely by the cessation of all karma as its cause: "When for him everything has become the Self alone.
Others, however, think thus:
Phenomena are of two kinds: those consisting of existence and those consisting of non-existence.
Among these, those consisting of non-existence do not obstruct non-duality, as for example—
“[It is] one, immortal, and unborn.
For the cessation of difference, arising, and passing away is not some [separate] entity that would bring about duality.
And if bliss (*ānanda*) were an existing thing (*bhāva*), then if it were the substratum (*dharmin*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) would be its attribute (*dharma*).
Now, if consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the substratum (*dharmin*) and bliss (*ānanda*) is its attribute (*dharma*),

it is not logical for a single entity to possess two forms, because that would involve contradiction. In that case, in the statement "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," since bliss and Brahman— existing as attribute and substratum respectively— are distinct, non-duality (*advaita*) would be destroyed.
It might be argued:

"The property (*dharma*) is also not different from the substratum (*dharmin*), because if they were different, the relationship of property and substratum would be untenable, as in the case of a cow and a horse.
That is incorrect; for even if they were non-different, that relationship would still be untenable, just as it is with the nature of the substratum itself.

Therefore, the property (dharma) is somehow distinct [from the substrate]. Consequently, the scriptural teaching of the absence of absolute difference—“one only, without a second”—would not be tenable. This is likewise true for one who maintains that a single entity possesses two forms.

Therefore, the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) is merely a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the absence of suffering in Brahman, which is of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-ātman*), just as words such as "neither coarse, nor subtle, nor short" have as their limiting adjuncts the absence of coarseness and so forth.
Nor is there absolute identity between consciousness and bliss, because that would render the employment of two distinct words redundant.
And how can oneness be denoted by words that are not synonyms? Therefore, the meaning of the word "bliss" (ānanda) in the context of Brahman is simply the cessation of suffering.
To this, it is replied:
There is no fault here, because the two words convey a distinguished light whose nature is bliss, just like the lunar light;
as in the expression, "The sun is the supreme light."
Thus,
the words "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*) and "light" (*prakāśa*) are not synonyms;
nevertheless, by means of these two, a single specific object— a particular kind of light— is conveyed.

For there is no excellence in the sun other than its nature as light, nor is its nature as light anything other than its excellence; rather, a distinction within the light itself is perceived through the means of two words.

Likewise, in the passage "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," a distinction within bliss or a distinction within consciousness is understood by means of the two words to constitute the very nature of Brahman.

Furthermore, some maintain that this [bliss] is supreme because it lacks the nature of suffering characterized by dependence on external means and the nature of suffering characterized by perishability.
Furthermore, because one understands according to the word, they do not accept that [Brahman] is an object established by verbal testimony (śabdapramāṇaka).
For, since it is impossible for its own nature to be something other than itself, it is not logical for that [nature] to be metaphorical due to the non-association with a contradictory [quality].
Therefore, it is correct that Brahman has as its very essence a self-nature that is preeminent in self-luminosity.
And thus, O worldly one, it is appropriate that this [worldly pleasure] is merely a measure of that [supreme bliss], because of its limitation;
however, this is difficult to reconcile in the case of the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, the Self is of the nature of bliss, because it is the object of supreme love.
For it is heard that [the Self] is the locus of supreme love, as in the text: "This very Self is dearer than a son.
And this is also perceived;
for instance:
This desire for self-preservation belongs to everyone, even to a worm: "May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist.
And this desire is possible only with respect to what is dear; moreover, love is directed toward that which is of the nature of happiness.
It is not suffering, nor is it devoid of both [pleasure and pain], because there is indifference toward hatred.
Others, however, claim that there is an experience of pleasure in the self during deep sleep, based on the subsequent reflection, "I slept happily.
For such a reflection would not occur in the absence of an experience, and yet the state of deep sleep is accepted as occurring.
Nor is there a reflective awareness that "there is happiness" in the absence of experience;
nor is there anything other than the Self to be experienced therein.
And thus, the attainment of the world of Brahman day after day is heard in the scriptures.
Regarding this, others say:
"Since such a conceptualization is established even from the cessation of suffering, the state of being happy is not established with absolute certainty.
To them, they reply:
It is logical that the word "happiness" (sukha) refers to the cessation of suffering when a change of state is understood; otherwise, its primary meaning alone would be appropriate.
Regarding this, they say:
since we observe designations in both ways and since both are logically consistent, the actual state of affairs cannot be established by mere designation alone; enough of this excessive detail.

[6,i] Here, some maintain that the scriptural teaching of oneness is based on figurative usage caused by the absence of distinctions of genus, place, and time; for otherwise, there would be the establishment of experience, the logical possibility of the distinction between the liberated and those in saṃsāra, the purposefulness of the power of vision (since it cannot act upon itself), the inference of a seer from the seen, and the perception of the division of the seen into sound and so forth, as well as its differentiation into pleasure, pain, and delusion.
And as for the statement, "The Self alone is all this," that is due to metaphorical usage based on the fact that everything has the Self as its ultimate purpose.
To those [who hold such views], it is replied: "One."
In the passage, "Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion" (*indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate*), it is clearly shown that the perception of manifold forms is based on *māyā*.
In that case, how could one say that unity is merely figurative? Likewise, the negation of plurality is explicitly stated: "There is no diversity whatsoever here" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*).
And there is the censure of the vision of manifoldness:
"He goes from death to death.
And there is the absence of the vision of difference.

The perception of difference, like an illusion, is indicated by the word "as if" in the passage, "He who sees here as if there were diversity"; this [perception] is not figurative, for it is inconceivable within the context of true unity.
Granted that unity may exist through metaphorical usage, yet there is no cessation of actual diversity.
If it is argued that this too is stated merely as a figurative expression (*upacāra*), we say no, because there is no purpose for it.
A figurative expression occurs when there is a basis (*nimitta*) and a purpose (*prayojana*).
And we do not perceive any purpose in employing a figurative expression for the cessation of plurality (*nānātva*).
And because of the opposite [case]:
the cessation of plurality would not be conducive to either worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) or the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

For that [cessation], by abolishing the distinction between the means and the end to be achieved and so forth, and by manifesting a sense of self-identity everywhere, would be in contradiction with those [aims].
For thus, there is no contradiction in the fact that for one who has desisted from everything, there is the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

Likewise, by means of the restriction "one only, without a second" and the word "without a second," the Veda is seen to aim at the cessation of all forms of difference through the repeated statement of that very same meaning;
for in repetition, there is an intensification of the meaning, as in: "Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful!"
Nor is there even a deficiency;
from afar indeed is it merely figurative.
As for the argument that "it is because of the regulation of experience," it is replied:
this is worthless, since the regulation of experience is established even on the basis of an imagined difference.
For instance:

Even with respect to a single self that is omnipresent, or one whose size is equal to the body, or one whose size is atomic, the regulation of experience is observed to be based on imagined distinctions— such as,
"There is pain in my foot," or "There is pain in my head."
For there is no connection with sensation for either the foot or the head, because they are insentient.

Even for the proponent of a self whose size is equal to that of the body, it is not the limbs alone that are the locus of sensation, since that would entail the consequence that the self is devoid of it [in those parts].
This might be argued:
In the case of a single self, there would likewise be a recollection of experiences in other bodies.
This is a different matter altogether;
for the time being, there certainly exists a fixed order regarding experience.

Moreover, even in that case, one part does not connect with the sensation of another part; likewise here too, the individual soul (*jīva*) does not connect with the sensation of another soul—thus the cases are the same.

Furthermore, just as in the case of gems, swords, mirrors, and so forth, a distinction in color and shape is perceived among the reflections of pleasure and the like despite the absence of actual difference, so too the distinction between the liberated and the transmigrating soul is logically established.
For instance—even though the Self is one, when it is joined with pleasure, pain, and so forth in certain locations, it is perceived as if bound there and as if liberated elsewhere.

This is just as a face reflected on a soiled mirror-surface is perceived as soiled, while on a pure surface it is perceived as pure; yet, apart from the mirror, it is understood to be untouched by the defects of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
It might be argued:
conceptual construction is a property of the cognizer's cognition and is not capable of establishing the reality of an object;
for objects certainly do not conform to the cognizer's cognition.
Furthermore, an effect cannot be produced from that which is merely figurative;
for a youth who possesses only a figurative attribution of fire does not burn.
However, the established rule has already been illustrated.
True; for that is indeed an error.
Here too, its status as an error is not prohibited by any staff.
Even an imagined snake-bite leads to the effect of death, and a reflected sun leads to the effect of illumination.

Furthermore, as for the claim that there is a distinction between the seer and the seen because the seer is inferred from the seen alone, and that there is a plurality of the seen due to the perception of distinctions such as pleasure and so forth— that too is incorrect.
It has been stated that there is no establishment of the visible object when the seer is unmanifest.
Furthermore, it will be explained later that there is no perception of distinctions among visible objects because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) lacks the power of limitation.
Moreover, the capacity of the power of vision possesses its purpose through its own self-utility.
Nor is there a contradiction in [the self] acting upon itself,
as it has been stated that this is like a lamp or like the fruit of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, this relationship between seer and seen is possible only in the case of oneness, because the seer himself— the conscious self— undergoes such and such transformations or manifestations (*vivarta*).
But if there is a difference—[if] the two have distinct natures, their respective essences are unmixed and unconnected—then what kind of relationship of seer and seen could there be?
For it is not logical that something can be perceived if it is not mixed with consciousness (*cit*).

If it is argued that a connection certainly exists when [the object] has transferred entirely into the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), we say no; because consciousness is pure, non-transforming, and non-transferring.

If it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*), being an object of perception, undergoes a transformation (*vivartate*) through the reflection of consciousness (*cit*) due to its proximity to it—then what is this "reflection" (*tacchāyatā*)? It is the appearance of something as having the nature of another, though it does not possess that nature.
In that case, the object of perception is not perceived in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
And if it is not perceived in an ultimate sense, it is difficult to maintain that there exists anything distinct from the perceiver.
Even he who thinks:
"The object is established as an object solely by its being perceived, not by a [real] relation;
and perception has as its object an external form, such as 'this'."
He should be told:
"It is true that it has as its object the form of another;
however, this occurs because of the various transformations or manifestations of the single self itself, like [the reflection] of a face in the surface of a mirror."
For instance, one perceives oneself as reflected on the surface of a mirror as if it were distinct from oneself;
however, it is difficult to comprehend how consciousness could perceive that which is distinct and unconnected with it.
And thus, the non-difference of the object of perception from the perceiver is declared in the sacred tradition:
“When the Self is known, all this becomes known.
Therefore, it is well said that [the Self] is one.

However, those who maintain that the self consists of momentary cognitions assert that the attainment of Brahman is characterized precisely by the cessation of cognition through the total eradication of the afflictions along with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Thus it is heard in scripture:
"After death, there is no consciousness."

Others, however, [maintain that liberation] is characterized by the arising of pure knowledge, in which the turbidity of objective forms has been shaken off due to the total eradication of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

For if it were without beginning and without end, there would be nothing to be removed nor anything to be added; consequently, the scriptures intended for that purpose and the activities directed toward that end would be rendered useless.

To explain: if its nature were already that of knowledge (*vidyā*), then nothing would need to be turned away from, nor would anything need to be attained, because ignorance (*avidyā*) would be non-existent and knowledge would already be present.
If its nature were ignorance (*avidyā*), then because it would be eternal, it could neither relinquish its prior nature nor acquire another nature.
Likewise, even if it possessed both natures, since knowledge (*vidyā*) would already be attained and ignorance would be impossible to eradicate,
[the author] says this to them:
"It is the nectar, the unborn.
Nor is there any futility in the scriptures or in the activities aimed at liberation, because ignorance is that which is to be removed.
Furthermore, in all philosophical systems, it is accepted that even though beginningless, ignorance must be destroyed.
We do not say that there is no destruction of that which is beginningless; rather, we mean the eternal nature of Brahman.
Now, if ignorance were not the nature of Brahman, it would follow that it is something other than Brahman.
Or else, it might not exist at all—in that case, what would there be to be removed? If this is your view—

Nescience (*avidyā*) is non-apprehension; how could it be a distinct entity? Nor is it something that cannot be removed, because the operation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has as its purpose the cessation of non-apprehension.
That too is incorrect, for it is removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), which consists in the apprehension of reality.
And that [non-apprehension] is eternal in Brahman.
Nor is there anything other than Brahman for whom the non-apprehension of reality might be removed from Brahman by knowledge obtained through effort.
For in the case of Brahman, simultaneous apprehension and non-apprehension are contradictory.
Alternatively, if there were no contradiction [between the two], ignorance would never be removed.

For one for whom ignorance is the apprehension of error, if that [error] were the very nature of Brahman, being eternal, how could it be removed? If it were not its nature, then it would become a different entity;
and it must be stated to what that [entity] belongs, since nothing exists other than Brahman.

If it is argued that it belongs to Brahman alone, there is a contradiction, because its nature is that of knowledge (*vidyā*). Or, if there is no contradiction, by what means would there be cessation?

To this it is replied: Ignorance (avidyā) is neither the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of Brahman, nor a separate entity (arthāntara), nor absolutely non-existent (atyantamasatī), nor yet existent (satī).
It is precisely in this way that this ignorance is called māyā and a false appearance (mithyāvabhāsa).
If something had intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), whether it be different or non-different [from that nature], it would be the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) itself, and thus not ignorance (*avidyā*).
If it were absolutely non-existent, like a sky-flower, it could not be a factor in conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*).
Therefore, it is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*).
All proponents must accept this point as follows:
for the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), seeing reality as it truly is regarding existence is not ignorance (*avidyā*).
If it were equal to a sky-flower, it would not be a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Even for the proponent of Consciousness-Only (*vijñānavādin*), there is no denial of the object as long as the existence of cognition corresponds to its manifestation; for the forms of the objects of knowledge, such as blue or yellow, are not denied when they manifest externally, since it is impossible for something absolutely non-existent to manifest externally, like a sky-flower.

Furthermore, even for the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), errors such as the appearance of permanence in impermanent things or the delusion of silver [in mother-of-pearl] could not be classified as ignorance (*avidyā*) if the forms that manifest were not actually existent.
If it were absolutely non-existent, there could be no conventional usage based upon it.
It might be argued:
"Let the appearing form not exist; however, the appearance itself certainly exists, and that is what is called 'ignorance' (avidyā)."
This is not sound:
if that which appears does not exist, its appearance as well cannot be established as real;
there would be only the mere appearance.
The notion that there is an appearance of that [object] is also merely an illusion.
Therefore, ignorance is neither existent nor non-existent.
For this very reason, its cessation occurs because it is of an unstable nature, being nothing more than a magical illusion (*māyāmātra*).

How could there be a change in that which is firmly established in a nature other than [the one it appears to have]? Because that would entail the loss of its own nature. Since in emptiness there is a spontaneous cessation [of all conceptual constructs], there is thus no loss of non-duality, nor is there an absence of anything to be ceased.
[10,i] As for the question, "Of whom is it ignorance?
we reply: "Of the individual souls (jīvas)."
But surely, the individual souls are not different from Brahman;
for thus it says:
"Having entered with this living self (jīva)..."
Truth is so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);
however, they appear differentiated through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
But whose conceptual construction effects this differentiation? It cannot be that of Brahman, for Brahman, being of the nature of pure knowledge (*vidyātman*), is devoid of conceptual construction.
Nor does it apply to the individual souls (*jīva*s), because such souls do not exist prior to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), which would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence:
for the division of souls is dependent upon conceptual construction, while conceptual construction is dependent upon the souls.
On this point, some say:
there is indeed a fault in the establishment of a real entity (vastu);
for an unestablished entity is not capable of producing another entity, nor even in the case of mere illusion (māyāmātra).
For there is no impossibility in illusion;
indeed, illusion consists precisely in that which is impossible.
If it were possible in its objective reality, it would not be an illusion, because it would exist as it appears.

Others, however, explain that because both ignorance (*avidyā*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) are beginningless— like the continuum of seed and sprout— they do not entail the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Thus it has been said by those who maintain that ignorance is the material cause (*upādāna*):
“Nescience (avidyā) is beginningless and purposeless.

In this regard, because it is beginningless, there is no fault of mutual dependence; and because it is purposeless, there is no occasion for questioning the purpose of the creation of the manifold diversity of distinctions.
As some [object] question:
“It is said that ‘even a fool does not act without a purpose’; therefore, the purpose for the Supreme Brahman in creating the phenomenal world must be stated.
It cannot be the favoring of others, because prior to creation there are no beings to be favored, and because creation is followed by suffering.”

There is no play or similar activity for his own sake, because his desires are already fulfilled; since such things are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), they find no occasion in him. For ignorance does not function by depending upon a purpose.
For illusions such as a city of Gandharvas do not possess a specified purpose.
Likewise, the statement, "There can be no impure transformation of the pure Puruṣa," is also applied to the division of creation which is based on ignorance (avidyā).
Moreover, the engagement in play and the like occurs only out of exuberance for those who have accomplished their goals and whose desires are fulfilled.
However, for those whose minds are drawn by longing yet who are deprived of pleasure, such play becomes undesirable.
Nor is there the fault of partiality or cruelty;
for a magician displaying various manifestations does not experience a division of passion and hatred based on the distinction between the completeness or deficiency of limbs.

Whether it be those who produce paintings, books, and so forth—creating various works according to the distinctions of being complete or incomplete—or children playing with diverse clay models and the like, there is no partiality or cruelty toward them on the part of the Lord.
And for the Teacher [Iśvarakṛṣṇa], there is no fault in His ordaining such diversity in accordance with the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*);
nor is there the fault of Him not being the Supreme Lord.
For a Lord who bestows different fruits according to the differences in service does not thereby become powerless;
likewise, even for that which is pure, there is an impure modification.
Indeed, there is no absolute lack of distinction between the primordial nature (prakṛti) and its modifications (vikāra).
The very relationship between material cause and modification would not exist.

Furthermore, one must consider the manifold differences between material causes and their modifications—such as the solid modification of liquid water into hailstones and the like, or the conscious scorpion arising from the unconscious cow dung—and so forth. Enough of this digression.
But surely, since the individual souls (*jīvas*) are not distinct from the reality of Brahman, they must be pure by nature;
so how can there be any room for ignorance (*avidyā*) in them? This is a trivial objection.
For a reflection in a sword or other such objects is not actually different from its bright original (*bimba*).
And yet, in that case, impurities such as blackness find an opportunity to arise.
If it is argued that this is an illusion (*vibhrama*), then the same applies to the impurity of living beings (*jīva*): it too is an illusion.
Otherwise, as has been stated, purity would be impossible to attain.
It might be argued:

"In the case of a sword and so forth, there is a cause for the illusion in the mouth; likewise here too, a cause for the delusion must be stated. To search for a cause in a beginningless delusion is, as it were, improper."
And thus, the objection—"How can the activity of ignorance, which is like that of dreams and so forth, be brought about?"—has been answered.

Now, one might ask: "If ignorance is innate, beginningless, and without a cause, how could it be destroyed? Indeed, all the scriptures are set forth for the very purpose of destroying innate ignorance.
Furthermore, the beginningless blackness of earthly atoms is removed by color produced through baking (*pākaja*).
But surely, even something innate might cease upon the occurrence of some distinct cause;

however, for one who maintains the doctrine of absolute unity (*aikātmyavādin*), since there is no adventitious object, how could there be cessation? Indeed, knowledge cannot be the very nature of the Self, because ignorance would then coexist with it, resulting in a lack of opposition.
Or, if there were opposition, the world would be eternally liberated due to the eternal cessation [of ignorance].

Nor can another adventitious knowledge (*vidyā*) serve as a contradictory counteragent, because in the doctrine of non-dual unity (*aikātmyavāda*), such a separate entity is impossible, and because it is illogical for something adventitious to be the very nature of Brahman.
As it has been said:
"No one is able to destroy innate ignorance (*avidyā*)."
For if one were to be reborn with a different characteristic, one's inherent nature would perish in some cases.
"But there is no distinct cause for the means to [attain] oneness.
To this it is replied:
This has been stated: that living beings (*jīva*) are defiled by ignorance (*avidyā*), but not Brahman. For Brahman is eternally pure, of constant luminosity, and its nature is not adventitious.
Otherwise, even for one who has attained the state of Brahman, ignorance would not cease.
In that case, there would be no liberation.
Furthermore, if Brahman alone transmigrates and Brahman alone is liberated, it would follow that when one is liberated, all are liberated.
This is because, through the perception of difference, Brahman itself transmigrates, and through the perception of non-difference, it is liberated.

And for those whose minds are defiled by innate ignorance (*avidyā*), the cessation of that ignorance occurs through the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) as a distinct cause; for there is no innate knowledge in individual souls (*jīva*s),
since it is indeed innate ignorance alone that exists.

There is the dissolution of that adventitious ignorance. Furthermore, although the individual souls (*jīvas*) are non-different from Brahman, the distinction between knowledge and ignorance is explained as being like that of an original object and its reflection.

By what means, then, is ignorance removed? It is by the means taught in the scriptures: the hearing, reflecting, and meditating [upon the teachings], along with the repeated practice of meditation, celibacy, and other such specific disciplines.

How so? This practice of meditation, preceded by hearing and reflection, directed toward the Self described as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*)—in which all the manifoldness of difference has been negated—is clearly the antithesis of the perception of difference and brings that to an end.
And while it dissolves the perception of difference in a general sense, it is itself dissolved along with the Self.

Furthermore, hearing and the other practices do not have as their object the cessation of one set of distinctions by abandoning another set of distinctions, such as the hearer, the hearing, and the object to be heard; rather, they function through the dissolution of difference in a general sense.
And likewise, when that [impurity] has also dissolved away, his self shines forth, clear and perfectly pure.

Just as water turbid from contact with dust, when the powder of a specific substance is thrown into it, brings about its own state of clarity while itself being withdrawn along with the other particles of dust as they are absorbed, even so, when the perception of difference is dissolved through hearing and the other means of knowledge, and the difference residing therein vanishes due to the absence of particularity, the individual soul (jīva) abides in its own clear and perfectly pure nature.
However, it is by ignorance alone that the individual soul (jīva) is divided from Brahman; upon the cessation of that [ignorance], it becomes the very nature of Brahman.
Just as, when the distinctions such as jars are removed, the space within them becomes the pure, supreme space itself.
This might be so—
How is differentiation itself withdrawn by means of differentiation? Because it serves as the antidote to differentiation, just as dust is removed by dust—so it has been said.

It is indeed evident that even when there is a lingering connection with ignorance (*avidyā*), the repeated practice of hearing, reflection, and meditation upon the Brahman that transcends differentiation serves as the antidote to the perception of differentiation.
Just as milk digests milk and itself is digested, and just as one poison neutralizes another poison and itself is neutralized;
as it has been said:
"He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together..."
"Having crossed over death through ignorance, one attains immortality through knowledge."
This is what is meant:
both knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā) are conjoined because they stand in the relationship of means and end;
there is no arising of knowledge without ignorance.
If it is argued that [the relationship] must then be established, and thus impermanence follows from the state of being produced, he says:
"By means of ignorance, death... The meaning is this:
Ignorance is not the means for attaining knowledge;
rather, it is through ignorance—characterized by hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—that ignorance itself is brought to cessation.
Death is said to be nothing other than ignorance.

When that [ignorance] has ceased, one partakes of the nectar characterized by the nature of knowledge, which is abiding in one's own true nature, just as a crystal gem [regains its clarity] upon the removal of the coloring caused by its proximity to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
One remains established in the very nature of knowledge without requiring any further effort.
This is another interpretation.
Ignorance does not exist as something devoid of knowledge;
for likewise,
even the perception of difference is not devoid of luminosity.
In the absence of that [Light], no differentiation would manifest.
Therefore, it is the Supreme Light itself that manifests in various ways,
as it has been said:
“Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined.
However, [the soul] is bound by ignorance, as it has been said:
“Every perception, though non-deficient and free from conceptual construction, is nevertheless imagined as such by this internal person.

Likewise, knowledge—characterized by hearing the teaching of the unity of the Self and so forth—does not exist without ignorance, because it is bound up with the distinctions between the hearer, the hearing, and so on.

In that regard, through ignorance itself—which is closely proximate to knowledge—one transcends ignorance and abides in one’s own eternal nature, which is characterized by knowledge, just as water turbidified by a reflection becomes clear upon the cessation of that [reflection].
It might be argued:

since division is unreal within the state of non-dual unity (*aikātmya*), how could the hearing [of the Vedas] and other practices—which have that division as their substrate—be effective for any purpose? Furthermore, the realization of the real from the unreal is itself false, just as the realization of smoke from mist when it has been falsely perceived as such.
To this, it is replied:
This is not an absolute rule—
that what is unreal cannot serve any purpose;

for illusion (*māyā*) is indeed the cause of both pleasure and fear, and the unreal serves as the means for the comprehension of the real, just as a line-drawn cow or written letters [serve as the basis for understanding the actual cow or the meaning].
It might be argued: "This [world] is real by its own nature, not empty;
however, for the proponent of monism (aikātmyavādin), even the means [of knowledge] are unreal by their own nature."
It is said: let them be real in their own nature;
however, that form in which they are expressive is unreal.
The reality of an intrinsic nature devoid of utility for a purpose is useless.
Furthermore, even the means for perceiving non-difference are not false in their own nature, because Brahman alone is their very nature.

In that regard, Brahman itself, when bound by ignorance, serves as the means for attaining Brahman; just as lines and other marks indicate letters and so forth through forms that do not actually exist, such as "this is the letter *ka*" or "this is a *gavaya*."
Even he who thinks:
"A line-drawn cow is not the cause for the cognition of other gavayas as being *gavaya*s by virtue of its being a *gavaya*, nor is a line [the cause] by virtue of its being a letter;
rather, it is through similarity"—
"The gavaya is like this [cow]," and the convention regarding the lineage-mark:
"Upon seeing such a line, this letter is to be remembered. This contradicts common worldly experience.
For instance:

in the world, children are indeed instructed that lines are themselves letters, and there is a designation [of them] as non-different by both the speaker who says, "This is a gavaya," and the listener.
“‘This gavaya has been seen by me’— in this way,

the inference of the cause of the reflection, which resides in a specific location and is not itself seen, from a reflection that is unreal, is not false. Likewise, from an eternal word, the comprehension of distinct objects characterized by divisions such as long and short, though they are unreal, is not erroneous.”
Likewise, a false snakebite is a cause of death;
consequently, the inference of death, fainting, and so forth from it is not erroneous, just as it is from a real snakebite that is subject to differences in time and other factors.

For one for whom momentary cognition alone is the self, liberation would be impossible because there can be no addition or removal [of qualities], and thus the treatises on liberation and the activities undertaken for the sake of liberation would be rendered futile.
This is because that which is momentary extinguishes by its own nature, and because it cannot have any excellence added to it;
furthermore, since there is no distinction between particular and non-particular states within a single moment, a moment is indivisible.
If it is thought that there exists something within the continuum that can be added to or removed from it, that is incorrect;
for the transmigrating being is both the agent and the enjoyer.

Furthermore, the continuum (*santati*) cannot be the agent or the experiencer because it is not a real entity (*avastu*). Or how could liberation and bondage belong to that which is non-existent? Now, if it is thought:

"The continuum is neither absolutely non-existent nor existent; rather, it exists through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), and for the sake of its liberation, the scriptures and spiritual practices are undertaken."
In that case, it is the imagined [self] that transmigrates and is liberated.
Furthermore, both transmigration and liberation, whose objects are imagined, are themselves merely imagined.
Why is this, which we are stating, not acceptable to you? This has already been said:
Samsara and liberation pertain only to imagined objects, not to the supreme ultimate reality.

Moreover, even if one were to accept that consciousness is momentary, it is nonetheless the beginningless and endless continuum itself that is admitted as the basis for liberation and samsara. For instance:
Because the continuum is beginningless and because cyclic existence is not a real entity, there is no arising.
Nor is there cessation, because it is not a real entity and because a final moment is logically untenable.
For would that final moment initiate some effect, or not?
If there is no beginning, there is no end; therefore, because of the absence of that [end], there is no annihilation.
If there is no commencement, then due to the lack of all causal capacity and by virtue of the definition of non-existence, that [beginning] would be non-existent.
When that is non-existent, then by this very sequence, all members of the continuum (*saṃtānin*) would likewise be non-existent.

In the absence of that [final moment], the continuum itself does not exist; of what, then, would there be an interruption? Now, if the final [moment] indeed initiates an effect in another continuum—the omniscient one—then, given the existence of the causal relationship, how can it be "another continuum"? There is nothing other than the causal relationship that establishes a single continuum.
Nor is the establishment of a single continuum based merely on the causal relationship, but rather on the relationship between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect.
And the final moment is not the material cause of the omniscient cognition.
For that [object] is the objective condition (ālambanapratyaya),
and the appropriation (upādāna) is the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya).
Furthermore, omniscient knowledge is produced by an immediately preceding condition that has fallen within one's own continuum.
The final moment is its objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
If [the cause] were of the same kind as the effect, there would be no such thing as a homogeneous cause for the liberated mind or the omniscient knowledge;
for even one who thinks thus—

If it is argued that the cessation of the continuum occurs when there is an effect of a different character, then there would be the undesirable consequence of *nirvāṇa* occurring for that [consciousness] during a continuous stream of visual cognition simply because of a cognition of another object.
How, then, could there be no *nirvāṇa* when there is equality of the mind? Enough of this excessive elaboration.

However, some— desiring the true self (*ātmatattva*) to be a quality of consciousness (*vijñāna-guṇa*) while having the nature of non-consciousness (*avijñāna-svabhāva*)— declare that its abiding in its own essential form, with all specific qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*) completely uprooted, is the attainment of Brahman (*brahma-prāpti*). For that state of his, being unconditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body and senses, is vast (*bṛhatī*) and is thus celebrated as "Brahman."

Furthermore, if [the Self] were of the nature of knowledge, being omnipresent, independent of body and senses, and eternal by its very nature as knowledge, then there would be a vast cycle of transmigration due to the presence of various distinct objects of knowledge in close proximity.
If, on the other hand, it does not cognize anything at all, then it is not of the nature of knowledge;
for the meaning of the verb "to know" is necessarily transitive, and it is not tenable when there is no connection with an object.
He replies to them:
"Consciousness.
Why? For it is heard in scripture:
“Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite”; “It is consciousness and bliss,” and so forth.
Nor is the aforementioned defect applicable;
for just as fire, though inherently burning, burns only that combustible object which is brought near to it, and not that which is not brought near or is not combustible.
And just as crystal, mirrors, and the like—though transparent and luminous by nature—display whatever object is placed before them that is suitable, by assuming its reflection;

so too this Puruṣa, residing in the body which is the locus of experience, experiences sounds and other objects presented by the sense organs, which are the instruments of experience, by assuming their reflection, even though his consciousness is eternal.
And for this reason, there is no consequence of everyone seeing everything.
Moreover, there is no enjoyment of external objects in liberation.
It might be argued: "For that which is omnipresent, everything exists as an object."
In this regard, what is to be brought forward? It is said:

Even for that ignorant person for whom knowledge of the self (*ātman*) is produced by the conjunction of the mind (*manas*) and so forth, how can there be a fixed rule for experience (*upabhoga-vyavasthā*), given that all minds are in conjunction with all selves? For, through the medium of conjunction with the mind, all objects of those [minds] exist as objects for this [self]. Now, if it is argued that because experience is bound by karma, the fixed rule is caused by karma, then that [rule] is not at all barred even for one who maintains that the self is of the nature of consciousness (*citirūpa*).

Moreover, through the perfection of the vision of non-duality, when everything has become one's own self-nature (*ātmabhāva*), there is no seeing precisely because of the absence of an object to be seen. Even though its nature is that of a seer, it does not see, just as fire, whose nature is burning, does not burn in the absence of fuel; nor does it illuminate, just as light does not illuminate in the absence of an object to be illuminated.
As it has been said:
"For there is no loss of the seer’s sight, because of its imperishability."
"But there is no second thing, other than that, separate from it, which one might see"—as stated in passages such as "But when for him everything has become the Self alone.
Furthermore, liberation, characterized by the cessation of specific qualities such as consciousness and the like, does not differ from the position of annihilation;
for the absolute absence of perception, even of something that exists, is not distinguished from non-existence itself.
Furthermore, who would desire the non-existence of the self, which is dearer than anything else? Thus, liberation would not be a human goal (puruṣārtha).
This might be argued:
because it brings about the cessation of manifold sufferings, even the annihilation of the self is sought after by a person.
For indeed, those seized by severe diseases and evil are seen striving for their own destruction;
truly, with all happiness uprooted by the growth of illness, they bear a form as if composed entirely of suffering.
But this is not so for those in cyclic existence (*saṃsārin*), who partake in various and manifold joys, such as those of the gods.

In this regard, just as there is the status of being a human goal (*puruṣārthatva*) because of the cessation of various sufferings, so too there would be the status of not being a human goal because of the cessation of various pleasures.

However, for one whose state consists in the experience of supreme bliss from which all traces of suffering have been wiped away, that alone constitutes the absolute human goal; enough of this digression.

The term "syllable" (*akṣara*) expresses its nature as sound, because it specifically characterizes the universal; or else it denotes its unchangingness, since in the case of transformation, there is a "perishing" (*kṣaraṇa*) due to the cessation of prior attributes, and this is excluded here.
How, then, is it the nature of sound? From such scriptural passages as: "The syllable *oṃ* is both the higher and the lower Brahman."

Nor does this depend upon a denoted object, because a word ending in the suffix *kāra* refers to the phonetic form of the word itself; for we observe the suffix *kāra* even after a collection of phonemes that do not begin with the vowel *a*, as in:
"What is the purpose of the particle *eva*? and "What is the purpose of the particle *ca*?"
But surely they explain this quite differently:
since Brahman, which transcends all particularities, cannot be an object of meditation, this is an instruction regarding a symbol (pratīka);
one should meditate upon Brahman by means of this support.

Just as it is possible to perform direct worship of a deity, one performs the ritual of worship upon its emblem—whether in wood or stone—with the thought that it is the deity itself; likewise, the meditator thinks, "That deity is pleased.
Or, by this designation, that [emblem] is to be meditated upon, because the *praṇava* is its name.
It is said:

"Contemplate the Self as 'Om'," and "One should apply oneself with 'Om'"—in such cases where the status of being a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*) is heard, it is thus. But where there is no hearing of "one should apply oneself" and so forth, and the sentence culminates in identity itself, it is not so.
As for example: "Om is Brahman; Om is all this."

For here, by showing that the syllable *oṃ* is the essence of speech (*vācas tattvam*) because it follows all speech and is not abandoned by it, [the text] concludes with "All this is indeed *oṃ*"—since the manifold of forms does not abandon its nature as speech.

Even where there is the scriptural statement, "By means of this very [syllable], one should meditate upon the Supreme Person," that too is preceded by the demonstration of the state of being the self of all.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that the state of being the self of all is merely figurative for the sake of praise, since there is no contradiction even if it is taken in its primary sense.
For it is not contradictory that this form, which is not ascertainable through perception and other means, is to be understood through scripture;
indeed, the non-apprehension of something by one means of knowledge does not deprive another means of knowledge of its object.
Furthermore, the phrase "therefore the wise man" indicates that the instruction on meditation is intended only for one who knows the Self of all.
Nor does it come from anything else;
therefore, the sentence concludes right there.
Following that, for one who has realized the universal self-nature, the instruction on meditation is given.
Alternatively—in passages such as, "Speech indeed gave birth to all beings; speech alone enjoyed this; speech spoke"—the universal selfhood of Speech is heard in scripture.
Likewise, in the Vāk-sūkta, the universal selfhood and the lordship over all of Speech are demonstrated.
“I move with the Rudras and the Vasus”—this was by means of speech alone;
just as it was by Vāmadeva, who had awakened to the Self, [who said]:
“I became Manu and Sūrya.”
Moreover, modifications are endowed with the form of their material cause,
and the world is endowed with the form of speech; therefore, it is understood that the world is either a transformation (*vipariṇāma*) or an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of speech.
How is there conformity with that [object]? Because it is to be experienced by a consciousness colored by that [object].

For thus, everyone clearly perceives the difference between the cognition of an object from a word and the cognition "there is fire here because of smoke," which, due to its different locus, is manifestly distinct.
And for this reason as well, it is so:
As for the relationship of qualifier and qualified that is perceived between two words, such as in "a blue lotus," this resides solely within the objects [themselves].

Otherwise, just as in the case of "it is a post because it is upright and a crow is perched on it," where there is a cognition of a distinct object through two mutually exclusive meanings, so too would it be here.
Furthermore, since a word is a cause of comprehension like smoke, there could be no certain determination of the object through the form of the word itself.
Furthermore, the ascertainment of fire through smoke or another means of valid cognition does not conform to the form of the smoke itself.
However, even when an object is ascertained through another means of valid cognition, that ascertainment involves a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the form of a word.
Observing this, we conclude that even when there is comprehension from a word, the comprehension occurs in that same manner; it is not a delusion caused by immediate succession.
Furthermore, this activity of even infants toward the breast and so forth, which occurs by avoiding other objects, could not exist for those who do not ascertain "this is [that].
Activity based on one of two possibilities—such as a post or a person—is not possible when there is no ascertainment.

Nor is an ascertainment devoid of the coloring of words; therefore, even for them, whose mental impressions of words from previous births persist, cognition is determined as being precisely colored by the form of speech.
And thus we perceive that the world, which is grasped as having that [Brahman’s] form, is its vivarta (illusory manifestation).
Moreover, there exist empirical objects whose reality is nothing other than a transformation of words;
by analogy with them, others too should be understood in the same way.

For example, injunctions and prohibitions such as "one should act" and "one should not act," the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), a collection (*samūha*), and non-existent things such as a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*) or a rabbit's horn—
among these, injunctions and prohibitions do not pertain to past activity and cessation, nor to the present, nor to the future; for if they did,
there would be no distinction between [the statements] "he cooked," "he cooks," and "he will cook."
If it is argued that [the object] is an effect (*kārya*), we say no; for "effect-ness" cannot be established apart from the three times (past, present, and future).
Therefore, injunction and prohibition must be mere appearances (*pratibhā*) devoid of objective reality (*avastuka*), conforming respectively to engagement and withdrawal.
Furthermore, it is not logical that a manifestation (*pratibhā*) should be without an object (*anālambana*), because its nature is that of cognition.
Nor is it devoid of the conceptual determination (*parāmarśa*) of the form of words.
Therefore, it is correct to maintain that the very reality of speech (*śabdatattva*) manifests itself in various ways in accordance with engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).
Such is the meaning of the sentence:
a relation is nothing apart from the relata; it is not something distinct from the nature of the relata themselves.
Nor is there a cognition devoid of an object of cognition.

It is not logical to claim that a conceptual cognition is devoid of the coloring (*uparāga*) of the form of speech, such that it is the reality of speech itself that evolves (*vivartate*) in various ways.
This same principle should be applied to collections such as forests and the like, as well as to non-existent things such as a whirling firebrand.

Furthermore, although there is a cognition of the notes of the scale (*ṣaḍja*, etc. or of cows and so forth prior to the word, it is not of the same kind as that which occurs at a later time following the application of the word.
For prior comprehension is undiscriminated, whereas later it becomes more distinct and possessed of discrimination.
Thus, cowherds, shepherds, and others apply designations in order to achieve discriminative knowledge.

And so, since an excellence of understanding is observed when an object is touched by a word, and since even things that have been consciously perceived become as if unconsciously perceived when that [word] is withheld—just as grass and such are disregarded by one walking on a path—the very capacity for cognition of the mind is dependent upon the form of speech.
Alternatively, consciousness itself is the power of speech (*vākśakti*).
Even when that [consciousness] is withdrawn, some maintain that the subtle power of speech remains.

In any case, the cognition of an object of knowledge is dependent upon the form of speech; therefore, every object of knowledge is understood as being endowed with the form of speech, and thus it is either a modification (*vikāra*) or an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) thereof.
Just as pots and other objects are [transformations] of clay, or as the moons in ripples of water are [reflections] of the moon;
however, others— on account of the observation of examples such as clay— maintain that Brahman is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*).
That is refuted by the word "imperishable" (akṣara).
Why? Because of the scriptural declarations found here and there that it is "firm" (dhruva) and "eternal" (nitya).
Now, it might be thought: even though there is transformation (*pariṇāma*), its permanence is not contradicted because its essential nature (*tattva*) remains unimpaired.
As it has been said:
"That which does not lose its essential nature even when it undergoes modification is also eternal.
True;

nevertheless, since that pure form of the Self is non-existent [in such a case], if there is transformation in its entirety, there is impermanence; if there is transformation in only one part, then because it possesses parts, both its permanence and its unity are contradicted.

This very purity, eternity, and unity are possible only in Brahman, which is like space (*ākāśa*). Even when a limitation is imagined, space remains unconditioned and unlimited despite that imagined limitation.
Furthermore, since any transformation of an imagined portion is merely a product of imagination, it has been well said: [that it is not real].
Regarding the term "the Imperishable" (akṣara):
some, based on scriptural passages such as "He who is all-smell and all-taste," have arrived at the conclusion that Brahman is the self of all.
And thus, since the enjoyment of objects is possible, it is logical that objects should manifest for the Self, whose nature is luminosity;
for if they were other [than the Self], the manifestation of insentient things would be impossible.
To those [who hold such a view], he says:
"It is not the whole.

Why? Because of the negation of all limiting adjuncts (*uparāga*) through the statement, "neither gross, nor subtle, nor short," and because there would be no liberation due to the non-separation from all such limiting adjuncts.
For it is impossible to separate a thing from its own nature, just as fire cannot be separated from heat.
Even if it were somehow separated, since the continuity of the manifold of difference would not be severed, there would be no liberation, and thus there would be eternal transmigratoriness.
In every respect, this [Self] has hunger, thirst, and so forth, as its manifold nature.
Furthermore, the destruction of its phenomenal proliferation (prapañca) is not accepted [by the former].
In that regard, for the proponent of a single self (ekātmyavādin), there is no liberation;

however, for the proponent of the plurality of selves (ātmabhedavādin), there is a distinction between the liberated and those in saṃsāra, such that for one the [proliferation] is destroyed while for another it is not.
Therefore, Brahman does not consist of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*); it is established that phenomenal proliferation is merely the play of ignorance (*avidyā*).
If, then, phenomenal proliferation is indeed the play of ignorance, then the emptiness of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca-śūnyatā*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Let that alone be Brahman, because it is the ultimate reality;
and thus its nature is made known precisely through the negation of the phenomenal world, as in:
"This is 'not this, not this,'" and "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long."
To this he says: "All.
This is what is meant:
Brahman does not possess the nature of being the self of all things;

rather, everything has Brahman as its self. It possesses form by virtue of having the nature of Brahman, and is not a mere void, because that would entail the consequence of its being eternally liberated, which in turn would render the teaching of its purpose and the activity [of scripture] toward that end futile.
If it is argued that even if there were eternal liberation, transmigratory existence is caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), [we reply:]...

If non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*) were ignorance (*avidyā*), how then could *saṃsāra* be based upon it? For that [non-apprehension] would be equally present even in liberation (*mukti*), and consequently, nothing at all would manifest, just as in that state.
Alternatively, if ignorance is the apprehension of things as they are not (*ayathārtha-grahaṇa*), then there is no universal emptiness (*sarva-śūnyatā*).

This is because of the Vedic revelation: "All this is filled by this Puruṣa," and because of the teaching that the Self is everything—"All this is indeed the Self"—and because emptiness itself is denied by the text: "How could being be born from non-being?"
For an entity, not manifesting as it truly is, appears with a superimposed form that does not exist;
however, in the case of the void (*śūnya*), where could there be superimposition, and what could possibly manifest? Thus, it would result in a state of total groundlessness.
Furthermore, because of the scriptural teaching of its nature as "consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam*), Brahman is not a mere absence of everything, but rather the Self of all.
[20,ii] However, some maintain that because pure happiness is never observed and is invariably accompanied by suffering, there is no state free from contact with suffering;
for no living being is ever found to be exclusively happy, nor exclusively suffering.
Pleasure exists only for one who possesses suffering;
the touch of sandalwood is pleasant only for one who is afflicted by heat.
To this, he says:
Regarding the term "fearless":
the state of Brahman is indeed entirely free from all fear.
Nor is there even the slightest affliction therein, as is repeatedly heard in such scriptural passages as, "Brahman is indeed fearless."
For indeed, fear cannot be inherent in Brahman, because that would contradict its nature as bliss;
nor can it be adventitious and caused by something else, because of the absence of a second entity.
As it has been said: "From a second, indeed, fear arises."
Furthermore, pleasure is not of the nature of the cessation of suffering, such that pleasure would remain as pleasure only for one who is suffering; this has already been explained at length above.
Another way [of explaining it]:
In this regard, some maintain that even those considered liberated are subject to the fear of returning.
For here, the conscious selves (vijñānātman) must either be distinct from Brahman or non-distinct.

Furthermore, they must either be differentiated by Brahman itself—either for the sake of experience, for the sake of sport, for the sake of manifesting its power, or by its very nature—or [they must be so] inherently.
Alternatively, their distinction is based on ignorance (*avidyā*).
Or rather, it is the cognizing selves (*vijñānātman*) alone that are denoted by the word "Brahman," and there is no other Brahman.
For them, transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is based on karma and ignorance, or else it is based on the mutual compatibility between the seer and the seen.
In that regard, if [the manifestation] were based on capacity (*yogyatā*), then because that capacity is never lost, the fear of returning would remain unabated.
If, however, there is no return because the task has been accomplished, then once sound and so forth have been perceived, they should not be perceived again.

If it is argued that primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—possessing infinite modifications—ceases when perceived in its entirety, yet continues to function for the perception of other unmodified forms, [we reply: ...

In that case, because of its very infinity, perception [of the Self] cannot occur in its entirety; thus, even for one who possesses the discriminative knowledge of the difference between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*, a return to transmigratory existence might be possible.

Even if it were based on ignorance and prior karma, since saṃsāra is beginningless and karmas are infinite and their time of fruition is不定 (*aniyata*), the fear of relapse remains unavoidable even in the state of liberation, just as it does in the state of cosmic dissolution (*pratisarga*).
Furthermore, even if it were based on ignorance, since that ignorance is itself causeless and its activity is purposeless, by what could its repeated recurrence be prevented?
And likewise, in deep sleep, a return from the attainment of Brahman is observed.

However, in the case of an independent Brahman, it is not possible for the distinction of bodies and so forth to arise again—whether the individual souls (*jīvas*) were previously distinct or non-distinct—with respect to the causes of bodily experience and enjoyment, through such means as the distribution of those experiences.
For an independent Lord, like a worldly ruler, might bind [beings] again either for sport, to manifest His sovereignty, or by His very nature.
Now, this [bondage] depends upon karma; it does not possess independence with respect to karma.

Nevertheless, because karmas are infinite and because there is no fixed rule regarding the time of their maturation (*vipāka*), rebirth is possible even after the passing of hundreds of eons from those karmas whose time for maturation has arrived.
For the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) does not pertain to a single lifetime alone; indeed, its manifestor is not merely death (*prāyaṇa*), but also factors such as place and time.

For instance: even within a single body, the enjoyment of the fruits of karma is observed to occur sequentially; moreover, it is impossible for actions that cause the experience of contradictory births to arise and cease simultaneously; furthermore, there would follow the undesirable consequence that those who die in the womb would be liberated without having performed any karma. To this, it is replied:
Regarding the term "fearless":
this is heard to be the supreme attainment of security;
in it, there is no longer any fear of saṃsāra.
Rebirth in saṃsāra is not caused by karma alone, because even infinite karmas whose fruits have not yet been experienced are destroyed by knowledge, just as they are by expiatory rites.
For it has been said:
"The fire of knowledge reduces all karmas to ashes in that same way."
Likewise, it is said: "And his karmas are exhausted.
Alternatively, when ignorance is removed by knowledge, the distinction between agent, action, and fruit is simply dissolved;
how then could that [distinction] possibly exist?
Nor does it have ignorance (*avidyā*) as its cause, because there is no cause for its arising.
For ignorance is beginningless; precisely because it is beginningless, it does not depend upon a cause.
The operation of a cause occurs only with respect to a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); in the absence of prior non-existence, when could a cause ever operate?

For there is no causal function for that which already exists; however, ignorance (avidyā), having been previously non-existent, when it arises after being severed [from its cause], cannot arise without a cause.
In deep sleep (suṣupti), however, only the manifestation (vikṣepa) has ceased, while its latent impression (saṃskāra) and the non-apprehension (agrahaṇa) have not ceased at all.
Otherwise, it would not be distinct from the fourth state (turīya).
However, because there is an absence of even the slightest distraction, it is said that one attains Brahman.
Therefore, it is well said:
"Fearlessness."
[22,i] By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, is this object apprehended?
It cannot be by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that has as its object a diversity contrary to this [non-dual reality].
Nor can it be established by inference, because inference is preceded by perception. Nor by analogy, because its object is similarity, and that [similarity] is based upon difference.
As for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it applies to the contrary case; for no worldly transaction whatsoever is possible without difference.
For non-difference, too, is difficult to comprehend without the distinction between the knower and so forth.
Even non-existence is not sufficient for the comprehension of the reality that consists of existence,

nor for the comprehension of the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), because such [non-existence] is impossible as long as perception and the other means of knowledge remain operative.

Furthermore, scripture (*āgama*) does not apply here as something authored by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), because its subject matter is already apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is it independent, because it consists of injunctions and prohibitions, and these two are impossible once reality (*tattva*) is established.

Nor can its validity be established independently of those [other means], having as its object only an already existing thing, since, in the case of being a mere restatement of what has occurred (*bhūtānuvāda*), it would depend upon other means of valid cognition.
The understanding of the capacity of words is also derived from common worldly usage.

In that regard, words are employed only with reference to what is to be done (*kārya*), among objects connected to that which is to be done, because they possess meaning only in such a way. For speech devoid of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) has no purpose whatsoever.
Moreover, the understanding of the relationship of a word does not arise from the mere restatement of what has already occurred, but rather from that which prompts action.
