For it is through activity that one infers the cognition of the object, and thereby perceives the capacity of the word therein.
Thus, the power of words is not understood to apply to objects that are devoid of a connection to such activity.
That being the case, how could words whose capacity [to denote] is not already known cause that past object to be understood?
Furthermore, if that object has been ascertained by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the word possesses no authority (*prāmāṇya*) regarding it;
and if it has not been so ascertained, then all the more so.
For if it were not a word-meaning (*padārtha*), it could not be the object of a sentence;
indeed, it is only a word-meaning that becomes the meaning of a sentence by way of being qualified.

However, something entirely unobserved, which is not understood from a word, cannot enter into the meaning of a sentence—which consists of the relation between word-meanings—either as a subordinate or as a primary element.
Moreover, reality in which all limitations have dissolved is indeed beyond the reach of cognition.
For every cognition proceeds by means of exclusion, such as "it is thus" or "it is not thus."
Otherwise, no one would have attained realization.
To the question, "But how can there be realization when all specific attributes have vanished? he says:
"The wise declare that its establishment is through sacred tradition (āmnāya) and through common renown."
And its definition is by way of the dissolution of the proliferation of difference. (1.2)
[23,i] It will be explained that even though it speaks the truth, that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya) is not dependent on anything else;
nor are all utterances in the world restricted solely to what is to be accomplished (kārya).

For instance, pleasant reports such as "Congratulations! A son has been born to you" are seen to serve the purpose of producing happiness, neither for the sake of engaging in action nor for desisting from it.
Nor is an engagement in action enjoined there by saying "Be happy," because that [state of happiness] is established by the very power of the object itself, rendering further instruction unnecessary.
Now, if it is thought—
There is indeed a specific activity there, and the intention (*tātparya*) of the speech resides therein.
True;
however, the intention pertains to the production [of the cognition], not to its comprehension.
Practice, however, must be grounded in the actual state of reality (*bhūtārtha*).

Furthermore, it is not possible to postulate that the operation of a word—which terminates in the actual state of reality—has its limit of activity in mere activity (i.e., the mere initiation of action), even if that word possesses a purpose. Moreover, a person who has not yet engaged in a means is incited to engage in it; or else, one who has not previously engaged in the goal because the means were unknown is incited to it by way of making the means known.
In this case, there is no engagement with the means—the birth of a son—because that has already been accomplished;
nor is there engagement with the end—the happiness—because there is no further activity directed toward it.
Likewise, by the same logic, the words of wicked people, which communicate unpleasant news and serve only to cause despondency, do not enjoin either engagement or withdrawal.

Likewise, in the case of one who mistakes a rope coiled up for a snake, the communication of the truth is seen as a means to remove his fear; however, there is no injunction such as "Do not be afraid" in that situation.

For an injunction applies only where, having understood the purpose of the injunction, a person subsequently engages or desists through conscious deliberation, by the power of the injunction, or out of desire.
In this case, however, the cessation of fear occurs solely from the realization of the truth, due to the absence of any cause [for fear], independent of the desire for an injunction.

Furthermore, once fear has ceased, a person who has spontaneously engaged because it serves their own purpose is not one to be enjoined; nor is there an injunction regarding the means to that cessation, namely the realization of reality, because such realization arises from the word itself—as in "This is a rope, not a snake"—and because any subsequent activity following the comprehension of the word's meaning is dependent upon a formal injunction.

Likewise, accounts of events occurring in distant lands, provided for the sake of satisfying the curiosity of those who have asked about them, terminate in the description of facts as they are; they do not aim at rejection or acquisition.

Moreover, even in cases where avoidance or acquisition is possible upon the comprehension of a real object— such as, "This path is beset by obstacles" or "This portion of ground contains a treasure"— even there,
the word functions toward that avoidance or acquisition because it brings the real object to mind.

Having understood the real object from the word and having recollected its status as a cause of benefit or harm as known through other means of knowledge, one engages out of desire or desists out of aversion.
But surely the speaker, acting with prior intelligence, employs speech for the sake of inciting or deterring the listener;
thus, it culminates exclusively in engagement or withdrawal.
For in such cases, one would have employed [the words] "One should not go by this path" or "Take the treasure from here," yet these are not employed.
This is not sound.

For even a statement that culminates in a real object (*bhūtārtha*) does not have its status as an auxiliary to engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) obstructed by virtue of its function of making that real object known, just like perception and the other means of knowledge.

Just as perception and the others—whose operations are fully completed by the valid cognition of a real object—do not forfeit their status as auxiliaries to engagement and withdrawal despite not having directed themselves toward those activities even in the slightest degree, so too it is with the word; thus, nothing is impaired.

If it is argued that activity and cessation are intended by the agent [and thus constitute the meaning of a word], we say no; for words do not have their meaning through the agent’s intention, but rather through their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).
Otherwise, even the attainment of various human goals mediated by the discovery of a hidden treasure would be the meaning of the word, since that too is intended by the agent.

Furthermore, when something is investigated through perception and other means with a view toward either activity or cessation, then even though activity and cessation are intended, they are not the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) for perception and the rest.
Furthermore, even when directed toward those [objects], engagement and withdrawal are not the meanings of words.
This is also evident from the fact that one person has the intention to appropriate [an object], while another has the intention of indifference toward it.
For if all words were the meaning, there would only be the cognition of the material cause (*upādāna*).

Nor is the understanding of the relationship [between word and object] derived solely from the linguistic usage of injunctive sentences, such that the dependence on activity alone could be understood.
Because it is observed otherwise as well.

For instance, in the sentence "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with wood," a person who has not yet mastered the meaning of the word "wood" (kāṣṭha), but has mastered the meanings of the other words and the meaning of the case-ending, perceives that which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the act of cooking; such a person thereby comes to understand that the stem *kāṣṭha* denotes the instrument.
Similarly, mastery [of word-meanings] arises from explanations of reality that serve the purposes of joy, dejection, or consolation, regarding the causes of joy and so forth.

For just as, from the observation of a particular activity, one infers either a specific motivating cognition or the cognition of its cause—since no other cause exists and because it follows immediately upon the word, the capacity of the word for that purpose is postulated—so too, from the perception of joy and so forth, there is an inference of the cognition of the cause of that joy; and because it follows immediately upon the word, the capacity of the word for that purpose is postulated.

Furthermore, since the cause for joy—the birth of a son—has been apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and no other [cause] exists, one understands that this sentence, "A son has been born to you," was uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*) with respect to that birth of a son.
And one determines that it is precisely the birth of a son that has been cognized by him from this sentence.
Thus, through both the application [of the words] and the resulting cognition, one apprehends the capacity of the sentence with respect to this meaning.
Or, let it be granted that all speech in the world functions as a producer [of meaning], and from that, the comprehension of the relationship [between word and object] occurs;
nevertheless, this must be investigated:

Do words other than the injunctive word terminate in their own primary meanings alone, or do they terminate in a connection with a purposeful action (*kārya*), or do they terminate in a connection between the meanings of the words themselves?

In that regard, if they were to terminate solely in their own primary meanings, there would be an absence of the cognition of the sentence-meaning and the employment [of such sentences] would be futile.
Therefore, they must terminate in a connection with another meaning.
To that extent, when the causal conditions for the application [of words] are established, there is no evidence for a connection with specificities (*viśeṣa*).
For whoever postulates a connection with specificities, he likewise postulates a connection with distinct entities (*arthāntara*).
And thus, even without an effect, the cognition of a qualified object would be established through the mutual association of word-meanings.
This must necessarily be understood in this way;

otherwise, since in the world the connection between word-meanings is subordinate to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), the absence of such [intention] in the Veda would result in no comprehension of the Vedic meaning. Furthermore, if all [word-meanings] were connected only with the "thing-to-be-done" (*kārya*), there would be no mutual relation among the word-meanings themselves.
In that case, the injunction (*niyoga*) would not be understood as having a qualified object;

it would instead have only a single word-meaning as its objective. Alternatively, if the injunction does not have the application (*viniyoga*) as its object, it is because its object is something qualified.
In that case, there is first the *viniyoga* (syntactic connection), and afterwards the *niyoga* (the mandate).

What follows from this? There is a capacity in a word for connecting with meanings other than the mandate, independent of the mandate, because there is a connection with the mandate only after [words] have already been mutually connected.
Furthermore, it will be demonstrated that syntactic relation (*saṃsarga*) is not based on the requirement of a mandate.

Even that which has not been apprehended by another means of knowledge, and whose relationship [to its denotation] has not been previously grasped, can be defined by its own word through the negation of specific attributes; for the connection of specific words and the negative particle with their respective objects is already known.
Thus, it is taught in this very manner: "Not coarse," which transcends all specific attributes.
This conveys the following—
"By means of the dissolution of the proliferation of difference"—
and this will be explained later. [26,i]
There is another point.
As it was said— that reality, in which all particularities have completely subsided, is not an object of cognition at all— to that it is replied:
It is by the very exclusion of specific attributes that the thing is established in the intellect by means of that word, like the essence of gold (*suvarṇatattva*).
For the essence of gold is not perceived as free from the obscuring influence of various distinct forms such as a lump or a necklace;
nor are those forms themselves the essence of gold, since it continues to exist even when they are abandoned upon the occurrence of another form.

Moreover, even that which is free from the confusion caused by the distinctions of unperceived forms is itself realized by the intellect through the exclusion of differences, and is communicated to another;
this very process of realization has been shown by the Scripture itself in the words:
"This is not it, not it."
Likewise by others:
"That which remains at the end when the withdrawal of forms has occurred.
And similarly by others:
“Through superimposition and negation, the non-proliferated is proliferated.
Now, this is being investigated:
Does the entire Vedic corpus (*āmnāya*) define Brahman by means of the dissolution of the manifold of difference (*bhedaprapañca*), or is it only a certain portion of it? Regarding this, some say:

throughout the entire Vedic corpus, the dissolution of some particular difference is perceived in various places; for example, in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," there is the dissolution of the identification with the body as the self.

For here, the qualified agent (*adhikārī*) is understood to be one capable of enjoying heaven, which is distinct from the body; therefore, there is a dissolution of the identification of the body with the self.

Likewise, from the rule "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a milking vessel," there follows the dissolution of the distinction between different qualified persons due to the qualification of one already engaged in the primary act.
Similarly, even in the injunctions of prescriptions and prohibitions, there occurs the dissolution of natural activities rooted in passion and the like;
in the case of prohibitions, this occurs directly, while in the case of prescriptions, it occurs through the internal application of the mandate toward activity.

In the world as well, one is either directly prevented from an undesired path, or [deterred] by the instruction of an alternative path. Likewise, through the dissolution of the various natural tendencies rooted in passion and other afflictions, the injunctions regarding ritual action (karma-vidhi) are useful for the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (ātma-jñāna) by means of what is empirically perceived. For instance:
The vision of the Self is taught for one who is peaceful, self-controlled, and composed;
and this is possible.
For one who is being dragged away by sense objects, whose mind is intent on engaging in the means to obtain them, is not able to compose himself in the Self.

However, one who has desisted from innate activities and whose mind is restrained is qualified for the vision of the Self by virtue of his capacity; this is the opinion of others. [27,i] But others think thus:—
One whose desires are unfulfilled and whose mind is afflicted by desire is not fit for the vision of supreme non-duality (*paramādvaita*).

However, one who has extinguished their desires through ritual actions (*karman*) extending up to a thousand years attains the supreme non-duality as the Self from the state of Prajāpati. In both of these views, the entire sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) culminates solely in the knowledge of the Self.
ii] According to the view of others:

ritual injunctions, while having distinct purposes, lead a person into the qualification for the knowledge of the Self, because one who has not discharged the three debts lacks the qualification for that [knowledge].

“Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation. Others, however, maintain that through the principle of "separateness of application" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), all ritual actions (*karma*) enter into the qualification for the knowledge of the Self, based on the scriptural text, “They desire to know [Brahman] by means of sacrifice,” and also, “By whatever [means] one may sacrifice— even with a ladle-oblation— one becomes indeed pure-minded.”

[28,i] Others, however, describe actions as being for the purpose of human refinement (*puruṣasaṃskāra*), insofar as they touch upon the qualification for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna-adhikāra*), citing such passages as: "By the great sacrifices and by the [regular] sacrifices, this body is made fit for Brahman (*brāhmī kriyate tanuḥ*)," and "He for whom these forty sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and eight qualities of the self exist... and so forth.

[28,ii] Others, however, describe this very point in the opposite way, asserting that knowledge of the self alone enters into the qualification for ritual action by way of being a refinement of the agent.

Others, however, maintain that there is no connection whatsoever between ritual action and the knowledge of the Self, as they are mutually contradictory and have dualism and non-dualism as their respective objects.
Among these views, the first alternative is not tenable.
For injunctions regarding ritual action (*karman*) and the like, having attained their own effects such as heaven from their respective sentences, do not require another effect.

Nor does the injunction for the knowledge of the Self, which has no further expectancy once its means such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*) have been specified, require the injunctions for ritual action. In that case, how can there be a single qualification (*ekādhikāra*)?

Now, if one should think that injunctions regarding action and so forth have their purpose already understood because they are connected with heaven and the like as subordinate elements (*guṇa*), then one should explain to him the section concerning "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmādhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, if all injunctions and prohibitions were to terminate in the effect of the dissolution of name and form (*nāmarūpa-pravilaya*), then the prosperity and misfortune of living beings would be causeless and accidental, since they would not be caused by karma;
likewise, liberation (*apavarga*) would also [be accidental], and thus the scripture itself would be rendered useless.

Now, it might be argued that ritual injunctions, by means of their results such as heaven and so forth, lead into the domain of knowledge (*jñāna*), just as instructions for traveling through villages along a road lead into the instruction for reaching one's desired city.
That is incorrect. It is logical that the attainment of a village along the way should lead into the instruction for reaching a destination not yet intended.
For indeed, the attainment of the human goal does not occur through instructions regarding the path to a village;
therefore, because they are expectant [of something more], they enter into that wherein the human goal is attained.
However, there is no such lack of attainment of the human goal in the case of ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*), since heaven and other such results are desired by the person.
And in that case, since there is no further expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*), how can there be an entry into another [instruction]? Now, if it is thought:

"When someone, having been enticed by the presentation of the successive virtues of the villages, is led to the intended destination, then the instructions regarding the previous villages—having achieved their intended purpose—are themselves entries into subsequent instructions," [we reply:
even in that case, it is correct because the speaker's intention is apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For in that case, it has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): "When this person reaches this place, this desired object will be attained for the speaker; therefore, this is what he intends to say.
It is not, however, [apprehended] merely by following the operation of the word (na tu śabdavṛttimātrānusāreṇa).
For this reason also, it is so:

when there is an acquisition of wealth for both the speaker and the listener in every village, and the intention to reach another country has not been apprehended by any other means of knowledge, bystanders who are recipients understand the previous instructions as having only the previous meanings, while the instruction regarding the other country is understood as being restricted to its own specific purpose.

Even though, according to the actual state of things, the objects of the previous instructions benefit others, nevertheless the purport of the word does not lie there—just as, for example, the injunctions regarding the acquisition of materials and the like do not have their purport in benefiting the ritual injunctions, even though they do so assist them.
In this case, the intended meaning (tātparya) follows the literal function of the words, because there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Furthermore, in the case of instructions regarding routes and villages, both the journey there and the attainment of the goal occur precisely through the determination that those instructions are directed toward that [attainment]. However, if the instructions were directed solely toward reaching a foreign land, going there would not necessarily follow.
One might go [to heaven] even by another path, since that attainment is what is intended to be expressed;

nor is the attainment of the object mandatory, because even the mention of a purpose in passages devoted to something else is merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*). Therefore, in this context, if injunctions and prohibitions are directed toward other effects, they do not have heaven and so forth as their effects.
Indeed, the effect consisting of heaven and so forth is not equal to the effects of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, such that it would entail another effect [of its own].
And how can it be said that [the prohibitions] assist the qualification for the knowledge of the Self by means of a visible result alone?
If it is by way of obstructing activity directed toward visible objects impelled by passion and so forth, then let this be the case for the prohibitions themselves.
It must be explained how ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*) bring about cessation;
for they are neither exclusives (*parisaṃkhyāyaka*) nor restrictives (*niyāmaka*), because their objects are not at all [otherwise] established.
Indeed, an injunction whose object is already established is understood to have the result of excluding other alternatives.
Nor does cessation occur due to opposition based on having an identical effect;
for activities arising from injunctions have unseen purposes (*adṛṣṭārtha*) and their results are not fixed in time,
whereas natural activities, impelled by passion and the like, have seen purposes (*dṛṣṭārtha*).

Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the practice of *sāṅgrahaṇī* (the art of winning over) and service (*sevā*) as means to achieve a village, for the scripture provides authority only to this extent. In that regard, what contradiction is there for one who desires an abundance of results to perform both service and *sāṅgrahaṇī*, whether simultaneously or in succession? Moreover, if all activity directed toward visible ends were prohibited, even activities rooted in injunctions (*niyoga*) would be obstructed, because they are impossible for one who has not acquired wealth and thus lacks the necessary means.

Furthermore, when the status of being a means to desire is equal, there is no distinction between activity directed toward visible and invisible ends insofar as they are impelled by passion and the like.
For instance: the injunction "one who desires heaven" is a specific prescription made by way of restating an activity impelled by passion and the like.

And so, since the attachment to the manifold world (*prapañca*) is equal [in both cases], by what distinction does one [type of desire] conform to the nature of the Self, while the other is opposed to it? For the impulse of desire is no different for the mind.

Now, if one were not to consider that [the Vedic rites] are merely means to desire, then the previously described theory of spontaneity (*ākasmikatva*) would be abandoned, and the stated reasoning (*nyāya*) would be withdrawn. Furthermore, because they are based on the same functional result, any suspicion of contradiction or sublation would be cast far away and rendered groundless. Alternatively, it may be that the injunctions for ritual action, by bringing about the attainment of desires, dissolve those very desires and thus become conducive to the qualification for knowledge (*jñāna*).
As it has been said:
"When all desires that dwell in his heart are liberated, then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman even here."
This too is incorrect;
for the dissolution of desire does not occur through the attainment of desires, but rather through *prasaṃkhyāna* (discriminative discernment) born from the contemplation of defects.
If the mind is touched by desires even in their slightest degree, it is surely carried away by those things that captivate.
For it has been said:
"Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects," and "Passions increase along with the practice of enjoyment, as do the skillfulness of the senses."
Even on account of its being a non-means, one might turn away from sensual pleasures and take refuge in the knowledge of the Self, which consists in the pacification of all afflictions; however,
one who employs the various means indicated by the ritual injunctions for action would instead become attached to those very same enjoyments that captivate the mind.
One should recoil from the knowledge of the Self, which consists in the dissolution of that [world].
For even if the bliss in the Self has been heard of, if it has not been experienced, it is not capable of even weakening—let alone eliminating—the desire for the bliss based on experienced objects.
Therefore, discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) alone is the singular means for the eradication of desire; ritual injunctions, however, are causes of the opposite.

As for the claim that— in every single scriptural tradition (*āmnāya*)— there is the dissolution of some particular distinction somewhere, as for example in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," where there is the dissolution of the notion of the body being the self—
that too is incorrect, because [those passages] do not have that as their ultimate purport (*anidamparatvāt*).
For this statement does not have as its primary purport the realization of the true nature of the Self as distinct from the body.

If you argue that even though it has another purport, this meaning is nevertheless determined by implication (*arthāt*), that too is like inferring the presence of an elephant by the word "elephant" once the animal itself has been seen.
For, having begun with "not gross," the dissolution of the body and the senses is directly shown; and by implication, the Vedic [teaching] would be as hard as the knot of desire and the rest.

The second alternative as well is inconsistent, because desires lack the capacity to eliminate desire, and because there is no authoritative means of proof for the entry of those who have no further need for their own specific effects into another sphere.
If, however, they shared a single objective, there would be a combination of all ritual actions.
And that is impossible.
Even those who claim that knowledge and action share a single locus by way of inversion must also state the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the connection between knowledge and action.
It is not, first of all, like "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*).

For there, by virtue of the context, the word "rice-grains" (*vrīhi*)—which otherwise would be purposeless in its own literal form—indicates a connection with the apūrva of the rite currently under discussion, as it functions as an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for that apūrva.
Nor is it like "he whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood [attains merit]."
For in that case, even in the absence of a specific context (*prakaraṇa*), the connection with the ritual action—unerringly associated with the *juhū* ladle and so forth—brings the action to mind;
there, the connection is established by syntactical relation (*vākya*) alone.
Self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*), however, is not heard of within such a context.
Nor does the self possess an invariable connection with action;
therefore, its connection with action is difficult to maintain.
Thus, when the fact of being for another's sake is unknown, the mention of a fruit cannot be merely explanatory (arthavāda); consequently, there is a separate qualification [for each person].
Now, it might be thought:

because of the statement in the present tense, "And he does not return," and because there is no connection with desire (*kāma*), the fruit must be inferred by transforming [the literal meaning]; and that [transformation] occurs when there exists a requirement for it.
But when that [visible result] is already seen, there is no further desire for it.
And there is a visible fruit of the injunction to know the Self: namely, the engagement in ritual acts whose fruits are to be experienced in another body.
Therefore, the injunction to know the Self is like the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*).

For the injunction for the study and recitation of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*), being satisfied by the comprehension of the visible ritual action, does not seek a fruit from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); likewise, the injunction for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna-vidhi*) is also [satisfied] thus, and there is no separate qualification (*adhikāra*).
That too is incorrect, because this person described in the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣada-puruṣa*) is a different one who is to be investigated in the Vedāntas.
Furthermore, that knowledge is not the cause for the engagement in action;
for it possesses neither agency nor enjoyership.
Thus it is said:
"He does not eat anything at that time," and "The other, not eating, looks on.
But he who is the agent and enjoyer of actions is established by the direct perception of all;
he is not something to be known through scripture alone.
Is it not the case that the individual self and the supreme self are indeed one?
For thus it is said:
"By this living self."
True;
however, this form of that very *jīva*, characterized by its connection to ignorance (*avidyā*), is apprehended through direct perception, and it is the cause for the engagement in action (*karma*).
Moreover, it does not depend upon verbal testimony (*śabda*).
That which is self-luminous and devoid of all distinctions is what is intended to be known through the word;
and that [knowledge] is opposed to the engagement in ritual action.
How could the engagement in ritual action be a perceived purpose for the knowledge of that? For instance:

For one who realizes the Self as the one, non-dual bliss of Brahman, for what purpose or in what manner could there be any activity? For such a person has attained all desires and lacks any means such as ritual instruments. It might be argued:

"The knowledge of the Person taught in the Upaniṣads is indeed enjoined as an auxiliary to ritual action, according to the text: 'Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the Upaniṣadic insight, that alone becomes more powerful.

Likewise, beginning with the passage, 'O Gārgī, he who offers oblations in this world without knowing this Imperishable,' the text shows the finitude of the fruits of sacrifices and other rites, thereby demonstrating that the knowledge of Brahman serves that same purpose."
And by the statement, "Knowledge and action both accompany him," the conjunction of knowledge and action is shown.
First, this refers to the subject at hand, namely the *udgītha*, because of the introductory passage: "This syllable 'Om' is the *udgītha*.
Furthermore, the subsequent portion praises the knowledge of the syllable by means of a deprecation of ritual action.
Furthermore, there is a distinct simultaneous undertaking of both knowledge and action—
namely, that one who possesses knowledge undertakes knowledge, and one who possesses action undertakes action.
Therefore, even on this account, it is not the case that action and knowledge share a single locus of qualification.

[32.i] Furthermore, for those who maintain that action and knowledge are entirely unrelated due to their mutual contradiction— thinking that "action has duality as its object, while knowledge has non-duality as its object"— it follows that the non-arising of the knowledge of non-duality would result, because there is a contradiction between the distinction of means and ends (such as the instruments of knowledge) and the realization of non-duality. If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the means and the end do not exist simultaneously, then indeed every distinction is dissolved upon the realization of non-duality.
Nor is there any contradiction or lack of means, because the means exists at a prior time and is not dissolved at that moment.
Indeed, difference itself is the means for the realization of non-difference.
In that case, there is no contradiction even with ritual actions (*karma*), precisely because they serve as a means.
This might be so— since Brahman is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*), there is no utility for ritual actions (*karma*).
And it is heard in scripture:

“There is nothing uncreated by means of what is created. Furthermore, there is no utility for [ritual] action in the arising of knowledge, because knowledge is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor are ritual actions auxiliaries to knowledge, because knowledge has no other goal to be accomplished.
Liberation is not something to be accomplished for him, because that would entail [the soul's] impermanence.

If it is argued that what is to be accomplished is the severance of the cause of bondage—such that once that is severed, one is liberated due to the absence of bondage—then what is the cause of bondage? It is beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). In that case, the severance of that [ignorance] is not to be accomplished as a separate entity, because the very arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cessation of ignorance.
It might be argued:
let it be that the cessation of ignorance, characterized by non-apprehension, is the arising of knowledge, since the very existence of a thing is the exclusion of its absence.
Yet, the arising of knowledge itself is not the exclusion of erroneous cognition.
Indeed, the exclusion of one entity is not another entity;
nor are entities of the nature of mutual non-existence, for that would entail the consequence of their being non-existent.
If it should be thought:
It is not the case that error, which is caused by the non-apprehension of reality, will cease of its own accord upon the cessation of its cause;
for indeed, non-apprehension—which is a mere absence—is not the cause of anything, as this would lead to the absurd consequence [of such cessation] even in cases like fainting.
What, then, is the cause? It has been stated: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless and purposeless."
And in that case, the inquiry into a cause would have no scope.
Furthermore, since error (*viparyāsa*) and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are established as being in a mutual relationship of cause and effect, there is no fault.
Therefore, since the cessation of erroneous cognition is to be accomplished by means of knowledge (*vidyā*), there would be a requirement for a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*) for that knowledge.

And this is the correct view: indeed, those who have attained right knowledge regarding mother-of-pearl and similar objects after a preceding error do not exert themselves separately for its cessation, nor do they depend upon any other auxiliary cause;
because the very production of a contrary state is the destruction of the former, and not a void.
Otherwise, destruction would not possess a cause. Furthermore, knowledge is the opposite of erroneous cognition; when that [knowledge] arises, error is indeed destroyed.
Now, it might be argued: "Karmas are the causes of bondage;
their destruction results from knowledge that depends upon auxiliary factors."

And how could that [karma] possibly exist when there arises a completely purified knowledge in which all particularities have been wiped away? Thus, through error and doubt, karmas are considered to be equal [in their effect]; for it is said: "The knots of the heart are rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and one's karmas are exhausted when That, which is both high and low, is seen."
Thus [it is said].

Now, if it is argued that there is a dependence on something else for the sake of purifying consciousness, that too is futile; for doubt and error, which are the impurities of cognition, cannot exist in a consciousness arising from a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Now, it might be thought:
"A perceptual cognition other than verbal knowledge is also admitted—one that grasps without the apprehension of distinctions and transcends all conceptual constructions.
For Brahman is the object of that [perception], not of verbal knowledge, which grasps the connection between distinct word-meanings."
Regarding its arising, there is a dependence on karma, meditation, and so forth.
But what is this distinction for which that [dependence] is required? It is the quality of appearing clearly; however, that [dependence] has no utility for that purpose.
For knowledge exists for the sake of pervading the object of knowledge, and once verbal knowledge has arisen, the object of knowledge is already fully attained.

If it is argued that because valid cognition (*pramiti*) culminates in perception (*pratyakṣa*), and because there is no further expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) regarding that [perception], it is for the sake of that [perception] that [other means] are sought—then once the object of knowledge (*prameya*) has been apprehended, what else would be expected? If you say "another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntara*), we say no; for that expectancy exists solely for the purpose of establishing the object of knowledge.
If you argue that it is for the sake of establishing it again, we say no; for it has already been established repeatedly by the previous [means].
And when that which is already established is expected to be established once more, there is no reason [for such a demand].

If there were another means [of knowledge], then one would have to depend upon that other means. However, regarding the object of cognition, there is indeed a state of complete satisfaction. If it is a particular kind of pleasure, that is accomplished even by the perception arising from a previous means of valid cognition.
There is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of establishing that [object].

Even if something is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it might still be sought after by others because of the possibility of its existence, since there is no distinction [in this regard].
Furthermore, the capacity to produce certainty belongs to the other [means of cognition] as well, because they possess the nature of valid cognition.
If it is argued that perception alone has as its object that which is capable of being abandoned and so forth, because its object is proximate, while the others do not;
then let proximity itself be regarded as the cause [of such capability].
It is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), for the valid cognition is already established.
And regarding the object of cognition under discussion, this distinction does not exist.
If it is argued that words and the like have universals as their objects, whereas perception has particulars as its object,
then the object of perception is indeed something not yet apprehended by the word.
Certainly;
this has already been stated—
that Brahman is not the object of verbal cognition.

If, then, Brahman is not apprehended through the word, how can meditation (*upāsanā*) proceed with respect to it? Nor does something else become directly realized when something other than it is being meditated upon. For what purpose, then, would there be the injunctions for sacrifices and the like? The injunction for sacrifices and so forth is logically justified for the sake of the direct realization of the Self, whose nature is Brahman—characterized by unsurpassed bliss, freedom from evil, and so on—as revealed by the word. Once that which is the human goal has been made manifest through an unerring means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and its opposite has been dispelled, nothing further remains to be sought.

[Objection: Even when the identity of Brahman and the Self has been understood through the words "That thou art," there remains a perception of the attributes of transmigratory existence as before; therefore, there must be a dependence on something else for their cessation.

[Reply: This is not sound. For how could one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self, who knows the true nature of the Self, be joined with those attributes caused by false perception? And it is heard in scripture:
“He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself.
Furthermore, there is no room for them in Brahman, which is free from all evil.
Likewise—
“If a person were to know the Self, realizing ‘This am I,’ desiring what, or for the sake of whose longing, would he suffer along with the body?”
Likewise: "Indeed, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless.
The connection with a body is caused by false identification;
when that [identification] ceases through the vision of reality as it is, there is bodilessness.
In this regard, the non-connection with the pleasant and the unpleasant is explained.
Therefore, one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self does not participate in the attributes of transmigratory existence as he did previously;
for whoever still participates in them has not realized the identity of Brahman and the Self.
To this it is replied:
even when reality has been ascertained through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), false appearances may cease in some cases, yet in others they persist due to specific causes.

Just as for those who have determined the true nature of the directions and the moon through the authoritative word [of a teacher], the appearances of two moons, the misperception of directions, and so forth, continue to persist;

likewise, for one who has understood the reality of the Self from the tradition free from doubt, the persistence of false appearances continues due to the power of potent latent impressions accumulated through the practice of beginningless false views.
For the cessation of that [persistence], something else must be relied upon.
And that practice of the vision of reality is established in the world, while sacrifices and the like have scripture as their authority.
For practice, by strengthening a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and obstructing previous impressions, continues its own effect;
whereas sacrifices and the like do so through some unseen mode.
Others hold that it is by way of destroying the impurities that obstruct the highest good (*śreyas*), because obligatory rites (*nitya-karmans*) have the purpose of destroying evil (*durita*).
This might be so—
let false appearances continue to persist.
Certainty, however, arises from valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And worldly activity proceeds according to reality and according to certainty.
Therefore, for one who has realized the true nature of the self, no engagement whatsoever—whether auspicious or inauspicious—is possible.

It is said: even when the vision of reality has arisen, if no latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the cloth has been established, and there remains a stronger latent impression born of false perception, then even certainties will have false objects—
as is seen in the case of one who is disoriented regarding directions and has not kept in mind the words of a trustworthy person, yet proceeds as before.
Likewise, even when a rope has been measured as such, if one does not reflect upon that measurement, fear arises through the delusion that it is a snake.

Therefore, even though reality has been perceived through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), they maintain that one must practice the perception of reality in order to overcome or eradicate the extremely firm latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the habituation to beginningless false perception.
Accordingly, it is said: "It is to be reflected upon; it is to be meditated upon" (*mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*).
And there is the prescription of means such as tranquility, self-control, celibacy, and sacrifice;
otherwise, what would be the purpose of that instruction? It might be argued:
"The knowledge of reality arises precisely from the performance of the means such as celibacy, as taught in the sacred tradition."
That is incorrect,
because comprehension arises from the mere word itself.

For prior to specific means of proof, the sacred tradition (āmnāya), which aims at the comprehension of reality, is neither non-expressive nor non-conclusive, since it dispels all doubts without exception.
Otherwise, even regarding the means taught by that [teacher], comprehension would be difficult to attain.
Furthermore, even when there is no such ascertainment, actors like Bharata on the stage become causes of grief, fear, and so forth through a false appearance.

Even when the sweetness of molasses is ascertained, the false appearance of bitterness therein causes pain as if it were real, because one rejects it with a spitting sound, just as one would reject something truly bitter.

Therefore, for the sake of its cessation, even one who has ascertained the identity of Brahman and the Self must still rely upon means of realization. Just as liberation is not something produced by a means when reality is manifested through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too it is not produced by means even when there is a particular manifestation [of that reality]. The scriptural passages, however, refer to the stage of perfection attained through practice; or they may depend upon words, means, and knowledge, because the latter [perfection] has those as its cause.
Enough with this excessive detail.
Even though ritual injunctions have distinct purposes, they lead one into the domain of knowledge, because only one who has discharged the three debts has the qualification for that.

Even that is not mandatory, because the Smṛti records an option regarding the stages of life (āśrama): "Some [teachers] hold that there is an option of stages for him," "He may dwell in whichever he desires," and from the Śruti: "Or otherwise, one may go forth from the stage of studentship itself.
"This, indeed, they say..."

For we see the renunciation of ritual action in such passages as: "Therefore, the wise of old did not perform the Agnihotra," and likewise, "What shall we do with offspring? and "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we sacrifice?

This shows that for one who has entered the householder's life, yet considers himself to have accomplished all that is required through the knowledge of the Self alone, and thus disregards the discharge of debts, the sin arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties acts as an obstacle to the dawning of knowledge—this is shown by the text:
"Having discharged the three debts..."
[36, ii] But this is logical:

even for those ritual acts that have no further requirement for another effect, there is the status of being auxiliary to knowledge because of the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), as in the passage: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas and through sacrifice."
That [knowledge] also serves the purpose of origination, not by means of a physical application like the *prayāja* offerings,
because knowledge has no other effect;
or rather, it belongs to the category of refinement (*saṃskāra*), according to Smṛti.
For knowledge arises from the refinement [of the self].
Thus it has been said:
"And because it is enjoined, the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-karma) must also be performed."
[36,iii] Is it not the case that the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) occurs precisely upon the arising of what has been seen?

In that regard, let the very procedure (*itikartavyatā*)—namely, the specific means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*) which obstruct mental distraction—be expected; for from a concentrated mind, there arises the clarity of knowledge through its manifestation.
But sacrifices and the like are not [the cause], for that [knowledge] can arise even without them through repeated practice.
True;
and thus, it is accepted that for those in the higher stages of life (ūrdhvaretas) who have restrained their vital energy, the dawning of pure knowledge occurs even without those [sacrifices].
However, there is a distinction made by time:
for through a particular means of realization, that [nature] is manifested quickly or even more quickly;
and in its absence, it is manifested after a long time or even longer.
As it has been said:
"And there is a need for all [works], because of the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse.
This is the meaning:

Because of the scriptural statement, "By sacrifice, by charity," ritual actions are required even for knowledge that is obtainable through practice, just as, although the attainment of a village can be accomplished even without a horse, a horse is required for speed or for ease.
[37,i] But is it not the case that Brahman itself is of the nature of knowledge?
Knowledge is not other than Brahman; and that is eternal and uncreated. In that case, how could anything be required? It is said in reply:
Just as a crystal gem whose form is concealed by an adjunct requires the removal of that adjunct for the manifestation of its own true nature, so too should it be understood here.
For the original form of the crystal gem is not destroyed due to the proximity of the adjunct, nor does another [form] arise when that [adjunct] is removed.
Indeed, the arising of a preceding moment of a similar kind, which has been interrupted by many dissimilar moments, is not possible without a cause.
For when the fire has vanished, there is no further continuation of the series of wood from the embers.
Therefore, just as the color of the crystal—which is not its actual effect—depends upon the removal of the substrate, so too does the nature of the self.
It might be argued as follows:
In that case, cognition is dependent;
and that [cognition] is an effect distinct from the crystal.
For human effort there is directed toward the purpose of cognition.

Furthermore, is knowledge sought for its own sake, or for the sake of establishing the nature of the object? It is not for its own sake, because worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is conducted by means of the object. Activity is not based on mere consciousness alone, as that would lead to the absurdity of it occurring even through false cognition. If, however, knowledge is sought for the sake of the object's nature, then the operation directed toward that object is what is truly sought.
Furthermore, there is no modification of the object resulting from cognition, because the two are unrelated;
for [otherwise] the suitability of the location would exist everywhere,
and it would follow that all cognizers would know [the object].
And because that [manifestation] is impossible in the case of things already destroyed or those yet to come;

therefore, just as the reality of the Self (ātmatattva), though not actually concealed, appears as if concealed and as if being manifested in dependence upon effort, so too it is fully established that it is manifested through effort as if it were concealed.
Therefore, with all distinctions withdrawn, it is described as having the nature of a universal, like gold indicated by the withdrawal of distinctions such as bracelets and other ornaments. (1.3)

And since that [Brahman] is defined by way of the exclusion of specific attributes (*viśeṣapratyastamukhena*), it has therefore been defined as having a universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*) by other authorities devoted to the knowledge of Brahman:

"That very one is the Great Unborn Self, characterized by pure existence (*sattālakṣaṇa*)," and likewise, "Existence alone is the source of all distinctions, the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*)."
Just as the reality of gold, when examined by setting aside its specific forms such as bracelets and rings, is understood as that universal;
or, for those who assert non-existence, saying: "A universal cannot exist without particulars, like a rabbit's horn," it is said in reply to them:
Regarding the phrase "in which all distinctions have been withdrawn":
if you are proving that [Brahman] is devoid of any generality (*asāmānya*), then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

For in the absence of particulars (*viśeṣa*), of what could there be a generality? Furthermore, by the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādibhiḥ*), "generality" is used figuratively (*upacārataḥ*) because it is defined through the negation of particulars.
Now, if non-existence itself were the probandum, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of this [reason] due to particularities that are themselves devoid of further particulars.
[Thus ends the Brahmakāṇḍa in the *Brahmasiddhi* composed by the venerable Maṇḍanamiśra.
{The Tarkakāṇḍa}

[39,i] But surely, since the intrinsic natures of entities are understood through perception and other means of valid cognition as being mutually excluded, a word is not a means of valid cognition regarding a single non-dual reality, because it would contradict perception and the rest— just like a statement concerning such things as stones floating on water.
To this it is said:
The wise say that perception is an affirmer, not a negator; therefore, scripture concerning oneness is not contradicted by that perception. 1.4
[39,ii] Now, it may be argued that human statements, being dependent on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), are rightly considered non-authoritative when they contradict them.

But why should the Veda (*āmnāya*), which is independent and functions without requiring other means of valid cognition, be non-authoritative even when it contradicts them? Furthermore, why do perception and the other means of valid cognition not lose their status as valid cognitions simply because they contradict the Veda? Since both are equally independent, there is no reason for such a distinction.
In that regard, the labor spent on avoiding contradictions with other means of valid cognition is in vain.
Regarding this, some say:
The scripture (*āmnāya*) is weaker when it contradicts perception and the other means of knowledge, because it is dependent upon them.
For indeed, the scripture depends upon perception and the others precisely for the sake of establishing its own nature.
Consequently, their validity must be accepted; for if they were sublated, its very nature would remain unestablished.
But there is no such dependence on perception and the other means of knowledge regarding the Veda.
This is because deviation is observed in the case of verbal testimony, whereas no deviation is observed in the case of perception.
Furthermore, between that which has scope and that which has no scope, the one without scope is stronger.
Furthermore, perception and the other means of knowledge are without scope [for such a view], whereas verbal testimony has scope through a figurative meaning.
For instance,
it is possible to describe the scope of the scriptural texts concerning oneness and non-difference as being figurative.
Alternatively, there is the scope for the recitation (*japa*) of those Vedāntas whose meaning is not intended to be expressed;
it has been described that the Upaniṣads are the Vedāntas.
Furthermore, because the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is confused, whereas perception and the other means of knowledge are not confused.

For ritual injunctions depend on difference, whereas the Vedāntas depend on non-difference; thus, they are mutually contradictory and their authority is difficult to establish even in the absence of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
How much more so when there is a contradiction with an unimpeded and firmly established authority?
Therefore, an effort is made here toward their reconciliation.
And because of their primacy;
for perception and the other means of knowledge are primary,
whereas the sacred tradition (āmnāya) comes at a later time for a person who has already been born.

With its objects already established by those [means of knowledge], the object to be conceptualized is deprived of its domain and is thereby sublated; or rather, it must conform to them in its conceptualization of the object.
Furthermore, direct perception and the other means possess primacy even in terms of their objective referents.
The determination of the meaning of the Veda depends upon the distinction between words and word-meanings, and that distinction falls within the scope of direct perception and the other means.
Therefore, one should strive for non-contradiction.
Others think: [40,i]—

Even if perception and the other means of knowledge were of equal strength with the Veda (āmnāya), since an alternative (vikalpa) regarding a real entity is logically impossible, there would be doubt in the event of a contradiction;
therefore, non-contradiction must be established.
Another view is that the Vedic tradition alone is authoritative when there is a conflict with it:
"In a sequence of earlier and later, the earlier is weaker, as in the case of the archetypal rule."
“For the arising of a subsequent [cognition] is not established without the non-sublation of the preceding one.
To explain: indeed, for everyone, the determination of distinct objects is innate and based upon perception and the other means of valid cognition.
But dependent upon that [innate ignorance], there arises for some a non-innate, adventitious realization of non-duality preceded by that [innate ignorance].
Being unable to arise without first submerging that [innate ignorance], it arises as something that sublates it.
And for this reason as well—
Because perception and the other means of knowledge can have various causes of error, whereas the Veda is free from any suspicion of defects;
for defects, which reside in persons, cannot exist in the Word when the person is absent.

Indeed, it is possible to conceive of and ascertain that the beginningless impressions of ignorance—which are the cause of error in perception and the rest—exist within them, just like the conceit of the body being the self.
But in the case of a word that is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), there is no suspicion of any defect whatsoever;
or, were such a suspicion to exist, it would simply not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for perception and the other [means of knowledge], their validity is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), because as long as the latent impressions of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃskāra*) persist, there is no subversion of worldly practice.
And where there is a contradiction with worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), there is no validity (*prāmāṇya*).
In the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*), however, since defects are possible, its validity does not consist in revealing reality (*tattva*),
nor in the absence of contradiction with worldly convention.
Because its purpose is unperceived (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), and because one observes that [cognition] contradicts worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) due to defects;
however, since perception and the other means of knowledge do conform to worldly practice, it is not possible to postulate a defect as the cause of a cognition that contradicts worldly practice.
For such a defect would only be postulated on account of a failure in worldly practice.
However, because it is the adversary of the vision of reality born from the Vedānta, the beginningless connection with ignorance is postulated as the sole cause for the obstruction of that reality.
Therefore, there is no contradiction between the persistence of defects and [the scripture's] validity;
for verbal testimony, being subject to the possibility of defects, would be one whose validity is difficult to obtain.
For it is observed that from defects arises the production of a cognition that contradicts practical activity (*vyavahāra-visaṃvādi-jñāna*).

In that case, because the contradiction with practical activity is suspected due to the suspicion of defects, and because there is an obstruction to [the apprehension of] reality, validity does not consist in the revelation of reality, nor does it consist in non-contradiction with practical activity.
Therefore, it is correct that when the validity of a word is accepted, it possesses greater force even in the face of a contradiction with another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
As for the argument that [the Veda] depends upon perception and other means of knowledge, it is replied:

the dependence of the word [of scripture] upon perception and the rest does not exist in respect to its being a valid cognition (*pramiti*), but rather in respect to the establishment of its own nature (*svarūpa*).
Otherwise, it would not be a means of valid knowledge at all.
And thus, because it depends upon its own causal factors, it is not inferior to perception and the other means of knowledge.
For even perception and the others do not depend on anything else for the establishment of their own nature. Indeed, dependence regarding the effect does not detract from one's capacity.

As for the claim that their validity must be inferred, who indeed says otherwise? That [validity] is characterized by non-contradiction in worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), not by the revelation of ultimate reality (*tattva*). From the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), which is established as possessing empirical validity alongside perception and other means of knowledge, the vision of reality arises; and because of its opposition, it sublates only the aspect of the vision of reality within those [empirical means], not the aspect of non-contradiction in worldly practice. Moreover, it is observed that a subsequent cognition possesses greater force than a preceding cognition, even when the latter is required as a cause for the former.
Just as, in the case of trees standing at a distance, the cognition of trees arises from the cognitions of elephants;
for the cognitions of elephants are required as causes for the distinct cognition of the trees.
That [cognition of trees] does not arise from the mere contact of the sense organ with the object, because it is absent at the initial moment.
Nor does it arise from a specific location, since it arises for one who is situated in that very place.

Therefore, it should be understood that this [cognition] is produced by the contact of the sense organ and other factors, accompanied by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) consisting of a reversal of the eastern direction, in one whose mind is fixed upon the trees standing before him.
In the same way, cognitions such as "twenty" and so forth, which result from the disappearance of cognitions of "one" and so on, should also be cited as examples.
And thus, as some describe it—
the realization of the meaning of the Vedāntas is itself contradicted:
non-difference cannot be apprehended without difference.
For its realization occurs through the means of differentiation;
in that case, non-difference is understood only as having implicitly included difference— thus there is a contradiction—
but this is rejected.
For practice implies a means;
it does not imply that the means possesses ultimate reality, since the realization of truth can arise even from false knowledge.
Moreover, the conventional reality of differentiation is indeed accepted [by us].
The observation of deviation is common to both verbal cognition and perception when they arise from fallacious reasons;
likewise, non-deviation is equal for the other two as well,
and so too is the absence of occasion [for doubt].

If, indeed, the meaning of the Vedānta is one and non-dual, what other scope (*avakāśa*) is there for those [other scriptures]? Alternatively, if their oneness is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), or if their meaning is not intended to be expressed because they are useful only for recitation (*japa*), then there is no contradiction at all, and thus the consideration of relative strength (*balābala*) does not even arise. Why, then, would weakness be attributed to them on the grounds of having a [limited] scope? And how can there be a figurative scope that bypasses the primary meaning? Furthermore, when the word has its innate status as a subordinate element (*śeṣabhāva*) with respect to its meaning—

Is it because [the Upanishads] have already been seen to have their purpose in the understanding of ritual action—as in the statement "for its purpose is seen to be the comprehension of action"—or because "the meaning of a sentence is non-distinct" [from that of other means of knowledge], that they are considered to have no intended meaning? If you say this is so because of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is a trivial argument.
The validity of a means of valid cognition does not depend upon another means of valid cognition, such that it would abandon its natural force (*svarasa*) in the face of contradiction by the latter.
For if it were dependent on that, it would function in accordance with it.

For that which is independent [of other means of knowledge], what reason is there for following after another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*)? However, since worldly words denote their own objects by depending on other means of knowledge, it is logical that their operation follows such dependence. But if independence is equal [in both cases], why is the reverse not the case, or why is there invalidity due to the contradiction between the two, or why is there sublation of the earlier—according to the principle that "in a sequence of prior and posterior, the earlier is weaker"—just as in the case of the cognition of silver? Indeed, the cognition of mother-of-pearl is not rendered objectless or otherwise because of its opposition to the cognition of silver. How then is there figurative praise (*guṇavāda*) in the Veda?

Where the accomplishment of the object of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) through the primary meanings of words is impossible, there the words are seen to function through a secondary sense (*vṛtti*), and by that [secondary sense] they obtain their objective domain. However, where words obtain their objective domain by their own natural force (*svarasa*), they do not turn away from it due to contradiction with another means of knowledge. For the object of these [words] is not dependent upon another means of knowledge, such that they would have to turn away from it under its influence.
[42,i] Now,
it might be thought:
it is postulated in this way precisely for the sake of favoring both.
For in this way, verbal testimony as well as perception and the other means of knowledge are supported;
otherwise, perception and the others would be utterly sublated.
This [objection] is not sound.

Some conceptual construction regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) may arise in accordance with the capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, regarding the means of valid cognition itself, there is no basis for a conceptual construction that abandons what is established by its own inherent nature.

Therefore, the arrangements of alternatives (*vikalpa*) and combinations (*samuccaya*) are postulated in accordance with the means of valid cognition, not for the sake of favoring both [the means and the object].
There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that neither [of the two] should be assisted.

If it is argued that those very [cognitions] are the means of valid cognition—if this is your view—then a means of valid cognition does not require assistance from another means of valid cognition; rather, it is self-evident (*svataḥ*).
For it is precisely because of its being a means of valid cognition that the object is established by it;
the object must be established in such a way that it is understood from it.
In this manner, the cognition becomes supported by that object.

Otherwise, it would be contradicted. Furthermore, the determination of an object would lack a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), because [the object] is not perceived through its own nature, because there is no other [means of cognition], and because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

For the perception of another object established by validity must be postulated through the impossibility of explaining validity otherwise, and the validity [of that means] depends on that perception.

In the case of a meaning obtained through its own inherent force (*svarasa*), however, its validity arises from the very fact of its being cognized; thus, there is no circularity (*itaretarāśrayatā*).

Therefore, when there is a contradiction, it is the sublation (*bādha*) of the prior [cognition] alone that accords with the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because such is the way it is perceived. It is not the case that the subsequent [cognition] must have its object postulated as something different.
Indeed, another object is not postulated for the cognition of the mother-of-pearl fragment for the sake of supporting the cognition of silver.
Nor is there a lack of scope for perception and the other means of knowledge simply because they have no other resort;
for whatever is the resort of errors such as that of silver, that is the resort of these [means of knowledge] as well.
If their object is metaphorical or conceptualized, then that is also the case for perception and the other means of knowledge.
Alternatively, if [the object] is non-existent, then they have no object; thus perception and the others likewise lack a real referent.
Therefore, the conclusion—that the meaning is not intended to be literal, or that the meaning is metaphorical—is indistinguishable for both.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: "In common worldly usage, when a word contradicts another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it is observed that its meaning is either figurative or unintended;
therefore, when the Vedāntas contradict perception and the other means of knowledge, they must likewise be so [figurative or unintended], because such is seen even in perception and the others."
As for the claim that the Veda has its scope sublated by things established as primary,
it is for this very reason that it is the sublater, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl.
Nor can it be justified by assuming a meaning in accordance with those [other means of knowledge], because it is independent.
Its status as a valid means of knowledge does not depend upon them.
There is no joint operation with them, nor is there a state of syntactic unity between the Veda and perception and the other means of knowledge.
For the arising of cognition in both cases is independent of one another;
in such a situation, it is logical that the stronger [cognition] prevails.
As it has been said:
“Let it be understood that in those cases where cognitions arise independently of one another, the subsequent indeed possesses greater force than the preceding.”

[43,ii] However, where there is a state of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) through cooperative operation, and the primary sense remains established by its own natural function because no contradiction has arisen, the subsequent words—being unable to achieve that status as a single syntactical unit through their first mode of operation due to the impossibility of offering a meaning required by it—offer the meaning required by the preceding word through a second mode of operation, by virtue of the power of the single syntactical unity. Thus, the primary sense is stronger. As for the argument that it is "because of confusion," to that it is replied:
There might be confusion if the injunctions regarding ritual action were intended primarily to establish difference;

however, they rely upon difference as already established, and their primary purpose is to instruct persons on how to achieve their welfare by stating, "One should accomplish this by means of that in this manner.
This may be so.

If there is no distinction [between the injunction and its object], then because the three constituent parts have ceased to exist, how can there be instruction for the sake of welfare? It is said in reply:

Just as indeed in the case of the hawk-sacrifice and others, although the element of the "thing-to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) has ceased due to the prohibition "one shall not harm any living beings," there is still an instruction; so too in all cases, even when all constituent parts have ceased.
For instance:

How indeed could violence, which results in the arising of what is prohibited and harmful, be something to be accomplished? Now, it may happen that for someone whose mind is overcome by intense anger, whose discriminative wisdom is obscured by the rising darkness [of delusion], and who—perceiving even what is harmful as beneficial—transgresses the instruction of the scriptures, [violence occurs]. Likewise, in rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, there are three components presented by innate ignorance for those who are unawakened; it is with reference to these that they are instructed. However, those who are awakened are not instructed by means of ritual injunctions, just as those who have conquered the enemy of anger are not instructed by the injunctions for the Śyena sacrifice and the like.

Thus, although there is a perception of difference in those injunctions for ritual action which rely on distinctions established by conventional usage, nevertheless, because they do not have that [difference] as their ultimate purport, they possess no authority regarding it—just as the words of an *arthavāda* have no authority regarding historical narratives.

And so, how could there be a contradiction of the Vedāntas by them, or of them by the Vedāntas? Moreover, contradiction is observed only within the realm of perception and the like, due to the observation of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator in cognitions such as those of silver and a fragment of mother-of-pearl; for everywhere, both the cognition of difference and the cognition of non-difference are found to coexist.

Thus, even though the Veda possesses such authority, there may be one of dull intellect who, observing that worldly speech often has figurative meanings when it contradicts perception and other means of knowledge, concludes that the operation of words in the Veda is like that in the world. Or, there may be another who, due to the dense and deep-rooted darkness of perceiving duality, considers perception and the other means of knowledge alone to be authoritative, because he observes them subverting worldly speech. To awaken such persons, contradiction is refuted; for it is not the case that one who is bitten by a scorpion with mild venom and dies is not treated by medicine.
In that regard, there are three alternatives concerning perception:
the affirmation of the essential nature of an object, the exclusion of other objects, or the cognition of both. Regarding both of these as well, there are three varieties:
simultaneity, affirmation preceded by exclusion, and exclusion preceded by affirmation.

In that regard, if there is the exclusion of another entity, or if both [exclusion and affirmation] are present, then difference (*bheda*) falls within the scope of perception; thus, a contradiction arises. However, if there is merely the affirmation of its own nature (*svarūpa-vidhi*), devoid of the exclusion of anything else, then difference is not the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for indeed, the establishment of difference does not occur apart from exclusion. And perception has as its operation mere affirmation; therefore, there is no contradiction. How so? It is said:
When something has acquired a certain form in some respect, it is precisely that which is negated;
therefore, without a prior affirmation, a negation is impossible. (1.5)

[44,ii] The operation of perception does not consist merely in exclusion, nor does it consist in both [exclusion and affirmation] simultaneously, nor does it consist in affirmation preceded by exclusion; for when an object is already established, only that which is established in form is negated—
such as "this is not here" or "this is not that"— as when a jar, being already established, is negated on an established ground, or a horse on a cow.

A negation is not possible without that which is to be negated and without the object of the negation. How, then, is there a negation of things that are absolutely non-existent, such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*) or a sky-flower? For in those cases, there is no negation in any place or time because of their absolute nature; nor is there any establishment [of them] from anything, because of their absolute non-existence.
Regarding this, some say:

First, when space and so forth are established, flowers and the like of that same nature are negated in relation to them; likewise, in the case of the primal cause of the world, properties such as being composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion, or being a differentiated effect, are refuted by the statement, "Pradhāna does not exist.
However, others [hold a different view]—

They explain that, due to some cause, the external negation of those forms which have been apprehended by the intellect is performed; otherwise, what negation could there be for that which is prohibited by fate and has not attained a form? Or, if it had attained a form, how could there be an absolute negation? Furthermore, if exclusion were a negation of an object that is not required [for cognition], then emptiness would be the meaning of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not differentiation, because everything would be negated everywhere without distinction.

However, that exclusion which serves for differentiation depends upon the establishment of the two things to be differentiated; and since that establishment does not occur apart from affirmation, affirmation must be sought first. Furthermore, negation is accepted as being preceded by affirmation.
Nor is there an exclusion preceded by affirmation, because—
The sequence of the action of a single cognition does not cohere with reason; for that [cognition] which arises from what is present is produced without the apprehension of anything else. (1.6)

Indeed, it is not logical for affirmation (*vidhi*) and exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) to be successive operations of a single cognitive act (*pramāṇajñāna*), because of its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
