For if the two operations were successive, the latter would not be an operation of that [cognition], due to the intervention [of time]. Furthermore, the very arising of cognition—which consists in the apprehension of an object—is its operation. If that [cognition] arises in the form of affirmation, then affirmation alone is its operation; for simultaneity is precluded, and what has already arisen cannot arise again.

Moreover, perception, which has a proximate object as its support, cannot manifest an object that is not proximate; nor is it capable of delimiting a form that is not being manifested. For if that which is to be delimited were not being manifested, there would be mere delimitation, but no delimitation of anything at all—or else, there would be delimitation of everything.

Therefore, there can be no delimitation when the object to be delimited is not being manifested; and it is not logical for an object that is not proximate to be manifested by a perception that has a proximate object as its support.

How, then, can perception be subverting? For in that case, it is accepted that within a single cognition there is first the negation of a prior object followed by the affirmation of another, and there is the appearance of a negandum that is not present. Therefore, this is not a fixed rule: namely, that negation must come first, that there must be a sequence within the operation of a single cognition, and that perception must involve the appearance of an object that is not present.

This is not sound. For even in that case, regarding the silver and so forth established by a prior cognition, the negation—expressed as "this" with respect to the general form of the object present before one—is necessarily preceded by an affirmation; whereas the affirmation of the mother-of-pearl is said to be preceded by the negation of its opposite. Furthermore, it is stated that negation is invariably preceded by affirmation, but it is not denied that affirmation can be preceded by negation. Moreover, there is no sequential operation of a single cognition in that instance, because both forms arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, because it is attained through prior cognition, there is no impossibility regarding the object and that which is excluded; and since exclusion operates upon an object already illuminated by prior cognition, there is no consequence of the appearance of a non-proximate object, for that [subsequent cognition] arises in dependence upon the former.
Moreover, it arises with two forms precisely through dependence on the former; otherwise, it would arise with only a single form.

Furthermore, for one who rejects all exclusions, what exclusion is intended, by means of which one might be opposed? If you say, "That is established in the world," then why is this not also established in the world?
Is it that "a horse is not a cow, nor is a cow a horse"?
As for the view held—
Exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*) is indeed nothing other than a single positive determination (*ekavidhi*). To explain:

just as perception, by assuming the form of that [object], establishes its nature, so too, through the restriction to that single form, it excludes others, thinking, "It is this, not another. And the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—"this" and "not this"—which are brought forth by the power of that [perception], set in motion the conventional usage of existence and non-existence.
For there is no exclusion of one thing from another that is distinct from a cognition restricted to a single form and not associated with anything else.
To this it is replied:
"The affirmation of one thing itself is the exclusion of others; it does not have something else as its object."
Let there be no lack of distinction, nor let there be a lack of unity for those who share a single cognition.

A specific restriction [of one thing] cannot be the cause for the certain determination of the absence of others, because it would follow that there is no distinction between that which has reached the conditions for perception and its opposite; for such a restriction consists in the non-connection of that [thing] with what is other than itself.
And if exclusion were to occur through such non-connection, then, since there is no distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible, both would be excluded.
Now, it might be thought: "It is indeed so;

for as many non-selves (anātman) as there are, perception excludes them by way of a specific restriction to that [particular] self. And thus, there are no other selves for this [object], though there may be others belonging to its place and time, since there is no contradiction, as in the case of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. In this regard, the condition of being accessible to perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpti*) is the specific feature for determining the exclusion of those other places and times. For it is possible that a non-self belonging to that place and time remains unperceived even when another [self] is perceived, just like the other cases; otherwise, it would not possess the same fitness for apprehension."
This distinction is indeed true; however, it does not possess the capacity to establish the restriction of perception.

For instance, even though perception occurs in a specific place, time, and form, since that perception functions solely by way of affirming those [specific] forms, it does not exclude taste. Likewise, the restriction of perceiving a portion of the earth, because its operation consists solely in the affirmation of that portion of the earth, would not exclude the visibility of a jar either; or, if there were such exclusion, there would be the exclusion of everything.
Therefore, even when there is the exclusion of the perceptible, another means of proof must be employed, rather than mere restriction to perception alone.

Likewise, the exclusion of other selves does not achieve establishment through that [perception]. Granted, since a positive injunction consists in the exclusion of the non-existence of the object to be enjoined, its absence might indeed be excluded; however, the existence of another self is not [excluded] in that way, just as the existence of something unperceivable is not excluded by the non-perception of it in a certain place or time.
If it is argued that there are not many selves for a single [entity], then the exclusion [of others] must arise from contradiction with something else;
it does not arise from the restriction of perception.

And if there is no exclusion, how can there be multiplicity, or how can there be contradiction, or the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*)? Therefore, the affirmation of one thing is not the exclusion of another.

Furthermore, if there were an exclusion of others based on the restriction of one thing, then in the case of variegated [colors] and the like, the difference between blue and other [colors] which are the objects of a single perception would not be established, because there is no restriction of cognition to a single [object] due to its connection with a single cognition.

[47,i] Now, it may be argued that entities are indeed different by their very nature; perception, by producing those specific forms, distinguishes them from one another, for distinction is not something other than that which possesses distinction.

In that case, even in the affirmation of that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), that [exclusion] is indeed affirmed; for whatever entity is the nature of something, it must be affirmed by that very nature, otherwise there would be no affirmation of it. Furthermore, entities with excluded natures appear according to their respective ways in various philosophical systems; therefore, they are affirmed in that very same way.

Even here, since the two objects of perception appear without being touched [by each other], and thus possess untouched natures, the exclusion remains in the same state due to the lack of distinction between them.
Moreover—
Difference is not the nature of a real entity, for that would entail the consequence of its non-existence;
moreover, it is not possible for a real entity to be differentiated by means of what lacks a nature.

Exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things; indeed, that [exclusion] is asserted and recognized as residing in one or many [entities]. And thus, if that single exclusion, which resides in many, were the intrinsic nature of things, there would be no difference among things either; for it is not logical for something to be different while having an intrinsic nature non-different from a single [entity], just like that [exclusion] itself. Now, if it is argued that this fault must not occur and therefore exclusion is accepted as being a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), even so, because exclusion is formless (*arūpa*), entities would not be excluded by their own nature.
Another alternative:
difference is the nature of mutual non-selfhood; if that were the nature of things, it would follow that things are non-existent, because [difference] is asserted to have the nature of non-existence.
Another way:
If difference were the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, then no entity whatsoever would be unitary, because unity is contradicted by difference.
Even an atom would not be a single entity, as it would possess a manifold nature due to its differences.

Consequently, even its manifold nature—which consists of a collection of those [parts]—would not be tenable; since neither unity nor multiplicity is possible therein, and a third mode being impossible, it follows that the entity would be devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
There is another explanation for the second half [of the verse]:

it objects to the dilemma of whether [the universal] is distinct or non-distinct [from the particular], asserting that this distinction—namely, being of the same nature (*tatsvabhāvatva*) or being other (*anyatva*)—pertains to real entities (*vastu*). It cannot apply to a difference (*bheda*) that is a non-entity (*avastu*), whose body is constructed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For instance:

that which is indefinable as either identical to or different from [its counterpart], its form manifested by conceptualization (vikalpa) based on the material cause of beginningless conceptual impressions (vāsanā), brings about the conventional usage: "This is different from that," or "This is the difference between these two. There is no such thing as "difference" (*bheda*) that exists as a real entity (*vastu*), of which one could investigate identity or difference.
In this regard, the following point arises once more:
And it is not possible for a real entity to possess difference by means of a formless [distinction].

If, then, difference is formless and devoid of intrinsic nature— since it does not exist according to the actual state of things, but is displayed solely by conceptual constructions— then [how can it be real]?

In that case, there is no difference in the entity itself, because from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha) there is an absence of difference; for it is not logical that a thing possesses a quality by means of an imagined (kalpita) nature, as that would merely be imagined itself.
Why do you not accept this which we are saying? We too say exactly this:
difference does not exist in reality; this is merely the play of beginningless ignorance (avidyā).
[48,i] As it was said:
"If a thing consists of difference, there is an absence of a single entity; and because of that absence, there is also the absence of the other," they say in response to this:

We maintain that the differentiated nature of an entity is dependent upon another, not dependent upon itself, such that there would be an absence of a single entity due to contradiction; rather, a single entity is one in its own essence but distinct in relation to another.
To this, it is replied:
"Indeed, dependence is a human construct and does not follow the nature of the entity."

[48,ii] Dependence (*apekṣā*) is not some real property (*vastudharma*) by which things could be established. Indeed, it is not logical for things that have arisen through their own causes and are established by their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to depend on other things for the sake of maintaining that intrinsic nature.
In this regard, dependence is merely a property of human conceptualization.
Furthermore, entities do not conform to human conceptualization, because they are established in their own specific natures by their respective causes.
Therefore, the nature of an entity is not determined in accordance with that [conceptualization].
It is only logical that its determination follows the already established nature of the entity itself, since the former is preceded by the latter.
Furthermore, if there were mutual dependence while the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity remains fixed, it would result in the fallacy of reciprocal dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Alternatively, regarding what was stated— that because [the universal] is not distinct from the difference of one [particular], it follows that there is an absence of difference in the entity— they reply:

Difference is not one, because its forms are contradictory; and if it were one, then by virtue of that [single] cause, all things would become one. Therefore, difference varies with each individual thing. How then can there be a dependence on multiple substrata? It is through relative dependence (*apekṣā*); for its own nature is established in dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Thus, all things are distinct through their respective differences, which are essentially identical with themselves yet depend upon counter-correlates.
To this, it is replied: "That which is produced by man" (*pauruṣeyīm*).

For a person, having grasped one object, requires another for the sake of accomplishing a task; but what need do entities have for anything else when they have acquired their complete nature from their own causes? Is it not for the sake of establishing their own nature? For the natures of entities are manifold; among them, some are established in their reality only through dependence on a counterpart, such as this very [concept of] difference (*bheda*). If that is so, then an entity does not acquire its complete selfhood from its causes, because the form called "difference" depends upon a counterpart.
Furthermore, because it would be produced subsequently from another cause that serves as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin), difference could not be an intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
This might be argued:
An entity arises from its causes as possessing an entirely complete form.

Among these, the form known as "difference" (bheda) is dependent upon its counter-correlate (pratiyogin); it is never independent, because such is its very nature. Therefore, it arises together with that very [counter-correlate] of its own kind; thus, there is no manifestation of an incomplete form. To this, it is replied:

Let it be granted that such a thing may appear; however, the meaning of "dependence" (apekṣā) must be stated. For when something depends upon another in some respect, it is said to be "dependent" on that [other]; no other distinction is discerned that establishes the difference between the dependent and the independent. In this regard, production does not depend upon the counter-correlative (pratiyogin), because [the effect] is produced from its own causes in their entirety.
Nor does causal efficiency (arthakriyā) depend upon it, because its causal efficiency is observed even in the absence of that [counter-correlative].

If it is argued that [difference] is perceived—namely, that difference is not perceived without depending upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—then it follows that the nature of difference itself is not dependent.

Once that [difference] is established, the perception, occurring at a time subsequent to the actual state of the thing, depends upon the counter-correlate as a distinct object; just as color and other qualities, whose natures are established as independent, are not said to have a dependent nature merely because they depend on the eye and other faculties for their perception.
Furthermore, because they are mutually dependent, even the cognition [of difference] cannot be conceived as existing through mutual reliance.
Nor can difference be established from a mere entity when its distinction has not been apprehended, for that would entail the consequence of such difference existing even in a single thing.
Therefore, when there is dependence on human agency, it does not follow the nature of the entity; thus, it is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the entity—this is the meaning.
[50,i] Another explanation:
difference is not the nature of a real entity, for it is perceived as being relative.
Furthermore, in the case of dependence, a thing does not conform to the subjective cognition of a person, because it is preceded by an established reality.

How then is it that fathers and so forth exist? For they do not exist without dependence, yet they are not like sky-flowers or cities of Gandharvas, since they are established in the world as being part of non-contradictory worldly practice.
It is said:
Why is it that difference, in this same way, is not also established by worldly consensus?
Moreover, with respect to [objects such as] one's father and so forth, the expectation is produced by [the fact of] procreation and the like. // 1.9 //
Through a single specific action, there is a mutual dependence between the short and the long;

for while the capacities of being produced and producing remain fixed as the respective denotata of the words "father" and "son," those two nevertheless apply themselves to the same objective sphere of the act of procreation due to a difference in their intrinsic natures.
Therefore, there is dependence only where there is equality;
this is what is meant:
in that case, it is the word-meaning that is dependent, not the actual object.
Furthermore, in that case, there exists a common action (*sādhāraṇī kriyā*) even for two entities that are already established;

however, when there is a difference in their states (*bhāvabheda*), this is an investigation into the true nature of things (*vastutattva*), and no such causal factor of dependence (*apekṣāhetu*) is perceived.

This should be understood in the same way regarding short and long [measurements], where, despite a single type of action, there is a state of deficiency or excess in the occupation of space (*deśavyāpti*).

[50,v] If, then, dependence is established even from the difference of effects, then— alas!— the mutual difference of entities will be proven simply from the difference in their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Furthermore, since the establishment of difference occurs through perception even when [difference] is not [explicitly] present, we infer the difference of causes precisely from the difference of effects, because [perception] functions solely through affirmation (*vidhi*).
If there were identity [of cause and effect], a distinction between effects could not be conceived, because the distinction between effects depends upon the intrinsic nature of the cause.
If its intrinsic nature is the production of that [specific effect], it cannot produce anything else. Therefore, the arising of another effect must come from something else.
Thus, this attempt to establish difference through difference itself is not very clever. Moreover:
"When difference is established by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), no difference in form (*rūpa*) is obtained. (1.10)
Fire is not differentiated by the distinction between burning and cooking;
nor is a difference in the nature of entities perceived through a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) based on mutual dependence, nor can such a difference be inferred.
There would be merely a difference in designation, since even in a single fire, a difference in effects such as burning and cooking is observed.
Now, it might be thought: fire is a collection of color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities;
therein, illumination arises from color-form, while burning arises from touch (*sparśa*).
Granted that burning and cooking result from contact alone;
yet these two are distinct perceptions in the world despite the commonality of the modification of the substances in conjunction.

Furthermore, it should be considered that a single action is the cause of conjunction, disjunction, and latent impression (*saṃskāra*); likewise, the self is the cause of desire and so forth; and the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, being individually non-distinct, are the causes of lightness, manifestation, and so on; while color-form (*rūpa*) and the other qualities are the causes of specific cognitions and of their own homogeneous moments.
Now, we do not assert a difference merely on account of a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); rather, it is because of [an efficiency] that is impossible there and has not been observed.

For example, even though the eye is present, there is a difference between the sense organs because auditory cognition—which is unobserved in the eye and impossible there—is absent in the deaf person.
And entities generally possess mutually incompatible effects, since the effect of one thing is not seen in another.

Now, how is the impossibility of an effect to be understood? [If it is argued: "It has already been stated that it is because it is not observed there. [We reply: In that case, there is no impossibility. For one for whom the world is non-dual, the entire collection of effects is seen in one place alone; so how can there be "non-observation"? In that regard, if difference were established, then there would be non-observation there; and if there is non-observation there, then difference is established. Thus, because of this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), there can be no inference of difference.
Now, if it is thought that [the cause exists] because an unseen thing is seen,
that is incorrect, because we observe successive effects even from a single [cause].
It might be argued:
if there were absolute non-difference, the observation and non-observation of effects would not be tenable, because there would be no distinction.
In that case, the difference among effects does not subvert [the fact of] non-difference.
Without subverting that [nature], there would be an inference of a mere particularity (*viśeṣa*).

And we do not at all disregard that as being within the domain of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because it is impossible for it to be a real entity (*vastusat*), given the impossibility of its being either identical to or different from that [nature].

But for one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*) and does not admit that the particularity is identical [to the nature], how could an effect with an identical nature be produced in the absence of a non-difference in the nature of the cause?
Now, even for those things that perish without leaving a trace (*niranvayavināśa*), the effect is identical because it is non-different from the object of conceptual construction (*kalpanāviṣaya*).
Alas! In that case, since the difference in effects is established precisely through the difference in the objects of conceptual construction, the postulation of a difference in causes is futile.

Alternatively, if one were not to require a non-difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the cause when there is no difference in the effect—since a single effect can arise from auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) of different intrinsic natures, just as the cognition of form arises from the eye and other [causes]—then [the argument fails].

In that case, just as a difference in the nature of the cause is not required for the sake of a non-difference in the nature of the effect, so too a difference in the cause should not be required for the sake of a difference in that [effect].

Moreover, even when a single effect is produced by multiple causes, the distinction in the objects of the causal operations has been described by him himself in the case of the cognition of color (*rūpa*), as follows:

The restriction of the eye to the apprehension of form, the nature of perception derived from the immediately preceding cognition (*samanantarajñāna*), and the assumption of the object's form [by that cognition]—if the similarity of the effect were not produced by the sameness of the cause, there could be no inference of the cause from the effect, since it is possible for a similar kind of thing to arise even from a cause of a different genus. If the non-difference of the cause does not entail the non-difference of the effect, what could prevent the production of a heterogeneous thing from a homogeneous one? In this regard, just as the non-difference of the effect follows from the conventional non-difference [of the cause], so too the difference of the effect follows from the conventional difference; thus, there is no distinction between the two cases.
It might be argued:
if difference is imagined, it cannot be capable of producing a difference in effects;
for there is no characteristic other than causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) that defines what is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*).
This is the same even in the case of non-difference.
[52,i] This is also the view of one who thinks—
The cognition of difference arises from observing contradictory purposeful actions occurring simultaneously. For instance,
the universe is perceived at one time as endowed with various contradictory properties, such as birth and death, growth and decay, staying and moving, sorrow and joy, and so forth.
It is understood that it possesses those distinctions; and for this as well, the same answer applies by way of repetition:
"through the distinction between burning and cooking."
How so? First, he should be asked this:
what is the meaning of "contradictory"? If it means impossibility in one place, that is unproven (*asiddha*).
Or, if it means having mutually exclusive natures, such that production and the rest consist in the negation of each other's nature; [then...]
In that case, difference is not established from this [reasoning],
because even in a single fire one observes both the properties of being a burner and being a cooker.
Indeed, there is no plurality of properties without mutual exclusion.
If there were a difference [between them] on that basis, then nothing could be both one and possessed of multiple properties.
Alternatively, if contradiction consists simply in having the nature of mutual non-existence— namely, that in a single thing, it both exists and does not exist— [then this is our position].
From that, there would be a determination of difference;
but that is incorrect.
For it is not the case that these two properties themselves [are different]; how, then, could there be an apprehension of difference due to a contradiction between them?
Furthermore, in the case of sky-flowers and the like, because both [properties] are absent, there would be the undesirable consequence of both [contradiction and non-contradiction].
Now, if contradiction is defined as the relationship between the victim and the executioner—
such that joy destroys sorrow and sorrow destroys it, and so it is for the others as well— [then...]
Even in that case, one thing that has not yet arisen does not destroy another, nor does it have a different substratum.
Therefore, it must be stated that it destroys [the other] by existing within a single substratum.
And thus, since those two are observed to share a single substratum, the inference of a difference in substrata based on that observation is not non-deviant (i.e., it is valid).
Now, properties consisting of a positive form and its exclusion— such as permanence and impermanence, or corporeality and incorporeality—
are contradictory; from their connection, the cognition of difference arises.
That too is not so; for it is not necessarily the case that whatever exists in a certain place pervades it.
Indeed, chariots and the like, or their conjunctions and the like, do not pervade space, nor do they pervade other conjoined things such as the earth and so forth, because they are limited in extent.
Thus, although delimited phenomena depend upon an undelimited and infinite object, they do not pervade it;
therefore, there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence even within a single entity.
But one might think:
"The distinction between objects consists in the difference in their causal efficiency;
from that, the cognition of difference [arises]."
For if there were identity, no distinction would be possible;
and thus, oil would come from milk, and curd from sesame seeds.
Likewise, when one thing is born, everything would be born, and when it perishes, everything would perish.
Otherwise, it would be merely a difference expressed by another word.
As it has been said: "There would be simultaneous arising and perishing, and everything would be applicable everywhere."
To this, too, the same answer applies:
"by means of the distinction between burning and cooking.
If the diversity of effects were the basis for establishing difference, one would not thereby perceive a distinction between sesame seeds and milk.
Now, the established rule is that curd is born from milk and not from anything else.
That which is sought to be known through this established rule cannot enter into the definition of "otherness," for that would result in the rule itself being unestablished.
Therefore, the established rule consists in the capacity of milk to produce curd and the absence of that capacity in other things.
From that follows difference; for it is not possible for one and the same thing to possess both power and incapacity with respect to a single object.
Furthermore, this conjunction of contradictory properties, which was cited as the cause of difference, has just been refuted.

Just as indeed long-duration entities, when connected with phenomena of limited duration—whether possessing those properties or not—do not become subjects of contradiction, so too do infinite entities [behave] when connected with phenomena of limited space. If it is asked, "How can there be a finite property of the infinite?", there is no room for doubt regarding its impossibility, whether one assumes their difference or their ineffability.
Even in the case of non-difference, it is like a limited duration belonging to a long duration.
Furthermore, for one who does not understand the point even after a long time, this should be recited again:
"by way of the distinction between burning and cooking.
Even though fire is a single entity, it burns some things and cooks others.
And likewise, the burner and the non-burner are not distinct;
similarly, it does not produce other burnings or other cookings upon that very same object to be burned or cooked.
Likewise, although seeds and so forth are individually capable, they do not produce other sprouts, nor does the causal complex (sāmagrī) produce them.
And thus, there is both the state of being a producer and the state of not being a producer.

Now, if the power to produce resides in one [moment] alone, why does it not produce another—whether past or future? Or, if its capacity lies only in that specific [moment], and not elsewhere, even in what is of the same kind?
Why? Because that [milk] itself arises, and because capacity is to be understood through its effect.
Thus, there is no contradiction between potency and non-potency.
If that is so, then even in the case of non-difference, there would be no contradiction when milk does not produce curd from sesame seeds.
For instance:

first of all, that curd which has its origin in milk does not fail to arise from sesame seeds, such that there would be a distinction [between them] due to a contradiction between power and powerlessness.
Why? Because sesame seeds are non-different from milk.
Now, it might be argued that there is a contradiction because another curd cannot arise [from the same milk].
But that is not so; for just as with seeds and the like, there is a capacity for one thing in one place and a lack of capacity elsewhere.
Indeed, a cause does not produce everything of the same class simply because it is capable, for if it did, it would follow that all effects of the same class could arise from a single cause.
Now, it might be thought: we determine difference because of their distinct application to purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*).
For milk is applied for the sake of curd, but sand is not.
That too is inconclusive, because even when there is unity, we observe a distribution [of function] by way of differentiation.
That very same objective entity is employed when accompanied by auxiliary factors, not when it is alone.
Now, if it is thought—
That [entity] is indeed distinct, due to the difference in conditions (*upādhi*) consisting in the proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).
If it is argued that the distinction is then merely conditional, residing only in the cognition (*pratyaya*), and not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), we reply:
such a distinction between entities is indeed admitted.

Even for one who asserts distinction on the basis of momentariness, since that distinction is equal [in all cases], everything would be applicable everywhere, or else nothing would be applicable anywhere, because their causal capacity has not been observed [to be restricted].

If it is argued that its establishment [of restriction] follows from non-distinction from the object of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then for the opponent as well, it follows from such a distinction; thus, there is no difference [between the two views], as has already been stated.
Furthermore, regarding one who maintains both [distinction and non-distinction] for a single entity—

[He asserts] both difference and non-difference; therefore, for one who accepts the entry of contradictory properties even in a single entity, it is impossible to distinguish between sesame seeds and milk on the basis of their being respectively the producer and the non-producer of curd.
Thus it is so—
This is the majesty of the One alone, which is incapable of being divided.
When there is a conceptual construction of a difference in states, as in the case of fire, then it is futile.

Because a difference in action is perceived in a single [entity], because the impossibility [of such perception] is unproven, and because the observation of what was previously unseen lacks the power to subvert non-difference; because that [difference] is merely a cause of specific qualities and is therefore a locus for conceptual construction, being indefinable as either identical to or different from the reality; because, just as non-difference arises from such [a cause], so too does difference arise from a similar cause; because contradiction is either inconclusive or unproven regarding the established order; because the difference in application is inconclusive; because its establishment occurs through imagined difference just as through non-difference; and because if both difference and non-difference were to coexist in one place, then the coexistence of capacity and incapacity, or application and non-application, would be possible within a single substratum—then this certain, inconceivable excellence of power belonging to the One alone, which is capable of producing the entire manifold of diversity, becomes the cause, just as fire is the cause for the distinction between cooking and burning; at that time, the postulation of difference is groundless, since it is established even from the One.
Thus concludes the preceding section.
This very point has been declared by a Ṛgvedic verse:
"Such is his greatness."

This is the extent of His power— that even though He is one, He is the locus of the various activities and functions of diverse and seemingly contradictory attributes as indicated in the two preceding verses, such as "the thousand-headed" and "that which has been and that which is to be. How is this so?

“From this”— that is, from that which is regarded as perceived, or from that which is indicated by the statement “The Person alone is all this,” or from the phrase “and also of immortality”— the Person is greater than each and every member of the manifold world, whether distinguished as the realms of gods or humans, or taken as a whole. Therefore, it is not possible for finite things— even those considered contradictory— to be contained within that Infinite.
He demonstrates that very superiority with the words, "All this is one foot of Him.
Even the entire expansion of the elements is but a smaller portion of Him; how much more so, then, each individual part?
For instance:

"Three-footed" (tripāt)—meaning immeasurable, infinite, and devoid of the qualities of the phenomenal world such as death—His form abides "in heaven" (divi), that is, in the state of radiance or in the state of supreme bliss, within the solar orb or in the celestial realm.
For it is there that He is to be meditated upon.
For that is the locus of its perception; therefore, it is said "therein. Another interpretation:

Even if [the cause] is imagined to be distinct, why does another effect not arise from the distinction of the state of the effect and so forth, or from the distinction of the cause? Or why is there no confusion, or rather, why is the established order reversed? Even though milk is distinct [from other things], why is oil produced only from sesame seeds and not from sand? And although they are distinct, the eye, light, and so forth, as well as arrows, horns, and so forth, produce a single effect. Furthermore, even though there is a distinction, oil comes from sesame seeds and curd from milk, but why is oil not produced from milk, or curd from sesame seeds? If it is thought that this is due to the inconceivable potencies of entities (*bhāva-sāmarthya*), [then we reply:]...

The causal capacities of entities, which are inconceivable and beyond logical derivation, are established through the observation of their effects—answering the questions "Why? and "How?"—and consist in the differentiation and the specific arrangement of those effects, not their opposite.
If this is so, let that excellence of capacity belong to a single entity alone.
Since that which is established as manifold and non-erroneous is the effect,
and since that [effect] is established by that alone, the postulation of entities for things that lack any means of valid cognition is groundless.
It might be argued:
even in the case of fire, the difference in effects is based on a difference in its potencies;
therefore, multiple effects do not arise from a single [cause].

In that case, if fire also is a cause, how is it that multiple effects do not arise from a single [cause]? Now, if you intend to say that it is the potencies alone that possess causality, it is said in response: "Just as the undivided form is the substratum for the distinct potencies... (1.12).
Likewise, why is a form that serves as the cause for various distinct actions not accepted?
Because it is contradictory for a single entity to be connected with multiple effects, a diversity of potencies is postulated.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction in one thing being related to many [things], then how is it that a single entity is related to various powers (*śakti*)? In that case, just as a single nature of an object is joined with various powers, why is its connection with various effects not likewise admitted? If you claim there is a contradiction in the connection with various effects but not in the connection with various powers, you must state the specific reason for this distinction. Furthermore, because powers are non-different from the entity itself, a single thing is thereby accepted as having a manifold nature.

In that regard, it is well said: "Oneness is contradicted by the multiplicity inherent in its own substratum; however, it is contradicted by the multiplicity residing in other substrata belonging to the effect! Now, if the powers (*śakti*) are indeed distinct entities, then the meaning of their "substratum" (*āśraya*) must be stated. If it is "conjunction" (*saṃśleṣa*), then since they are distinct, there can be no conjunction characterized by the non-separation of form; for if they were conjoined, there would be no distinction at all.
There is no such thing as "immediacy" [of power], because it would follow that any other substance conjoined with a substance possessing that power would also possess that power.

For a substance does not become separated from its power simply by being adjacent to it. Indeed, it is not the case that color is not immediate to the substance of the eye simply because it is adjacent to it.

Furthermore, because space and the other [elements] possess omnipresence (*vibhutva*), there would follow the consequence that they possess all powers, since there is no obstruction to their capacity for all objects.
Therefore, the substratum [of these powers] must exist due to some specific assistance (*upakāra*).

In that case, just as a single entity, despite its diverse powers, produces distinct assistances based on those differences in power, why is it not accepted that it likewise produces effects? Thus, first of all, there is no apprehension of difference through inference, nor through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
[56,ii] But as for those who think:
"This is true; perception is not sufficient for the apprehension of difference."
For the distinction between entities consists in the aspect of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and that is not within the range of the senses;
"for the sense organ is indeed capable of contact only with the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) of things.
Likewise, it is not even accessible through an inferential mark (*liṅga*), because its connection [with any such mark] has never been perceived.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) would also have to be based on the establishment of effects;
however, since that [establishment] is impossible when difference is unproven, it is untenable in that case.
Therefore, a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) must be employed for non-existence, rather than those causes consisting of the perception of existing things.
Alternatively, there is indeed another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called non-existence (abhāva) which functions as an exclusionary determinant;
for it is based upon this that the non-confusion of the intrinsic natures (svabhāva) of entities is established.
As they have said:
“And the establishment of the non-confusion of entities depends upon their validity.
To those [who hold this view], it is replied:
Because they are mutually dependent, difference does not establish another means of valid cognition.

There is no cognition [of exclusion] without the distinction that "this is not in this" or "this is not that. Indeed, there can be no comprehension of an exclusion without the apprehension of both that which is excluded and that from which it is excluded.
There is no negation that does not depend upon an object and a thing to be negated.
It has been stated that one should bring about the emptiness of existence itself, not its differentiation.
Their words also say:
"Having apprehended the real existence of the object and having recollected its counter-correlate..."
"Non-existence is known by mental cognition, independent of the sense faculties."

And if there were no cognition of those two as having unmixed natures, but rather as mere entities, then— due to the absence of a distinction between the object to be excluded and the limit of exclusion—
negation would be impossible, for there is no negation when there is an undifferentiated mere object.
When something is required as an objective referent, it cannot be the object of negation.
When something is intended as an object of negation, there is no specific qualification of the object;
in that case, the negation would be absolute.
And it has already been stated that such a negation is not compatible with either established existence or non-established existence.

If, for someone, the cognition of difference from something were to occur only with respect to a particular thing, then there would be a cognition of difference for everything from everything, because there would be no distinction [between cases].

Therefore, having cognized two distinct things by means of this unmixed intrinsic nature (*asamkīrṇasvabhāva*), one must cognize the exclusion—“this is not here” or “this is not that”—with regard to the object and the thing to be negated, because of both possibility and necessity.
Otherwise, there would be no state of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*); for when a post is perceived as a general object, there is no cognition of the absence of a person.

And thus, by accepting both the established object and the object to be negated, the cognition of non-existence—which effects a mere exclusion—is observed within each individual. Furthermore, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*):
the knowledge of non-existence presupposes non-confusion, and from that, the establishment of non-confusion [is derived].

Furthermore, the cognition of non-existence does not arise from the mere non-arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because such non-arising occurs even during deep sleep and other states.
Therefore, it is accepted that when the causes of a means of valid cognition are present, the non-arising of that means of valid cognition is the cause for the cognition of non-existence.

Nor does this [non-arising] possess any specific difference in its own nature (*svarūpa*) by virtue of which it could be a cognizer through a superior capacity, like the eye and other senses; rather, it is so because of its invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyakatva*).

Without the absence of the object of cognition (*prameya*), there can be no non-arising of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when the causes for such means are present; however, when they are absent, it would occur due to that absence even if the object of cognition were present. Thus, like a logical mark (*liṅga*), [the non-arising of the means] depends upon cognition to produce comprehension. And if that [cognition] is the cognition of another entity, it cannot be established unless the difference between entities is established.
For the distinction among cognitions, which are themselves inferable from their objects, is indeed inferred from the distinction among those objects.

Thus, the comprehension of the distinction between absences is preceded solely by the establishment of the distinction between positive entities; this constitutes the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Alternatively, it might be argued that [the distinction] is the non-modification (*apariṇāma*) of the self.
That is not a state of stagnation, because when there is no cognition of anything at all, no absence whatsoever can be apprehended.

Therefore, even though there is a transformation into the form of the cognition of another object, the absence of that specific transformation into the form of the [target] cognition is the cause for the cognition of absence.
Nor can this distinction be established prior to the establishment of the difference between objects; thus, it is indeed a case of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
[58,i] But as for those who say:
"The distinction between entities is established through perception alone."
For it has been stated by one who refutes the view that non-conceptual perception has a universal as its object:
"That is incorrect, because a distinct form is perceived in each individual substance."
As for the confusion that arises from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), it is removed by the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva*);
however, those [arguments] have already been refuted previously.

There are also those who maintain that it is another perception itself— arising from the sense organ aided by the recollection of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) and the performance of the procedure— that functions as the delimiter, following upon an initial affirmative perception;
just as a determinate perception arises later than the apprehension of the object and is preceded by the recollection of a word.
Nor is it non-sensory, because that [cognition] arises from the sense organ when assisted by a specific mode of operation (*itikartavyatā*)—
this is what those who say even the cognition "it does not exist" maintain.
To them, this very point must be said:
Due to mutual dependence, difference is not established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The meaning is that it is not established by another instance of perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The cognition "this is not that" is either a perception or another means of valid cognition.
In every way, negation is impossible without the distinction between the object and that which is to be negated.
Furthermore:
In things that possess a single, uniform nature as they are being measured, there is no room for negation.

Furthermore, when only existence (*sanmātra*) is perceived everywhere in things that possess that very nature, there is no non-arising of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding one thing as being other than what is intended to be other, because both possess the nature of existence (*satsvabhāvatva*).
Moreover, the term "existent" (*sat*) applies everywhere because of the presence of a means of valid cognition in all cases.
"Because there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the cognition of mutual non-existence.
Now, it may be argued that there is no single, undifferentiated form among objects;
for it is through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that such a form is understood.

Furthermore, for one who has perceived a mere object, there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the form "this is that very same [object]" with respect to another object, as there is for one who has seen a single cow when seeing another cow.
As for the persistence of the word and cognition "existent" (*sat*), it is based on etymological derivation (*yoga*), like the case of "cook" (*pācaka*) and so forth.
For that which is the object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is said to be "existent."
This is not sound.
If there were no cognition of an undifferentiated form, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would result in being entirely without an object,
because the cognition of difference does not occur without exclusion (vyavaccheda).
Exclusion is not alone, nor is it accompanied by affirmation; nor does the operation of the means of valid cognition occur after affirmation.
It has been explained that exclusion is not simply affirmation itself.
In that case, if even one of these were not understood, there would be a total absence of an object.

If it is argued that non-recognition occurs because of the difference from a cow, even though there is a persistence of the form of pure existence (*sanmātra*), then that [non-recognition] would not occur with respect to another cow either, due to its difference from Devadatta.
For the kind of cognition of oneness that arises upon seeing Devadatta again does not occur in the case of another cow.
Now, in that case [of Devadatta], there is indeed a synthesis of the prior and the subsequent, but not so for one existent thing in relation to another existent thing.
Furthermore, sir, unity arises from synthesis (*anusandhāna*), not from a cognition of an undifferentiated form.
Otherwise, an object existing at different places and times would not be one;
for it is only when there is a difference of place and time that there occurs the synthesis of "this is that" (*so 'yam*) between what precedes and what follows.

And even in the case of different locations, such as a cow-pen which is distinct from a buffalo-pen, the cognition of a single object is held to arise from the very first non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-pratyaya*), because it follows a uniform form.
Furthermore, since there is no difference in time in that instance, there is no reflective judgment (*avamarśa*) of the form "this is that.
As it has been said:

Even in non-conceptual cognition, there is the apprehension of an object that possesses a dual nature; this is called its "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa), yet it is apprehended by the knower in its pure form.
Furthermore, just as one who has seen a water-jar does not fail to recognize it in another jar, so too, upon seeing a bowl, one would not deny the presence of the universal "clay-ness" therein.

If that universal exists there as well, yet it is not as prominent as it is in another jar due to the greater abundance of common features there, this is because of the limited following of common features [in the bowl].
The same would apply even in the case of other existing things.

This will be explained in detail further below, so let us stop this digression. If it is argued that there are two cognitions appearing as distinct and non-distinct, let them be examined: [59,i] If it is held that there are two cognitions appearing as both distinct and non-distinct, let them be investigated.
If it is thought:
"Indeed, two cognitions—appearing as continuous and appearing as excluded—do exist;
for in their absence, the conventional usage of 'continuous' and 'excluded' would not be possible."
Nor is there any cause for the determination of objects other than consciousness and form;
if that [cause] were non-existent, even their non-difference would not be established.
This is not sound.
For it is not the case that the mere fact of "consciousness" establishes the reality (tattva) [of things];
for that too must be examined— whether it is not contradicted by reasoning, and whether it does not arise from valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Indeed, the determination of the reality of an object does not proceed from cognitions such as those of a firebrand-circle and the like.
It might be argued:
"Direct perception is not sublated by reasoning."
True.

It has already been explained that the cognition of difference is not indeed perception, just as in the case of the cognition of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) produced by the rapid conjunction [of the wheel] with all directions.

Although that [cognition of difference] exists, it does not arise from a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); though it resembles perception, like the cognition of things seen in a dream or a fire-brand wheel, it is not a cause for the realization of reality.
Now, it might be argued that the cognition of difference cannot arise from anything other than the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the manner already stated.
Who indeed says otherwise? For there is no comprehension of difference in an ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*).
If such were the case, how could difference be denied? Or, if it is denied, how can there be its comprehension?
It is a contradiction to say that there is nothing to be known and yet it is known.
What then is this? It is ignorance, a delusion. If the object of knowledge existed as it appears, it would not be a delusion, but rather right knowledge.
Furthermore, the apprehension of a non-existent thing is logically untenable.

Therefore, it is said that [the self] is not defined as existing from the perspective of ultimate reality, nor is it defined as non-existent, because it is established in the world according to all philosophical systems.
Moreover, regarding these two cognitions, four conceptual possibilities arise:
first, that there are two entities distinguished as universal and particular due to a difference in cognition, as the proponents of conjunction (saṃsargavādins) say;
or second, that there is a single entity consisting of both the universal and the particular, as the proponents of non-absolutism (anekāntavādins) say.
Or rather, only the particulars (*viśeṣa*) are real entities.
Because one is incapable of ascertaining their absolute difference, non-difference—which has those [particulars] as its basis and as its object—is the domain of conceptual cognition.
For the conceptualization of non-difference is indeed observed among distinct things, as in the case of the word "forest."
As those who maintain the doctrine of absolute difference have said:
"Non-difference is the ultimate reality;

however, because that which is undivided and infinite cannot be determined as such, and because ignorance is beginningless, there arise conceptual constructions of difference based upon it [ignorance] and having it as their object."
For indeed, a conceptualization of difference is observed in the moon, which is non-different, due to the distinction between its waves;
therefore, there can be no determination of reality without investigation.
In that regard, as for investigation—
First of all, duality [is not possible], because the manifestation of a single identity is inconceivable. (1.15)
If it is argued that this [cognition] is produced by inherence (*samavāya*), that is not so, because difference has not been discarded.
To begin with, the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) are not two distinct entities, because their appearance is non-different.
For these two appear as co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*), as in the cognitions "the pot is existent" (*san ghaṭaḥ*) and "the cow is healthy" (*gauḥ svastimatī*).
It is not [a case of] having different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), as in the case of "blue" and "yellow," or as in "the staff is Devadatta.
Nor is it [a case of] the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), as in "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*), because the relation does not appear [in consciousness].
Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible when the objects are distinct entities, even if a relation exists.
The two related entities are apprehended as qualifier and qualified by means of either two cognitions or a single cognition, but not as being identical with one another;
yet, here, their realization as being identical with one another is personally experienced by each individual.
Furthermore, there is disagreement regarding the difference between the universal and the particular.
Otherwise, they would not fall into error;

for when there is perception of the general, one might falsely imagine it to be perception of the particular. Otherwise, just as when smoke is seen, there would be a false imagination of fire being imperceptible.
It might be argued:
the cognition of difference does not arise from relation in general, but rather from a specific type of relation, namely inherence (*samavāya*);
for that [inherence] consists in the essential fusion of entities.

That is not so; for even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), the difference in form from those two [substrata] does not disappear, otherwise there would be no relation due to the absence of distinction.
And thus, manifestation as a single identity is not tenable;
yet this [manifestation] does exist.

Therefore, a difference in appearance that is contradicted by that [reality] is not capable of establishing a difference in the thing itself; for it is either self-contradictory, since it results in [the contradictory properties] having a single substratum.
But surely, even though there is difference, it is inherence (*samavāya*) that serves as the cause for their cognition as being identical with one another.
Indeed, this is its extraordinary capacity: that by which it conceals the difference of distinct objects, so that they appear as non-different.
To this it is replied: "If it is held that its capacity for the disappearance of difference exists even while difference persists," (1.16)
Ah! Why then is it not accepted that this belongs to a single entity alone, since it appears in such a way?

If you argue that the appearance of non-difference between two things that are distinct arises through the power of inherence (*samavāya*), then, alas, let it be admitted that the appearance of multiplicity belongs to a single reality due to its own specific capacity.
The postulation of a distinction between entities is useless.
For there is no distinction such that the manifestation of non-difference is possible for two distinct things, while the manifestation of multiplicity is not possible for a single thing.
But surely, such a capacity for conjunction is observed in cases like fire and iron balls;
since it is seen there, the appearance of difference among things that are non-different may arise from conjunction.
However, the appearance of multiplicity in a single thing does not occur, because it is never observed.
It is said:
This property of association is observed even when only one [of two things] is present in that manner. (1.17)
Just as a single variegated color appears manifold, so too does cognition. Indeed, it is observed that even a single thing can have various appearances, as in the case of a variegated color;
for that [variegated color] is certainly not merely a collection of blue and other colors.
For if one does not admit a distinct color in the inherence of those parts, it would follow that the whole is colorless;
yet the whole cannot be colorless,
because in the absence of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of color, it could not be perceived by the eye.
Nor does it follow that [the universal] is visible simply because of its inherence in a substance possessing color, as is the case with number, action, and so forth.
For it has been stated thus:
"Perception [of a substance] occurs when there is inherence in multiple substances and when there is color."
In this way, every whole (*avayavin*) would be devoid of color (*nīrūpa*).

If it is argued that this undesirable consequence does not apply because [the whole] is not perceived as being without color, then even a variegated [color] is likewise [not perceived as such], and thus it is not without color.
And its color consists in the appearance (*nirbhāsa*) of blue, yellow, and so forth.

Thus, proponents of the theory that cognition possesses the form of the object (*viṣayākārajñānavādin*) maintain that cognitions such as cities, the three worlds, and so forth, which appear in the forms of various objects, manifest even though there is no actual differentiation [in the external world].
Furthermore, because they are not distinct from the single reality of cognition (*buddhitattva*), the forms of the objects do not differ from one another, much less from the cognition itself.
It might be argued:
"Even variegated color appears as such only due to a relation characterized by inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-the-same-subject (ekārthasamavetasamavāya) resulting from conjunction.
That is incorrect.
For it is said:
"Nor is there a relation consisting of the connection between two related things, because of the intervention [of a third entity]. (1.18)
For conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*) is indeed contact (*saṃsarga*);
and from that follows the appearance of each other's forms.
And that [appearance] is possible only when there is no interval.

But not when there is an intervention by their own respective substrates. Even with the intervention of a single [substrate], there is no contact between the forms of the part and the whole; how much less so with an intervention by two?
Furthermore,

when all cognition in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)— which is conditioned by another— is conventionally valid (*vyāvahārika*) yet not in accordance with reality, then the conceptual construction (*kalpa*) of the differentiation of entities is futile. (1.19)

For one who holds that cognitions such as "the cow is white," which serve as the basis for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), are based on the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of substance, quality, and genus (*jāti*), these [cognitions] do not correspond to reality; for genus, quality, and substance are mutually distinct entities (*arthāntara*).

Consequently, linguistic usage is not grounded in reality, because that which is not presented by cognition does not serve as a basis for usage, whereas that which is presented by cognition possesses such a status.

Thus, since this conventional usage—both its exclusion and its inclusion—is constituted solely by an object produced by conditions, the postulation of a real distinction between entities is useless; for that [distinction], even if imagined, is of no utility in conventional usage, whereas the other [the object produced by conditions] is indeed useful.

For a real distinction between entities is postulated so that conventional cognitions may correspond to reality (*yathārtha*). But once that distinction is imagined, those cognitions cannot avoid being non-correspondent (*ayathārtha*), because they would then have that [imagined distinction] as their external condition (*paropādhi*).
[62,iii] This might be the case:

if there were no difference in the nature of things (*vastubheda*), then conventional cognition— which apprehends both the inclusive and the exclusive aspects even though they do not correspond to reality— could not arise, due to the absence of its cause.
Indeed, errors such as those of a person or silver with respect to a post, a fragment of wood, and so forth, are not without a seed, because they are based upon a commonality [of features].
It is said:
the seed of a cognition that does not correspond to reality is necessarily external alone.
For internal disturbances such as cataracts and desire have indeed been observed. (1.20)

[63,i] It is not from defects in the object alone—such as similarity—that there arises cognition that does not correspond to reality; rather, it also arises from internal defects such as cataracts, desire, grief, and so forth.

In that case, even in the absence of a difference in the external object, the internal defect characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*) is the seed of conventional cognition; thus, there is no need for a difference in the object itself.
[63,ii] Let it be, then, that one thing has a dual nature;
for in this way, the mutual apprehension of the universal and the particular is rendered possible.
Furthermore, one should not postulate an excellence in the causal capacity of an object that is contrary to reality;
worldly transaction is based on the actual thing, not on the erroneous functioning of conventional cognitions.
This might be argued:
The dual nature of a single entity is contradictory;
for it is a contradiction to say that something is both one and dual-natured.
Furthermore, a universal is that which follows after other particulars.
Therefore, difference has a nature that is excluded [from identity].
For the oneness of those two is impossible to establish due to their contradiction.
This is not sound.
Wherein do we have the conviction that something is "contradictory"? It is that which exists in opposition to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

But as for that which is apprehended by a means of valid cognition exactly as it is, if one were to designate it as "contradictory" while it exists in that very manner—on what basis, pray tell, could one establish the distinction between what is contradictory and what is not? Furthermore, a means of valid cognition reveals that a single entity possesses the nature of both the universal and the particular, because of the difference in the forms of its manifestation through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anuvṛtti*), and because of the apprehension of their co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
This is improper, because it is not logical for such cognitions of contradictory objects to possess validity at all, just like a cognition of doubt.
Otherwise, even the object of doubt would have a dual nature, since it possesses two appearances and those two appearances share a common substratum.

Now, it might be thought: there is no comprehension of a collection of forms in a state of doubt, as there is in the case of that which possesses both general and particular characteristics, because the cognition takes the form "this or that.
Let there be no collection; let there instead be an alternative (vikalpa).
That too is not the case, because conceptual construction is impossible with respect to a real entity (*vastu*).
In that case, even a single thing cannot possess a dual nature, because it is contradictory for a single thing to have a dual nature.

Just as doubt (*saṃśaya*) is not a valid means of knowledge due to its internal contradiction, so too is the cognition of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), because they would occupy the same locus (*aikādhikaraṇya*).
It might be argued as follows:
doubt-cognition is not invalid because of contradiction, but rather because it is sublated by determinate cognition.
In that case, however, where there is no definitive determination (*nirṇaya*), there must be the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpātmatā*).

Furthermore, just as in the case of sublation (*bādhā*) one [cognition] is rendered invalid due to its being refuted, so too in the case of contradiction (*virodha*), when two cognitions or even a single cognition assumes contradictory forms, their respective apprehensions of those forms mutually refute one another.
In that situation, upon the refutation of one, certainty arises from the other.

Since there is doubt when two [cognitions] of equal strength mutually exclude one another, the apprehension of either the universal or the particular from such a state of doubtful cognition is not distinguished [from it].
Therefore, the description of one's own position is that the cognition "the object here is non-conclusive" is well-ascertained.
Moreover,
if oneness and difference were to coexist without contradiction, there would be no dual nature [in the entity], just as a single part cannot be devoid of one of its two aspects. (1.21)

One who necessarily establishes the difference and non-difference of categories must state the definitions of difference and non-difference— for instance, as it is said that the universal is non-different while the particulars are different.
In this context, the opposition of form (*rūpavirodha*)—which is synonymous with mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)—is the characteristic of difference;
its opposite is the characteristic of non-difference.
For it is through the opposition of form, which is a synonym for mutual non-existence, that particularities (*viśeṣa*) are differentiated.
Even when those [particulars] are being divided, the universal remains undivided; it is the opposite of them.

In that case, if there were a contradiction of essential nature between the universal and the particular, consisting in mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*), then there would be no unity, just as there is none among distinct particulars relative to one another.

If, on the other hand, a contradiction of essential nature is accepted because the cognitions of the universal and the particular arise with a common substratum, then the one cannot possess a dual nature.
Because there is no contradiction in the intrinsic natures of the universal and the particular, duality is untenable in the absence of a distinction between them;
just as the aspect of the universal is not twofold, nor is the aspect of the particular, because there is no contradiction in their nature— since duality is absent in that single undivided entity.

Likewise, if there is no contradiction in their essential natures regarding the cognition of co-referentiality between the universal and the particular, then they do not exclude one another; in that case, duality would not be tenable.
If, however, there is a contradiction in their essential natures, then unity is not possible.
[64,ii] If it is thought:

"Plurality does not arise from a contradiction in essential nature (*svarūpa*), nor does unity arise from its absence; therefore, because there is no contradiction in the essential natures of the universal and the particular, they would not be two, just like either one of their parts."
However, it is through the difference and non-difference of forms as they are perceived by cognition (*buddhi*).

Since the universal and the particular are understood as being of the nature of one another, even though there is no contradiction in their own-nature (*svarūpa*) characterized by mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), duality arises from the difference of forms as perceived by cognition;
whereas in the case of the parts, unity arises from the non-difference of forms.
Therefore, because this entity is grasped by a cognition of two forms, it possesses a dual nature.
To this, it is replied:
if that were so regarding the object, then this [dual nature] would apply only to a portion of the cognition of a single essence.
If it does not exist, how can there be oneness? If it does exist, how can there be a dual nature? (1.22)

If, then, because cognition grasps a single form, there is no difference in the part, the object itself must be examined— in that case as well, does cognition grasp a single form with respect to the object or not?
In this regard, if cognition does not grasp a single form with respect to the object—

For an entity consists of both the universal and the particular; it is apprehended by two distinct forms of cognition. How, then, can there be oneness in the entity? This is because the characteristic of non-difference—the non-distinction between the forms of the cognitions—is absent, while the characteristic of difference—the distinction between their forms—is present. Alternatively, if the cognition of the entity were to apprehend only a single form, then the entity would not possess a dual nature, but would be merely a part.
Now, it might be thought:
"The definition of difference consists in the diversity of the forms of cognitions and the state of not being identical with one another.

In that regard, particulars such as cows and the like are apprehended by cognitions of diverse forms and are not identical with one another; however, this is not the case for the universal and the particular, because they are perceived as being identical with one another even though there is a diversity in the forms of their cognitions."
Even so, because the universal and the particular lack the characteristic of difference, they do not possess a dual nature, as has been stated regarding the case of parts.
If it should be thought:
The non-differentiation of form within cognition and the mutual realization of their own nature are the two characteristics of non-difference.
In that regard, on account of the non-differentiation of form, there is oneness of the part; however, because both are realized as having each other's nature, they are [one].
But for particulars, there is neither a lack of distinction in the form of cognition nor a mutual realization of each other's nature; therefore, they are distinct.

Even so, when there is a characteristic of non-difference consisting in the mutual realization of each other's nature, and when the characteristic of difference—which would entail the absence of both—is non-existent, there can be no dual nature.
Furthermore, it is not logical for a single non-difference to have two distinct characteristics;
for it is the non-difference of characteristics that establishes non-difference, while their difference establishes difference.
If reality exists despite a difference in characteristics, or if otherness exists despite a lack of difference in characteristics, then the characteristic itself would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, if there were no distinction between the universal and the particular, [the characteristic would likewise be purposeless].
Otherwise, another cognition would be rendered useless, as if it were merely one part [of the same cognition].
If you argue that its purposefulness arises from its diversity, then why is it not likewise useless due to its unity? (1.23)
The very occurrence of a distinct cognition [of the universal] refutes the identity of the universal and the particular as a single entity.
For that [distinct cognition] is meaningful—just as in the case of particulars—only when there is plurality, because it involves the apprehension of what was previously unapprehended.

But if there were unity, then just as no distinct cognition different from those already apprehended by their own respective cognitions is sought for the division between the universal and the particular, so too no distinct cognition different from the cognition of the universal would be required for the apprehension of the particular.
Likewise, a particular cognition does not lead to the apprehension of the universal.
Now, if it is argued that there is no absolute non-distinction between the universal and the particular, but rather there is indeed distinction,
then [it follows that] meaningfulness [of words] arises from that distinction.
That is incorrect.
Even so, why is it that meaningfulness follows from distinction just as difference does, whereas meaninglessness— like being a single part— does not follow from non-distinction?

For when difference and non-difference are equal, why should this be the case—that there is no apprehension by a single cognition due to difference, while there is apprehension due to non-difference, such that a further cognition would be redundant? Furthermore, it is established by nature that in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect; this is the general rule (*autsargika*).
Its exception (*apavāda*) is that when the cause is present, the effect is present.
In that case, since there is a causal relationship within non-difference, it is logical that both are apprehended by a single cognition alone.
It cannot be said that, despite their oneness, there is no cause for the apprehension of either one.
Even if it were somehow claimed that such a cause does not exist;
Nevertheless, there is still [the following]: because of oneness, the state of being an effect would arise from that which has the state of being a cause, since that [oneness] is the cause;
however, non-existence is not the cause of non-existence.
But the non-existence of the effect is established by its own nature. Its existence as an effect, which is dependent upon a cause, is what is negated.
And that cause exists, for now, in both cases.
Non-existence, however, is useless because it lacks causality.
Furthermore:
For the universal is not the essence of the thing, nor is the particular; rather, it is manifold.
Because that [universal] lacks continuity, this doctrine of particulars is merely another way of speaking through different words.

For one for whom a single entity possesses both natures, neither the universal alone nor the particular alone constitutes the essence of that entity; for if it were merely one or the other, it would follow that there is a difference between entities.
Therefore, the variegated nature of an entity consists of both forms combined.
Furthermore, there is no persistence of the variegated [entity] elsewhere;
and that which does persist is not of the nature of a real entity.
Thus, by resorting to another term, it is demonstrated that differences alone are real, or else, by means of another word or reason, that a single thing is dual-natured.
Because that which follows [the object] lacks the nature of a real entity, it is merely an object of conceptual construction.
This might be argued: "Let it not be a real entity; however, its being a part of that [object] is not denied."
