Otherwise, even conceptual construction would not exist without a seed.
But what, then, is this so-called "aspect"?
It is certainly not the thing-in-itself.
It has been stated that if a thing were of the nature of the *tanmātras* alone, there would be the consequence of its being differentiated.
Nor is the thing itself something other than a thing, for that would entail the consequence of three distinct entities: the universal, the particular, and the possessor thereof.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the thing itself is not a thing, nor is it something other than a thing.
By process of elimination, it is an object of conceptual construction, indefinable as either identical to or different from reality.
Now, an "aspect" (aṃśa) is neither an entity distinct from the possessor of aspects (aṃśin), nor is it that very same thing, because in either case the possessor would lack parts;
nor is it a non-entity, for the very same reason.
For a sky-flower does not become a part of anything. In that case, if a part were to follow [the whole], it would be the entity itself that follows, because of its non-difference from it.
This is not sound.
Is it not the case that the entity itself lacks persistence because another part does not persist?
Furthermore, its very lack of persistence follows from its being composed of a collection, since it would cease to exist even upon the absence of a single [part]. To illustrate:
Alternatively, the real entity (*vastu*) consists of either the universal and the particular in mutual dependence, or their collection.
In both cases, because the particular would be non-existent as a distinct object, there would be no persistence of the real entity.
If each were a real entity independently, then a single entity could not possess a dual nature; thus, it is well said:
Because there is no continuity [between them], this is a doctrine of difference, such as "this is a different word" and so forth;
or else, because all entities are non-different from that reality, one might resort to a doctrine of non-difference by means of another mode of speech. (1.25)
Alternatively, if the reality is followed through the persistence of its constituent parts, there is the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda).

For instance—a cow is a cow by its own nature; yet, through the persistence of the forms of existence, substance, and so forth, it is a cow, and through the persistence of the entity "horse," it is a horse.
Thus, in this way, there is both a cow and a horse.
Even the horse, by virtue of its conformity with the nature of the cow through its persistence in the form of existent substance and so forth, is a cow.
Therefore, in this manner, even the horse is both a horse and a cow.

Thus, it has been stated in another manner of expression that the world is non-dual (*advaita*), because all things are non-different from one another by virtue of their being that [very thing] or being other than that.
True; yet duality (*dvaita*) also exists, since there is non-difference through their being that [thing] or being other than that.
This is not sound.

If a cow were also a horse, and a horse were also a cow, how could there be any difference between them? [The phrase] "a cow and a horse" would likewise be a designation of distinction that is entirely without basis.

For this [distinction] is possible only when the difference between a cow and a horse is established. However, if each of them were individually both a cow and a horse, there would be no difference, and thus that [distinction] would be entirely without foundation.
[Objection: But surely, the establishment of their otherness follows from the exclusion of their specific parts.

And thus, the world consists of both duality and non-duality. Now, if difference is established through the exclusion of specific qualities, is there no conformity with another entity because an object possesses both forms? For instance, the entity that is a horse is not the entity that is a cow.

Now, if there is such a persistence [of identity], does a horse also become a cow? In that case, regarding the former alternative, it has been stated that this is the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*), because the entity lacks continuity and that which persists is not a real entity.
Now, if even upon the exclusion of specific differences that entity persists, then the horse would indeed be the cow.
How, then, can the existence of otherness be established? If this is your view—
The category of "cow" applies both to what follows [the definition] and what does not follow it;
thus, a horse is a cow,
whereas a cow is simply a cow.
For in that case, the entity "cow" (govastu) indeed exists;
from this, the establishment of its difference [from others] follows.

Now, how is the entity "cow" to be described? Is it that which is necessarily a cow, or is it that which is not necessarily so? In the former alternative, there is no persistence of the entity, and thus the entities would be non-continuous (ananvita).

In the second case, because one entity is concomitant with another entity, there is non-duality (*advaita*). However, since that entity which establishes this thing as "cow" rather than "horse" through a particular characteristic (*viśeṣa*) is not concomitant with those possessing that particular characteristic, there is the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*).

Now, if one does not rely on a particular characteristic due to the fault of non-concomitance, there is the doctrine of non-difference (*abhedavāda*); thus, the conceptualization of both duality and non-duality is untenable.
By this [definition], the viewpoints (nayas) that take substance and mode as their objects are refuted;
for even among those, there is either only the substance-viewpoint or only the mode-viewpoint. (1.26)

And those who hold that substance— such as clay, gold, and so forth— is eternal; and that its modifications, such as jars, earrings, and the like, which are called "particulars," are subject to disappearance and appearance, yet are non-different [from the substance].
And these [ornaments] are not merely the substance itself, because that [substance] possesses persistence;
nor do they deviate from it absolutely, because they are not perceived as distinct.
This is because the cognition occurs precisely of the substance in the form of the necklace and so forth.
Thus, an entity consists of both substance and mode (*dravyaparyāya*).

For if it were substance alone, then in the production of a necklace (*rucaka*) through the destruction of a bowl (*vardhamānaka*), nothing would have been produced or destroyed; consequently, joy and grief would not arise for those desiring [the respective objects].
On the other hand, if it were merely mode, one seeking gold would not remain indifferent.

For if it were merely a modification (*paryāya*), then since gold would perish along with its modification, how could there be neutrality (*madhyasthatā*) upon the destruction of that modification, or how could there be arising? Therefore, because a real entity (*vastu*) consists of both substance (*dravya*) and modification, the occurrence of arising, persistence, and destruction is possible within a single locus. Thus, they hold that neutrality belongs to the persistence of the substantial form, while joy and sorrow are accounted for by the arising and destruction of the two modifications respectively. That doctrine is also refuted by this very same method.
For instance— even if those [categories] were to inhere in one thing through another thing, they would be mere substance (*dravyamātra*) due to the absence of parts.

Alternatively, if the substance does not inhere [in the categories], because a thing consists of both substance and mode (*paryāya*), and because one mode does not persist in another mode, then things would be non-inherent and of an exclusive nature (*vyāvṛttasvabhāva*).

Since that of which persistence is postulated is merely a succession of states, being devoid of substantial reality (avastutva) in its mere form, it is nothing more than a conceptual construct (paryāya).
For only that which is stable is called a substance (dravya);
and yet, there exists no single entity whatsoever that is thus stable.
However, the conceptualization of a portion extracted from a real entity as having an independent status is merely a construction;
for the real entity is manifold, whereas that [extracted portion] does not exist in such a way.
Moreover, because arising, abiding, and destruction are co-present in a single entity, it would follow that joy, indifference, and sorrow would occur simultaneously; yet this is impossible. (1.27)

For one for whom modes are indeed distinct from the substance—the following systematic arrangement is possible: for one who seeks only the substance, there is neutrality because the substance neither perishes nor arises anew; for one who seeks the necklace (*rucaka*), there is joy because that [necklace] arises anew; and for one who seeks the bowl (*vardhamānaka*), there is sorrow because that [bowl] perishes.

But for one [who holds] that the substance is not other than its modes, nor the modes other than the substance—for such a person, when origination, persistence, and destruction are inherent in a single locus, there would be either neutrality on the part of one who seeks the substance, or there would not;
joy and sorrow would both occur, or neither would occur.
For that substance does not simply persist; rather, it perishes and something new arises.
In that case, because of destruction and the arising of what was previously non-existent, joy and sorrow would occur, and not neutrality;
and neutrality would have to arise from persistence—
thus a logical impossibility would result.
Likewise, for one desiring a *vardhamānaka* [vase], there would be grief due to its destruction;
yet it would not occur, because [the substance] persists.
And there would be joy due to the production of that new [form].
And it could not come to be, because of the persistence of the very same [entity] from before;
furthermore, there would be grief due to its destruction.
Now, if it is argued that there is also difference, then this fault does not apply.
Why does it not follow that there is also non-difference? Or, if there is no absolute non-difference, then there is no confusion [of categories].
But if there is no absolute non-difference, then even the established distinction [between categories] is not tenable.
Furthermore, for one who accepts non-absolutism (anekānta) everywhere and nothing whatsoever as being exclusively so, how can this specific distinction be stated?
"There is no absolute non-difference, and thus there is no confusion;
likewise,
there is no absolute [identity] of all entities from every perspective."
For this entire world everywhere has reached a state where there is neither engagement nor cessation. 1.28.
For when things are indeterminate in every respect, that being the case—

this world would not engage in action after determining that a certain means leads to a desired end, since it is not always exactly so; nor would it desist from action, since it is not always otherwise.
Likewise, he would not turn away from the cause of suffering, nor would he remain exactly as he is;
yet he would not fail to turn away, since he is not otherwise— thus, alas, he would fall into a miserable state.
Alternatively, regarding what was said—
that it is difficult to establish whether joy, indifference, and sorrow would or would not exist— in response to that, they might say:
Since all things are non-exclusive in every respect, what difficulty is there? For instance, joy, indifference, and sorrow do not exist exclusively, nor do they not exist exclusively.
To this, it is replied:
"Not exclusively so for all things.
For if the existence or non-existence of pleasure and the like were not indeterminate—
if it were not the case that one seeking pleasure would not engage in the means for achieving pleasure because pleasure already exists— then [the objection would hold].

Nor would it be the case that [the world] does not engage [in activity], because of the non-existence of that [desire for pleasure]. Likewise, one who seeks the cessation of suffering would not avoid contact with the means of suffering, because of the non-existence of that [suffering];
nor would it be the case that he does not avoid it, because of its existence.
"Alas! The entire universe has thus fallen into a state of neither engagement nor cessation.
[70,i] Thus, first of all, there are not two entities, nor is there one entity possessing a dual nature.
In this regard, two alternatives remain:
either difference is real and the conceptualization of non-difference is based upon it,
or non-difference is real and the conceptualization of difference is based upon it.
In this regard:
Since difference is relative, it is preceded by the apprehension of difference;
one does not perceive a single cognition as one, nor does one perceive difference, for that would entail the loss of reality. (1.29)
[70,ii] There is no conceptualization of non-difference based upon difference.
Why? Because difference is relative; it cannot be apprehended without depending on something else.
Furthermore, a difference that is not apprehended cannot serve as the material cause for the conceptual construction of non-difference.
Moreover, its apprehension is untenable if it is dependent upon another,
because the two distinct entities do not stand defined until their difference has been apprehended.
Furthermore, it has been explained previously that there can be no apprehension of difference without the establishment of a distinction between self and other.
Likewise, the apprehension of non-difference does not depend upon the apprehension of non-difference,
nor does it depend upon the apprehension of difference, for that would entail the loss of non-difference itself.
For when difference is apprehended, there is no room for non-difference.

In that case, having apprehended non-difference and taking it as a basis, the postulation of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is tenable only when one is unable to ascertain that [non-difference] correctly—just as one might postulate a division of parts in pots and the like which are grasped by a single cognition.
It is not the case that, in that instance, one postulates non-difference by taking difference as a basis.
For difference resides in atoms,
and they are beyond the reach of the senses.
But is it not the case that even unity is to be determined by a synthetic cognition?
And that [synthesis] does not exist without difference;
for if there were no contact with difference, what would be synthesized by what?
This has already been answered.
In that case, an object could not be one when its place and time are not distinct.
And if there were no single entity, upon what basis could there be a suspicion of difference, such that through the synthesis of which "oneness" is asserted?
Moreover, this is to be personally realized by everyone: that diversity has non-difference as its substrate.
For it is thus:
"The mere object is first perceived by a cognition arising from the initial encounter."
To claim that even a difference manifests without being conceptualized is an extreme act of temerity.

The first non-conceptual perception has as its object the mere thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*). It is known by everyone through their own experience that the subsequent conceptual cognitions, being preceded by that [perception], do not grasp specific particulars (*viśeṣa*).
This might be so—
Perception apprehends only that which possesses a specific form.
However, because that distinction is untouched by verbal expression, it is not perceived in the same way as it is in conceptual cognition.
This is incorrect, because it involves a contradiction.

Furthermore, it is a contradiction to claim that no distinction is perceived in perceptual cognition while a particularity nonetheless shines forth; therefore, this is stated with great temerity. As for one who disputes the very nature of consciousness, asserting that perception is a clear manifestation excluded from everything that is not the self—the following is the reply to him:
"It is said that perception is the means of establishing [an object]," and so forth; this has already been stated.
Furthermore:
And consciousness is established as having the mere object as its support;
however, even in the case of sensory cognitions, there is a lack of establishment with respect to particularities. (1.31)

Since two distinct entities cannot logically exist together and it is impossible for a single entity to possess a dual nature, one of the two must necessarily be considered false. It is logical that it is the appearance of the specific quality that is false, as this is observed in cases of error such as the perception of silver [where there is only mother-of-pearl].

It is not the case, however, that the appearance of the mere object is false; for nowhere is a deviation from the mere object ever seen in cognition, since at the very least, that object itself must appear.

The postulation of that [invalidity] is simpler for one who has already observed its occurrence, because the capacity [for invalidity] is already established, whereas in the other case it would have to be postulated.
This might be argued:
"Only mental cognitions possess the established capacity for falsity, not those born of the senses."
And [the claim] that these distinctions are to be apprehended by the intellect through the sense faculties is merely a rumor;
for errors follow from specific defects of the sense faculties.
Furthermore, as for the opinion that entities have excluded intrinsic natures (vyāvṛtta-svalakṣaṇa):
Therefore, those [entities] must be explained as having the nature of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), or as being qualified by it;
otherwise, the word "excluded" (*vyāvṛtta*) would not possess any meaning, because its basis is mutual non-existence.
In that regard:

It is not tenable for all things to consist of mutual non-existence; rather, they should be perceived as distinct only with respect to their limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and not by way of their intrinsic nature (rūpa). 1.32.
When one thing exists independently, another is established as having the nature of its absence.
However, all things cannot be conceived as having the nature of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), because that would involve a state of mutual dependence.
Alternatively, mutual non-existence may be considered a qualifier.
Granted, even though they do not have that as their essence, let them be understood in such a way due to the coloring by the qualifiers;
however, there would be no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
But surely, there is no such thing as "mutual non-existence" (*anyonyābhāva*) which could be either the reality or the qualifier of entities; this is merely a matter of establishing the object.
If there were no such thing as mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), then non-difference would be established.
Furthermore, it can be inferred that because the universe possesses the nature of difference, this difference must have non-difference as its substrate.
For indeed, a distinction [of the face] is seen in jewels, swords, mirrors, and so forth, even though the material cause—the face—is undivided.
Yet, there is no production of a separate entity (*bhāvāntara*) therein, because that would involve a contradictory transformation (*viruddhapariṇāma*).
This might be argued:
Non-difference, too, can be inferred as being based on difference, since the non-difference of a forest is based on the difference between its trees.
No; for that would entail the absence of all difference.
For in this way, not even a single atom would be non-different.

For even that non-difference would have difference as its substrate, like a forest and so forth; likewise, the non-difference of its parts would also [require further substrates], leading to an infinite regress.

Since in such an infinite regress no single entity exists, there could be no non-difference consisting of their synthesis. Alternatively, if it were to rest somewhere, that [resting point] would be the one [ultimate entity].
Thus, there is no deviation [in the rule] that non-difference does not depend upon difference;
this is stated as follows:
"Just as in the case of the reflection of a face in a mirror and so forth, difference has non-difference as its basis."
Non-difference based on difference does not exist in that way, because of the absence of such [difference]. (1.33)
Moreover,
because each is individually permeated by falsity, they are considered non-different from it.
Just as there is a distinction among waves, so too is there a distinction [of the moon] due to the distinction of its parts. // 1.34 //
Because each individual thing in the universe is permeated by non-difference, their difference is false—just as in the case of the moon reflected in the waves of water.

For there, although there is a distinction between each individual reflection, there is an underlying continuity of non-difference in that "this is the moon"; likewise, even though the universe is diverse, there is an underlying continuity of non-difference in each instance as "this," "that," "object," or "entity."
Although the individual tree is not false, the inclusive cognition "forest" does not apply to each one individually;
for there is no cognition of "forest" with respect to each individual tree.
Therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule] by that example.
And it is for this reason that "each one" was stated.
Furthermore—
Let there be the majesty of a single entity alone, which appears as if manifold; for this is more parsimonious than the view that distinct entities appear as if non-distinct. (1.35)
First, this proponent of difference (bhedavādī) must be asked:

how is it that there is an appearance of non-difference and a continuous linguistic usage (*anuvṛttavyavahāra*) with respect to particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that are mutually excluded? If [you say] it is due to similarity (*sādṛśya*), that is untenable in the case of things that are absolutely unconnected.
Or if [you say] it is because the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not perceived—
"For who is able to grasp the exclusion of color in the case of gunja berries, young sprouts, and so forth?"—
this is incorrect.
For that which has a nature distinct [from others], if it were not apprehended, there would be no apprehension at all.
If it is argued that this is because there is a difference in essence between determinate cognition (*niścaya*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*), such that there is no determination [by the latter],
that is incorrect, because we observe the practical application (*vyavahāra*) of both forms.
For instance, in the case of Kālākṣī, both the linguistic usage based on the universal "cowness" and the exclusion from other cows are observed;
and that [usage] is not possible unless there is an ascertainment of the exclusion from other cows.

"Now, [it might be argued that] because they perform the same purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*), there is a similarity due to the exclusion of what does not perform that action (*atatkriyāvyāvṛtti*).
This too is incorrect; for since purposeful actions themselves differ, it is impossible for the exclusion of what does not perform those actions to be identical.
There is no single purposeful action to be accomplished by another such that the exclusion of what does not perform it would be the same.

Furthermore, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities is not uniform because of the differences between individual things. If, on the other hand, they lack an intrinsic nature, how could their exclusions be uniform? If it is argued that [the cognition] is based on beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and does not depend on specific features residing in the objects, that too is incorrect, because of the necessity [of such dependence].
For indeed, in only certain individuals does a certain appearance of non-difference occur; this would not be tenable if it were based solely upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, one must postulate that by their very nature some entities are fit for the apprehension of non-difference with respect to something, while others are not—that is, entities possess specific capacities contrary to [the assumption of] a uniform nature.
This being so, such a postulation avoids the excessive complexity [of the alternative].
Let the greatness belong to the one alone, in that even the one appears as many, for this is a simpler conceptualization;
but it is not the case that distinct things possess such an excellence of capacity that they appear as non-distinct.

And the conventional usage of difference, just as it appears, is established for those who maintain difference; likewise, the conventional usage of non-difference is established [for us], just as it appears.
For instance—for those who maintain absolute difference—the conventional usage of non-difference is according to appearance, not according to the actual state of things.

Even for those who maintain the theory of inherence (*saṃsarga*), since the universal as an object is distinct from its particulars, the linguistic usage of non-difference regarding particulars occurs exactly according to how they appear.

As for those who maintain that [the universal] is not a distinct entity, since the reality is variegated (*śabala*) and that [variegation] lacks persistence (*ananvaya*), the dual usage [of both difference and non-difference] occurs exactly according to how it appears;
it has been demonstrated that this [usage] does not follow the actual nature of the thing.
Just as outsiders explain the establishment of conventional usage according to its persistence and according to its appearance,
so too do those who possess the discernment of the Vedānta speak regarding the application of the convention of difference. (1.36)
Thus ends the section on reasoning (*tarkakāṇḍa*) in the *Brahmasiddhi* composed by the venerable Maṇḍanamiśra.
[The Section on Injunction (*niyogakāṇḍa*) begins.]

Thus, because it would contradict perception and other means of knowledge, as well as conflict with the injunctions regarding ritual action, those who maintain that the Vedāntas possess only a figurative meaning when their literal sense is accepted—against them this effort has been directed for the sake of awakening them.
Now, however, [it is argued]:
the authority of the Veda pertains only to that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*), not to that which already exists (*bhūtarūpa*).
For it has been stated thus:
"Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*).
This means that the meaning of the Veda is to be known through the authority of injunctions.
And *codanā* is an injunction that prompts action; therefore, the Veda is an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding matters that are to be accomplished.
Even the Vedāntas, however, being authoritative with respect to the duty of realization, convey knowledge of the reality of the Self—which is subordinate to that [duty]—by means of that [duty];
thus, they too do not transcend the state of being grounded in what is to be accomplished.

And thus, having raised the objection as to how the ritual injunctions (*mantra*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), along with the Upaniṣads, can be authoritative, it was stated: "For an injunction [makes known] what has been, what is being, and so forth.
What is meant by this is that the injunction itself, while making known a purposeful action (*kārya*), also makes known such matters as what has already come to be (*bhūta*).
For those who hold such views, an effort is made to awaken them. There are three modes of realization regarding Brahman:

first, that which arises from the Word (Śabda); second, that which follows from having realized it through the Word and consists of a continuous flow of meditation, contemplation, and worship—terms denoted by words such as *dhyāna*, *bhāvanā*, and *upāsanā*; and third, that which, having attained perfection from the former, is free from all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and takes the form of direct intuition (*sākṣātkaraṇa*).
Regarding this, it is said with reference to the first [type of knowledge]: "The self-knowledge that arises from words and so forth is not something to be enjoined;
for it occurs spontaneously in one who has studied the Veda, just like the understanding of ritual action. (2.1)

[74,ii] Since Brahman has a nature that cannot be apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the knowledge whose object is his nature as apprehended through verbal testimony must be enjoined.
In that regard, the knowledge derived from the word itself is not subject to injunction, because it occurs even without an injunction, just like the comprehension of a ritual action (*karman*).

Just as the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" arises solely from the authority of that sentence itself and does not depend on another injunction, so too the realization of the Self arises independently of an injunction through the authority of the sentence that declares the nature of the Self. This is because, when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists, the cognition of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) arises by its very power. Indeed, when the complete means of valid cognition is present along with its auxiliary factors, even a person's desire is not required for the arising of knowledge; this is because one may have cognitions of things that are undesirable, let alone the case of an injunction. [75,i]
He demonstrates that very same independence of injunction regarding the comprehension of ritual action:

"In this cognition—'One desiring heaven should sacrifice'—no other injunction is required, because that would lead to an infinite regress; nor is this [injunction] required for the establishment of the ritual action. (2.2)

In the engagement resulting from the knowledge of the meaning of an injunction regarding ritual action (*karma-vidhi*), no other injunction is required, nor one that is contained within that very injunction.

This is because, if another were required, there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā-doṣa*), since yet another injunction would have to be required even for the knowledge of that [second] meaning; and because an injunction contained within the first lacks the capacity to enjoin the understanding of that [meaning], as its object is the ritual action itself.

Now, just as another injunction is required for their acquisition—namely, "One's own Veda should be studied"—and yet there is no infinite regress, so it would be in the case of understanding their meaning as well.
And there exists an injunction:
"The entire Veda is to be mastered."
This is an unequal comparison—

for even though one has not yet begun the study of the injunction for Vedic recitation (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), one proceeds to study that injunction as well as other sentences based on what has been studied by another person, just as one incorporates the subsidiaries belonging to other recensional branches (*śākhā*) through mere hearing. Indeed, it is not only the sentence one has studied oneself that prompts one to action.
As it is with one person, so it is with other persons as well; because [the Veda] is beginningless, its study is also like that of the Veda itself.
However, an injunction for understanding does not impel one toward understanding when the meaning has not been understood.
If the comprehension of that meaning were dependent upon an injunction, the injunction itself would not impel one toward it, because the meaning remains uncomprehended.

There would be a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): activity proceeds from the understanding of that meaning, and the understanding of that meaning occurs for one who has engaged in activity. Therefore, another injunction would have to be required, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Nor is the injunction "the entire Veda is to be mastered" an injunction for a previously unknown purpose (*apūrvārthavidhi*). Rather, the fact that "its purpose is seen to be the comprehension of ritual action" is merely pointed out as a matter established by reason.

Even if this were an injunction, and even if the knowledge of meaning—which is already implied by the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayanavidhi*)—were not [already] stated, nevertheless, no separate injunction is required for the cognition arising from Vedic sentences that declare the nature of Brahman, just as in the case of the sentences containing injunctions for ritual action.

Just as in the case of the general injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," once it is established, nothing else is required, because that would lead to an infinite regress, since even when an injunction exists, something else might still be required; and this [requirement for another injunction] does not apply here, because [the former injunction] has action as its object. Likewise, in sentences intended for the realization of reality (*tattva*), an injunction need not be expected, because the awakening to reality arises from the very power of the sentence itself.
Furthermore:

"The result [is known] from the understanding of what is to be enjoined, and the subsequent activity arises from the injunction; because of this mutual dependence, this is not a verbal cognition, and for us, it is not the ultimate [cognition]. (2.3)

The purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*) is that activity which follows from understanding what is to be done through the word; it is not, however, the very understanding of what is to be done that arises from the word itself, because of mutual dependence—since activity occurs once the meaning of the word is understood, and understanding occurs for one who has engaged in activity. Alternatively, if the understanding of the word’s meaning were to arise from the understanding of the word’s meaning itself, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
However, mutual dependence has been stated because both [alternatives] are equally untenable.

As for the realization of reality that arises from a sentence whose ultimate purpose is the realization of reality, this is not something subsequent to the cognition of the word's meaning; rather, it is that very cognition itself.

Moreover, once awakening has arisen, one is no longer to be prompted [to act], much less so when there is no awakening through a word; therefore, when certainty is not attained from that [word], one seeks it from another. (2.4)

If it is argued that the realization of the reality of the Self arises from the statement beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" and ending with "That thou art," because the words possess mutually connected meanings—then what further could an injunction accomplish? For one who has already engaged [in the inquiry] is not something to be incited to act. Alternatively, if the arising of the realization of reality does not occur merely from the mutual connection of the word-meanings, then he is all the more not to be incited to act, because the verbal realization of reality would be impossible [otherwise].
It might be argued:
"Even when the manifestation of reality has arisen from verbal testimony, one must be impelled toward certainty [thinking], 'It is thus.
That is not so.
If the certainty arises from that word itself, then it has already arisen [from the word].

On the other hand, if the certainty arises from something else, then the desire for another thing constitutes a dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); in that case, the word would not be the basis for the ascertainment of reality.
Thus, in the first place, an injunction is not required for the sake of ascertaining reality.
[76,iii] Now, if a positive injunction is sought in order to exclude the possibility that the meaning is unintended,
then when it is said "the meaning is to be known," it would follow that what is to be known is not something unintended. (2.5)

[77,i] Furthermore, it is held that even if there is a comprehension of meaning from a sentence, its intended purport (*tātparya*) is difficult to establish, because a statement whose primary object is an already existing fact would be purposeless.
Alternatively, there may be a state of doubt, because even a lack of intended meaning is observed in the case of *japa* mantras.
However, when an injunction (*vidhi*) exists, since the knowledge of the meaning is enjoined, the meaning cannot be unintended.
Therefore, an injunction must be sought in order to ensure that the meaning is intended.

[77, ii] That words in both worldly and Vedic usage are directed toward their referents is established, because there is the general rule: "But the meaning of a sentence is not distinct [from its parts]. (2.6)
The subordinate status of words with respect to their meaning is the general rule.
However, in common worldly usage, there is an exception where, due to other causes, the word's own form becomes primary and its meaning is not intended to be expressed.
The same applies in the Veda as well, because the capacity of words is understood through worldly usage.
As it has been said:
"But the meaning of the sentence is not distinct [from the meanings of its parts].
Moreover, the fact that the injunction for Vedic study has a perceptible purpose is not altered here; otherwise, the entire meaning of that injunction would be rendered unintended. (2.7)

Just as in the case of ritual injunctions, where it is said, "For its purpose is seen to be the understanding of the ritual," one does not postulate a different fruit from the study of those [injunctions] whose meaning is not intended to be expressed, so too it is with the Vedāntas, because the understanding of the reality of the Self is directly perceived. Nor will it be argued that there is futility in the comprehension of an existing reality; for this is equally true in the case of an injunction regarding comprehension.
And this must necessarily be understood in this way;
otherwise, together with the injunctive [word], the entire [text] would lack the intended meaning.
For while the intended meaning of other [words] is based upon the injunctive word, there is no such basis for the injunctive word itself.
And thus, if that [injunction] were to have its meaning unintended, the others would likewise be so.
Now, if the injunctive [word] is inherently intent upon the meaning because its purpose is seen [in the world], then the others would also be so; in that case, this injunction would be redundant.
An injunction is desired for the sake of establishing that knowledge is a human goal;
however, the claim that the status of being a human goal resides everywhere in the injunction itself is also unseemly. (2.8)

The understanding that the realization of the self is a means to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) depends upon an injunction; thus, even for the realization of the nature of the self—which arises from the words [of scripture]—the comprehension that it is a means to the human goal is due to an injunction.
This too is not tenable, because there is no fruit other than the knowledge itself, since [that knowledge] completely pervades the object to be known.
If it is claimed that liberation is something to be attained, it is not so, because it would entail a deviation from reality. // 2.9 //
For the visible fruit of knowledge is indeed the pervasion of the object of knowledge by the knower, that is, its manifestation toward the knower.
But that which is unseen and occurs at a later time—that for the sake of which an injunction would exist—is not [perceived].
This might be argued: liberation is also accepted as another fruit of the knowledge of the self.
That is not so, because it is not something that can be produced.
This liberation is not produced by causes, for that would entail a deviation from reality;
if it were an effect, it would be subject to destruction, and consequently, there would be a return to saṃsāra.
And the absolute cessation of *saṃsāra* is called liberation (*mokṣa*).
Now, one might object: "But even destruction, being an effect, does not perish.

True; however, this is said with reference to liberation as a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*) characterized by unsurpassed bliss and unsurpassed sovereignty, because there is an invariable concomitance between the destruction of an effect and the destruction of its positive substrate.
It is simply untenable that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*)—which is the absence of the future conjunction of body, sense organs, and intellect—should be an effect.

Although the cessation of the cause of bondage is indeed an effect, even as an effect it does not entail the consequence of being non-eternal; nevertheless, since this cessation is not distinct from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it is not something to be accomplished by that [knowledge].
For ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of bondage, and its cessation occurs at the very moment the knowledge of reality arises.
Alternatively, it is stated that liberation is abiding in one's own nature, as in the passage: "Having attained the supreme light, he remains in his own nature.
And if it were something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there could be no such abiding in one's own nature.
Therefore, one would fall away from the state of liberation.

As for the argument that even liberation as an effect must be eternal because of the authority of the Vedic scripture stating, "He does not return," one might resort to such a view— even though it contradicts what is observed— if there is no other way to account for the scripture.

But when, for one who perceives the non-dual, pure luminosity of the Self as the reality of the Self, ignorance has been completely uprooted, then—since bondage can no longer occur due to the absence of its cause—the Śruti merely restates an already attained fact through a statement in the present tense as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). In that case, how could there be an infinite fruit based on its authority? For instance, from the very fact of the statement being in the present tense, it is not understood that "non-return" is something yet to be accomplished;
nor is there any connection with a desire (*kāma*) from which such a state of being an end to be achieved (*sādhya*) might be inferred.
Therefore, it is an explanatory passage (arthavāda).

Furthermore, even the postulation of a fruit based on an explanatory passage is untenable, because knowledge is already satisfied by its directly perceived fruit, which is the manifestation of the reality of the object to be known.
And its status as a human goal will be explained later.
Others, however, say:
"Without a prescription, it is devoid of purposeful action; it merely restates an already existing fact."
And a statement would be a mere restatement when its object is within the scope of another means of valid cognition. (2.10)
Its validity transcends dependence on other means of knowledge; it is established in the sense of an injunction, which is not the object of other means of knowledge. (2.11)
Like injunctive sentences regarding ritual action, it attains the status of a means of valid cognition independently;
even in the absence of another's activity, that injunction exists solely for the sake of its own validity. (2.12)
Without an injunction (*vidhi*), there is no cognition of an instruction regarding what is to be done (*kārya*).

A thing as it exists is understood to be merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that which is already so. And since a restatement has as its object another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), a statement concerning an existing fact (*bhūtārtha*) is said to depend upon that [other means of knowledge]; thus, because of this dependence, it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*).

However, because the meaning of an injunction (*vidhyartha*) is not the object of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), a statement whose content is that [injunction] is an independent authority (*anapekṣa-pramāṇa*), just like a scriptural injunction regarding ritual action (*karmavidhi*).
Furthermore, the meaning of an injunction is not the object of any other means of valid cognition;
for there is no comprehension of it from anything other than the verbal cognition of the word "do" (*kuru*).

This being the case, although in a statement intended for the realization of reality (*tattva*), there is no activity subsequent to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning and thus no fruit of an injunction (*vidhi*),
nevertheless, for the sake of its authoritative status (*prāmāṇya*), it must be accepted as having an injunction as its ultimate purpose.
To this it is replied:
Is the state of being a restatement (anuvāda) due to the fact that its object has been established by another means of valid cognition, or is it because its object is already existent?
For even a statement whose object is an established fact [could be considered such]. (2.13)

It does not make that [object] known by way of having its object already obtained through another means of knowledge; nor is it dependent upon that [other means]. If this is what is intended by "reiteration" (anuvāda), [then our position stands]. (2.14)

What, then, is *anuvāda* (reiteration)? Is it the state of having a meaning not distinct from another cognition (*adhigama*), that is, the demonstration that [the object] has been apprehended by another means of knowledge (*māna*); or is it merely the fact of having an existent object (*bhūtārthatā*)? In the first alternative, let that which has a meaning not distinct from another cognition be dependent (*sāpekṣa*).

However, that which makes known even an existent object as not having been apprehended by another means of knowledge is not an *anuvāda*, nor is it dependent, because there is no comprehension [of it] through contact with a prior apprehension.
[79,ii] Now, another alternative:
if the fact that the object is established is pure, what is the cause for its being dependent?
The intermingling with another means of valid cognition is the cause for its dependence upon that [other]. (2.15)

In the case of the Veda, there is no lack of authority even regarding matters of fact (*bhūtārtha*), provided its origin is not untrustworthy. If it were merely a restatement of a matter of fact, it would be a mere *anuvāda*; however, being a restatement is not the cause for its dependence on other means of knowledge.
Indeed, the state of being a matter of fact itself is not the cause for dependence, because even perception and inference, though they concern matters of fact, are independent.

Therefore, whether the object is real or unreal, contact with another cognition is the cause for dependence upon another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because this is observed in the case of memory. For memory has as its object a thing mixed with another cognition; thus it depends upon the means that produced it. And in this way, a statement originating from human intellect—whether its object be real or unreal—is dependent [on other means].

For from that [human testimony], the cognition arises only with respect to an object already mixed [with the speaker's intention], and not independently with respect to the object itself without regard for what was previously apprehended.
As it has been said:
"Moreover, from a human statement, the cognition arises as 'this person knows it thus,' and not as 'the object is thus.'"

Because it does not originate from human intellect, even regarding matters of fact (*bhūtārtha*), there is no cause for dependence in the words of the Veda; for the confusion of prior cognitions is caused by connection with a person.
[80,i] This might be argued:

Even in the case of a non-human (apauruṣeya) scripture concerning a real object, there is dependence upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because such other means of valid cognition are possible regarding that object.
For instance, when another means of valid cognition is possible regarding that object, even the possibility of its contradiction [with the scripture] might be suspected.
Therefore, for the sake of its non-contradiction, corroboration by that [other means of knowledge] must be required.
However, when the object is of a nature that cannot possibly exist, there can be no suspicion of contradiction from any source; thus, nothing needs to be required.
To this, it is replied:
Nor can dependence on that [cause] be conceived merely by virtue of its possibility. // 2.16 //
For in that case, if those two were mutually dependent, no distinction between them could be perceived.

Since both can have the same object, why is it that the word is dependent on that [other means of knowledge], whereas that other means of knowledge would not be dependent on the word? If it is argued that in common worldly usage a word is seen to have an object already apprehended by another means of knowledge, then its authority is all the more impossible when the object lies outside the scope of that other means of knowledge.

For while it might be possible [for a word] to refer to the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because another means of valid cognition is available there, it would be difficult to achieve elsewhere due to the absence of such a means.

Now, if the fact that worldly speech has its objects already apprehended by other means of valid cognition were caused by its being of human origin, rather than by the inherent capacity of the word itself,
then the capacity of the word would belong only to an object that is not mixed with other means of valid cognition.

In that case, it is not only verbal testimony (*śabda*) that is dependent because of the possibility of other means of valid cognition; that [other means] too would be dependent on verbal testimony because of the possibility of verbal testimony therein. What follows from its being dependent? It would be non-authoritative (*apramāṇa*).
It is not logical for verbal testimony to be dependent on that.
For if that [perception] were authoritative, its correspondence or non-correspondence with [the object] would have to be taken into account.
However, since the word lacks authority, that [perception] is not authoritative by dependence on the word;
rather, it is indeed authoritative because it is independent.
Why is verbal testimony (śabda) not a means of valid cognition? Because it depends upon other means of valid cognition.

And the validity of that [other means] depends on its independence; yet the independence of verbal testimony [is said to follow from its] invalidity—thus there is a circular argument (itaretarāśraya).

For if verbal testimony were a means of valid cognition, then with respect to its object, that [other means] would also be dependent, just as verbal testimony is dependent when that [other means] is possible, since there is no distinction between them.
Now, even if sound occurs, it is not dependent on that;
and even if that occurs, sound does not possess dependence, because there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Moreover, in this way, perception and inference function with respect to each other's domains. (2.17)

It would follow that there is no distinction [between them] in their mutual dependence; for even a sense organ would be dependent upon another sense organ when it has the object of another sense organ as its domain. (2.18)

If dependence were based merely on the possibility [of another means of knowledge], then since perception and inference can both occur with respect to a single object, they would be mutually dependent, which would result in the undesirable consequence of their lacking validity.

Likewise, in the case of existence (*sattā*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and substance (*dravya*), which are perceptible by multiple sense organs, it would follow that each sense organ depends upon the other sense organs.
Now, if you claim that dependence applies only to verbal testimony when other means of knowledge are possible, then a specific reason must be stated.
If it is argued that this is because we observe that the object has already been apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), the answer to this has already been stated:

if this were a property of verbal testimony alone, then due to the impossibility [of novelty], there would result a lack of authority for perception and other means regarding that object, just as in the case of the statements of the Buddha and others. However, if such possibility exists, then authority is appropriate regarding the objects of the senses, just like the words of a trustworthy person.
As it has been said:
“If that [statement] comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object of the senses, it is indeed non-false.
Now, this dependence applies to human-authored dharma; it does not apply to the authorless (apauruṣeya) word, even when its subject matter is accessible through other means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, some inferences have objects already apprehended through perception; thus, the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) does not depend on perception in the same way that perception depends on it. For example, perception regarding the discrimination of musical notes such as *ṣaḍja* is preceded by scripture (*āgama*), yet not all perception is like that. Likewise, even if human words are seen to have objects already apprehended by other means of knowledge, this does not mean that the non-human [Vedic word]—which has a real object—is likewise [dependent]. Otherwise, since no other means of knowledge would be possible, its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) would follow even more strictly, as has been stated.
Moreover,
because the application of medicines and the like is impossible [in the case of the Veda],
it would follow that worldly [action] is independent [of human agency], whereas [Vedic action] is preceded by human cognition. (2.19)

In that case, there is an application [of the word] and thus a mutual dependence; however, in the Vedic context, even that [application] is not preceded by human intention, and therefore it is said to be independent. (2.20)

If the Vedic statements that are intent upon the *kārya* (the task to be performed)—because no other means of knowledge is possible regarding the meaning of an injunction (*niyoga*)—possess independence (*anapekṣatva*), then even worldly statements such as "One desiring freedom from fever should drink this medicine" or "One desiring heaven should eat sand," which are likewise intent upon a *kārya*, would attain validity as independent authorities. Now, if it is argued that the relationship between the end and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) in those cases is preceded by human intention, and therefore they possess dependence (*sāpekṣatā*), whereas in the Veda even the relationship between the end and the means is not preceded by human intention, and thus [the Veda] possesses independence; [we reply: ...
Alternatively, the relationship between the object, the person to be directed, and the injunction in worldly speech is constructed by human intellect;
however, in the Veda, there is only the injunction, which is not preceded by human intellect. This too constitutes its independence.
It is said:
"In this case, the very fact that it is preceded by human intellect is the basis for its dependence;
for even when other means of knowledge are impossible, there is dependence upon them in that regard. (2.21)

If it is argued that even in a sentence whose content is not established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is a state of dependence due to its connection with a person, then the very fact of being preceded by human intellect is the cause for requiring another means of knowledge, as demonstrated by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*):
because in common worldly usage, such a sentence is dependent when that [human intellect] is present, whereas in the Veda, it is independent when that [human intellect] is absent.
It is not the case that another means of knowledge is possible regarding the object itself; for even in the absence of such a means, we observe dependence in worldly injunctions.
[82,i] Now,
it might be thought:
"In the Veda, there is a focus on injunction (niyoga) and a predominance of application (viniyoga)."
There is no dependence on the Veda regarding the world, yet there is dependence on that [world] regarding the Veda. (2.22)
Vedic speech culminates in an injunction (*niyoga*), and since that is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is independent (*anapekṣatva*).

Mundane speech, however, is centered on the relationship between a goal and its means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), and since that is an object of other means of valid cognition, it is dependent (*sāpekṣatā*).
Such a distinction in the capacity of words is not merely a matter of verbal expression.
A word whose capacity is understood from common worldly usage is also expressive in the Veda. (2.23)
This is not yet a differentiation of the expressive power of the mere word— whether it is independent of or dependent upon a human agent—

in which "niyoga" (an injunction) is the meaning of the word in one case and "viniyoga" (an application) in another, as is the case with the word *go* signifying that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, and the word *aśva* signifying that which possesses a mane and so forth.
Since its capacity is understood through worldly usage even when it functions as a communicator in the Veda—

if the meaning of a word is its application in the world, then its capacity is apprehended precisely there, not in the *niyoga* (injunction). Therefore, even in the Veda, the meaning established by the authority [of the word] would be only its application.

Now, when a person, having known [the object] through another means of knowledge, employs speech regarding that object, then that [speech] is based upon it; the other, however, stands otherwise. (2.24)
[83,i] Now, it might be thought: this is not a differentiation of the capacity of the mere word itself.
For the inherent capacity of a word consists precisely in its culminating in an action;
for thus it is—
the meaning of an injunction (niyoga) is that which is to be accomplished.
Furthermore, the connection [of other elements] is perceived for the sake of another action,
but the connection of the action itself is not for the sake of anything else.
Therefore, because it is an action to be performed (*kārya*), the injunction (*niyoga*) has that [action] as its primary object.
A person, however, employs speech regarding an object that is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
yet, an injunction (*niyoga*) is not within the scope of another means of valid cognition.
Therefore, it is not fit to be employed therein.
However, because the application (*viniyoga*) exists in that manner, its employment there is appropriate.
Therefore, human speech has application as its primary concern;
whereas Vedic [speech], because the mandate (*niyoga*) is to be accomplished through capacity (*sāmarthya*), has that mandate as its primary concern.
To this it is replied:
Because it depends upon other means of knowledge, it is possible that there may be another means of valid cognition [for its establishment].
Indeed, this is its own domain; therefore, it has no dependence on other means of valid cognition.

If it is assumed that human speech has the status of being an object of application because a person employs words regarding an object already apprehended—since it depends upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—then its object is one for which another means of valid cognition is possible.

However, human speech is not dependent simply because its object is one for which another means of valid cognition is possible; rather, it is the nature of such an object that is the cause of its dependence.

Therefore, having ascertained [the truth] through another means of knowledge, a person employs speech in order to communicate it to another; it is not for no reason that he speaks of that [object]. (2.26)
The integration with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara-saṃbheda*) arises from dependence, not from possibility.

A person’s speech is for the purpose of making known their own apprehension; therefore, there is an integration with another means of valid cognition in that speech, in the sense that "this object was apprehended by me."
Therefore, in that case, one must rely solely on the possibility or impossibility of perception.

Where there is certainty regarding perception—namely, "its perception is possible, and he does not speak of what is imperceptible"—therein lies authority, as in the case of a trustworthy person regarding an object of valid cognition.

However, where perception is impossible, as in the case of the words of the Buddha and others concerning perceived objects, or where there is even the possibility of speech being uttered despite the object being imperceptible, there is no authority.
However, because other means of valid cognition are possible, there is no dependence on them even in the case of human speech.
Therefore, both the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatā*) and indeed the state of having a human author (*pauruṣeyatva*) [are relevant]. //2.27//
Since the causes for independence and dependence have been described by the wise, even that which refers to an existing fact is dependent; therefore, it does not arise from human intellect. (2.28)

For this very reason, the experts in logic have pointed out that being human-authored (*pauruṣeya*) and not being human-authored (*apauruṣeya*) are the causes of dependence and independence [of a means of knowledge], and they have demonstrated this through the effort to refute human authorship in the statement:
"But the relation of a word with its meaning is innate" (*autpattikas tu śabdasyārthena saṃbandhaḥ*).

Since the relation between word and meaning is innate, the word does not originate from human intellect due to its lack of autonomy; thus, the comprehension of meaning from a word is not conflated with other means of knowledge, and it is therefore independent.
[84,i] But is it not true that an effort has already been made— even though other means of valid cognition are impossible— by the statement: "When there is contact with the existent"?
True;
this is for the sake of establishing the restriction that "injunction alone is the means of valid cognition, and nothing else."
But it is not the case that it is *pramāṇa* alone.

Now, even if other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were possible, if the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is not undermined, what is the purpose of rejecting those other means of valid cognition? It is for the sake of the knowledge of the true nature of *dharma*.

For if other means of valid cognition were possible, then even the Dharma taught by those such as the Buddha—who are considered omniscient—might be apprehended; in that case, the true nature of Dharma would not be definitively determined.
This effort [of the Mīmāṃsaka] is for the sake of such a determination. It is for that purpose that the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is sought, not for the sake of some unseen result.

Alternatively, there would be a sublation of the injunction due to its contradiction by that [perception], or there would be doubt if they were of equal strength; therefore, the impossibility of that [injunction] is established.
It is not, however, because of the possibility of that [perception] that [the injunction] is dependent.
But surely, the absence of that [perception] would have to be depended upon?
Granted; however, a word does not convey its meaning by depending on another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
For that which conveys an object does not itself depend [on such a means].
That which is required does not establish that [object].
For the absence of a contradictory means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not a cause for comprehension.
Moreover, if invalidity were to arise from the mere possibility of contradiction, then even perception and the other [means of knowledge] would be subject to it.

Moreover, even if [the Veda] were restricted to action (*kāryaniṣṭha*), its lack of authority would be unavoidable due to the possibility of contradiction; for it is accepted that the cognition of an existing entity (*bhūtārtha*) occurs by way of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*). In that case, however, there is the possibility of contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), because an existing entity is the object of other means of valid cognition; therefore, [the Veda] is described as being restricted to action.
If it were indeed the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, being a restatement (*anuvāda*), it would convey its meaning by depending on that other means of valid cognition—
thinking "this has been apprehended by another means of valid cognition"— and not independently.

But in the case of its independence regarding the accomplishment of an action, it does not depend on other means of knowledge because that [action] is not within the scope of other means of knowledge.
Since there is no dependence in the manner described, it is well said: "Even though it concerns an existing fact, it is not dependent; therefore, it is not born of human intellect.

Now, since our categories of existence are by nature associated with one another, what need is there for an action? Even that [action] is easily found everywhere in roots such as *as* ("to be") and so forth. (2.29)
[85,i] If it is thought that there is no connection between the meanings of nouns without the meaning of a verb;
For action (*kriyā*) is the cause of the connection between word-meanings; in its absence, there would be a state of expectancy.

Therefore, established entities such as Brahman and the like are not within the scope of words, because a single word does not produce cognition when its conventional relation (*saṃgati*) is unknown. Nor are they the meaning of a sentence, because the meaning of a sentence consists of a relational synthesis (*saṃsarga*).
Furthermore, since word-meanings devoid of action do not enter into relation with one another,
let action be admitted in this way; and by means of that action, let the establishment of the relation between word-meanings be desired.
There is no purpose whatsoever for an injunction here;

moreover, that action is everywhere easily available even when not explicitly heard, such as the verb "to be" (*asti*), according to the principle: "The verb *as* (to be), in the third person singular, is understood even when not employed. In this context, a sentence whose primary aim is the realization of the nature of Brahman has its finality in the meaning of "is."
The connection between categories (*padārtha*) therein is based on that [Being]. And since Being is by its very nature primarily existent, the establishment of the qualified entity occurs through it.
On this point, they say:
there is no such thing as existence other than being cognizable by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For it is thus:
Regarding that which is apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the worldly convention "it exists," and in its opposite, "it does not exist.
Indeed, no other cause for the distinction between existence and non-existence is observed.
If it is argued that this distinction consists in the presence or absence of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*):
Nor does it depend on the presence or absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for those two;
for instance, if the conventional usage of "existent" with respect to an effect were itself dependent upon another effect, there would be an infinite regress.
Therefore, even at the end, the linguistic usage of "existent" (sat) arises solely from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the linguistic usage of "non-existent" (asat) from its opposite.
If this is so, then let the linguistic usages of existent and non-existent be based, right from the beginning, on the presence or absence of a means of valid cognition.

And thus, a sentence whose referent is the meaning of the verb "to be" (*asti*) makes its object known only by depending on another means of valid cognition, because being an object of a means of valid cognition is the very meaning of "existence."
To this it is replied:
An object is not considered to be such merely because it is cognizable by a means of valid cognition (*māna*).
For it is from pride alone that the notion arises: "I existed" and "I shall exist. // 2.30 //

For this [cognition] would occur regarding fire and so forth when they are inferred by means of smoke and the like; otherwise, it would differ at a later time, for it certainly does not arise in three ways. (2.31)
The meaning [of "exists"] is not the state of being cognizable by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is it the object of the cognition "it exists.
For it is from the means of valid cognition itself that three kinds of cognition arise:
"there is fire here because of smoke," "it has rained because of a particular swelling of the river," and "it will rain because of a particular rising of clouds."

In this regard, if cognition takes as its object the state of being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇaviṣayatā*), it would exist only when [the object] has already been cognized (*pramita*), not from the valid cognition itself. For prior to the arising of the valid cognition, there is no connection with a valid cognition;
yet this cognition is dependent upon that very connection with a valid cognition.
Now, if out of impudence one were to assert that this [cognition] belongs only to a subsequent time,
then the threefold division [of objects] would be untenable, because there is no difference in the relation to the means of valid cognition even with respect to objects existing at different times.
Even though a means of knowledge apprehends an object as being related to itself, it does not thereby become divided; nor, in this way, does it depend upon anything else. (2.32)
[86,ii] Now, it might be thought: an object is apprehended by a means of valid cognition precisely as being related to a self.

Therefore, even for the cognition "it exists," which has as its object a connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no posteriority [in time], because the object is perceived precisely through its connection with its own self.
Even so, the cognition "it exists" would occur in all cases;
there would not be a threefold division [of time], because the connection with a means of valid cognition is present at the moment of every cognition.

And in this case, there is no dependence upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in a statement whose object is an existent thing (*astyartha*), because the very connection with that means of valid cognition constitutes its being an existent thing. Alternatively, it might be maintained that its being cognizable by another measure is threefold by way of an inferential mark (*liṅga*).
If it is argued that the inferential mark (liṅga) might also be dependent [on something else], because its own establishment arises from that very same thing; 2.33.
If that lack of dependence is not prevented by punishments in the Veda,
then the following might be thought:

It is precisely the state of being cognizable through another means of valid cognition that is apprehended by means of an inferential mark (*liṅga*); therefore, there is no subsequentness [of the inference].
And since that means of valid cognition pertains to the three times, it is of three kinds.

What, then, is that? It is perception (*pratyakṣa*). For instance: when a vision has occurred, for someone it is a past perception; when it will occur, it is a future [perception]; and when the fire is present, it is a present [perception].
And this is untenable, because that [perception] does not exist in the case of what is eternally inferential.
Moreover, the inferential mark (liṅga) itself would likewise be non-authoritative due to its dependence on another means of knowledge.
If it is argued that there is independence because the existence of another means of knowledge is established from the inferential mark alone;
For instance: it is precisely when another means of valid cognition exists that the inferential mark (liṅga) is a means of valid cognition;
and in that case, nothing else is required.
The establishment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) occurs through the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This rule is not prohibited by a staff in the Veda;
even a Vedic statement that is focused on an object is authoritative only when there exists a means of valid cognition for that specific object.
In that regard, it is independent;
and the establishment of the qualified object occurs through the door of that means of valid cognition— this is the same.
Its occurrence [is] in the case of an inferential object (or a non-worldly object), like the meaning of the Buddha’s words, but not otherwise. // 2.34 //
In this regard, [the position] is inconsistent because it posits direct perception as the means [of knowledge].
It might be thought:
"The validity of the inferential mark (liṅga) is thus appropriate, because with respect to its object, another means of knowledge is possible."
For in the case of rain and such things, other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are possible; therefore, the comprehension of the object occurs through them.
However, this is not admitted in the case of Brahman, which transcends all particularities and is based solely upon the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*).

In this regard, just as the words of the Buddha and others—such as "this person knows thus"—do not possess authority regarding an object beyond the senses because knowledge of such supersensible matters is impossible for those whose cognition is restricted to [empirical] objects, so it would be here as well.

However, like the speech of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) concerning an object accessible to possible means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), validity is appropriate for an inferential mark (*liṅga*) even when its basis is a means of valid cognition.
That is incorrect, because even with respect to Brahman, direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) is admitted upon the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
But for those possessed of ignorance, it is said that its sole basis is the traditional scripture (āmnāya).
Moreover:
If being an object of cognition were itself existence, then how could there be a threefold nature of the means of knowledge?
Therefore, on account of that connection, a threefold nature of the object is not possible.

Furthermore, if a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is itself measured by an inferential mark (*liṅga*), and if being-measured is itself existence (*sattā*), then because it is being measured, every means of valid cognition is indeed existent.
And what exists is said to be present (*vartamāna*).
In that regard, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists with respect to every object, there would simply be "it exists.
There is no threefold nature of objects based on the threefold nature of the means of valid cognition, because that which is being measured is existent, and what is existent is present.
Furthermore, this person should be asked:

is existence (*sattā*) the connection with a present means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and non-existence (*asattā*) its opposite; or is it merely the connection with a means of valid cognition, independent of any specific time? In this regard: "Existence is the connection with a present cognition; non-existence is its opposite. (2.36)
If, in that case, non-existence were obtained regarding the object of memory, then there would be no connection with a present means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which is being remembered.
[Objection: But surely, because destruction is possible in the case of what is being remembered, the conventional usage "it exists" does not occur at all.
True.
Even "it does not exist" does not exist.

If existence (*sattā*) is the connection with a presently functioning means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then its opposite is non-existence (*asattā*); thus there would only be "it does not exist," and not "it exists."
Therefore, existence and non-existence are distinct from that;
if existence were merely the application of a means of valid cognition, then non-existence would be its opposite. (2.37)
The retention of honey is achieved by means of a jar that has been measured and then lost;
once it has been measured, there can be no further desire to know its existence or non-existence. (2.38)

If existence were merely the connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yoga*) without depending on a specific time, then even an object that has perished after being cognized would be "existent," and it would follow that it could perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*) just like an unperished object, because there is no difference in their existence. If you argue that this is not so because there is a distinction between the perished and the unperished, then that very distinction must be the cause for establishing the linguistic conventions of "existent" and "non-existent," just as it is the cause for the establishment of effects; it cannot be the connection with a means of valid cognition. Indeed, it is observed in the world that these conventions follow precisely that [distinction].
Indeed, the world does not metaphorically designate as "existent" that which has been cognized and then perished.

Furthermore, ordinary people would not seek to know whether an object already cognized is existent or non-existent, because its existence is already established by the mere occurrence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because existence is defined precisely by that connection with a means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, [the opponent's definition of existence as] "fitness for being an object of valid cognition" is unsatisfactory: it is lost in the case of what has perished, it fails to apply to what has not yet arisen, and it is unstable when applied to that which is being remembered. (2.39)
Now, it might be thought:
existence is not the connection with a present means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), nor is it merely that connection independent of time.
Rather, it is the capacity with respect to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And since that [capacity] has perished and fallen away, there is no consequence of its [the object's] existence.
However, in the case of something being remembered, because it has fallen away from some [means of cognition] but not from others, there is no non-existence of everything.
This too is not correct, because it results in the abandonment of what has been accepted.
For in this way, existence (sattā) is described as being nothing other than the very nature of the object.

Existence (*sattā*) is the nature of an object that is capable of being apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
