The distinction between the linguistic usage of "existent" and "non-existent" is based solely on the nature of the object itself, not on the adventitious condition (*upādhi*) of the presence or absence of a means of valid cognition. However, this [mention of the means of cognition] is merely a method of explaining it; there is no actual contact with the means of cognition. Just as when it is stated, "An object capable of producing a cognition with a blue form is blue," the word "blue" does not have the cognition of blue as its adventitious condition, so too, when that [object] is denoted by the word "exists," the sentence is grounded in the nature of the object or has the meaning of existence as its primary focus. How, then, could there be dependence [on other factors], given that there is no contact with the means of valid cognition?
It might be argued as follows:

let it be that the distinct intrinsic natures of objects alone are fit for the means of valid cognition and are denoted by the word "existent," rather than there being a single, unitary existence (*sattā*).
Let it not be so; this is not what is to be proven.
In every respect, the word "exists" (asti), which denotes the intrinsic nature of an object, does not have its cause in the application of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
For if there were contact with a means of valid cognition, there would be dependence [on something else].
But multiplicity does not entail any fault.

Moreover, if it were multiple, how could there be the application of a single, undifferentiated term? For instance, a single word would apply either by relying on a non-differentiated qualifier or indicator (*viśeṣaṇa* or *upalakṣaṇa*) among distinct things, or it would be a common term based on different causes, like the word "akṣa" [which refers to various objects].

In that regard, commonality cannot first be established with respect to things whose natures consist of infinite objects, because of the necessity of grasping a relationship [between word and meaning].
For words such as "eye" and so forth must either have limited universals (*jāti*) as their objects, or be characterized by limited indicators.
This might be argued:
"The word 'sat' (existent) is common to those objects characterized by the three generalities—substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth.
This is not so;
for whoever denies existence (*sattā*) necessarily denies substantiality and the others as well.
Indeed, for one who has seen fire, there is no tactile perception of it in water.
Moreover, universals, particulars, and inherence also truly exist;
the word "existent" applied to them is not figurative, because the cognition [of them] is not different [from that of other real entities].
Furthermore, there can be no metaphorical usage (upacāra) without a commonality (sāmānya).
Or, if such a commonality exists, that very thing is the referent of the word "existent" (sat);
and that itself is "being" (sattā), because the cognition [of them] is identical.
Now, it may be thought: in all philosophical systems, all categories of things are subsumed under certain limited properties;
thus, even for infinite objects characterized by those [properties], the common term "existent" (sat) applies.
That is incorrect;
for a collection does not exist without [at least] one member.

In that case, if the collection were by way of being the referent of the word "existent" (*sat*), such that it were said, "The referent of the word 'existent' has this many divisions," then there would be no exclusion of other objects.
In that case, there would be no inclusion of all objects; just as when it is said, "The meaning of the word 'cow' is ninefold," this does not imply the non-existence of other things.
Consequently, there would be no comprehension of the true nature of objects from various doctrines.
Now, it may be argued that the meaningfulness of these doctrines is not what needs to be proven.

We do not say that the meaningfulness of these various doctrines is what is to be proven. Rather, the proponents of these doctrines accept some single nature of an object, which serves as the basis for this collection of subdivisions such as "five" or "six.
For, without a single inclusive entity, there could be no application of intermediate numbers.

Now, if it is argued that "existence" consists in being fit for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇayogya*) or possessing causal efficacy (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), and that the referent of the word *sat* (existent) is indicated by these two alone—whether as fitness for a means of valid cognition or as causal efficacy—then the mention of specific, limited properties is redundant.
In that case, there would be only a general term, not a term with a common [specific] application.

Furthermore, if the grounds were distinct, as in the case of words such as "eye" (*akṣa*) and so forth, there would be doubt due to the difference in their grounds, rather than a cognition of a specific [referent].
For indeed, when encountering the various qualifiers such as "the pot exists," cognizers do not entertain doubt.
Just as the cognition "the cloth is white" is free from further expectancy, so too is the cognition "the pot exists.
As for the doubt as to whether [the object] is a substance, a quality, an action, form, or consciousness, that does not occur among ordinary people.
Ordinary people, however, perceive the sign as being undifferentiated.
Furthermore, the doubt arises from the meaning, not from the word. Why? Because the hearer’s sense of expectancy is satisfied even without the cognition of any distinction.

For where there is doubt due to the capacity of the object—as in the case of the command "Let the tree be cut," regarding tools such as an axe or a hatchet—there is a lack of expectancy even when the specific [tool] has not been perceived, because one may employ any of them; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress.
But where [the doubt arises] from the word itself, there is indeed expectancy in the absence of a cause for perceiving the specific [object].
Thus, a common term does not have multiple causes [for its application].

Even a single qualifier would have to be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). And it has already been stated that this is untenable even prior to the arising of a cognition permeated by the word "existent" (sat), as explained at length in the passage beginning: "Since cognition [arises] from a means of valid cognition alone."

Moreover, even from the effect, it is only the occurrence [of the cause] that is determined as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that case, how could there be a qualification by that [effect]?
For an object does not become qualified unless its qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is present.

Furthermore, when the absence of a qualifier has been ascertained, there can be no doubt permeated by the expression of the qualified object, just as there is no doubt such as "Is he a staff-bearer or not? once the absence of the staff is certain.
Yet, in cases such as empty cities where treasures have long been buried, even when the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is certain, a doubt arises as to whether they exist or not.
Therefore, an existent object is something other than that which is connected with a means of valid cognition; it is in regard to such an object that this doubt occurs.

Nor is "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) a defining characteristic (upalakṣaṇa). For in the case of things that have been cognized and subsequently destroyed, the word "existent" (sat) is not employed; and in the case of what is being remembered, there arises doubt permeated by the word "existent. If existence were merely due to being characterized by a means of valid cognition, then for that which has already entered into a relation with a means of valid cognition, there would be only existence—neither non-existence nor doubt.

Furthermore, for one who qualifies or characterizes the meaning of the word "existent" by means of causal efficiency (arthakriyā), there would be no application of the word "existent" prior to the observation of that effect.

Now, if one were to say that the very production of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) constitutes purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*), then the cognition "it exists" would not arise from the means of valid cognition itself.
Or, if it is held that this [cognition] is conceptual and occurs subsequent to the means of valid cognition, then it could not arise from a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Furthermore, if it is argued that the object is simply followed by the logical mark as something whose relationship with its effect is already known, then in that case, there would be no object of cognition (*prameya*).
For instance— the meaning of "existence" (asti-artha) is indeed "having an effect" (kāryavattā), and that [existence] has already been apprehended.
To claim that "having an effect" is understood solely through "having an effect" is logically untenable.
Furthermore, because cause and effect cannot exist simultaneously, a specific qualification (viśiṣṭatā) is untenable.
If it is argued that [the qualification] is merely an indicator (upalakṣaṇa), then it would follow that even a past thing exists.
Moreover, it has already been stated that there could be no doubt regarding something that is being remembered.

Therefore, just as the referent of words such as "blue" is the intrinsic nature of the object (*arthasvabhāva*), and is not characterized by its effect nor characterized by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— because that would lead to an infinite regress—
but rather its own form is established and determined according to the means of valid cognition;
so too it is logical that the intrinsic nature of the existent object is likewise [established].

For if the distinction between the conventional usage of "existent" and "non-existent" were based on the presence or absence of a causal means of valid cognition (*kāryapramāṇa*), then that very distinction would never function; for it would follow that the distinction between the usage of "existent" and "non-existent" regarding the causal means of valid cognition itself would also be dependent upon that same [further] means, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, the knowers of Brahman maintain that existence is the singular intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the object.
Now, it might be thought: "Capability is not the intrinsic nature of the object, but rather the existence of the causes of valid cognition;
and for non-existent things, the causes of valid cognition do not exist."
That is incorrect—
for that which is buried in the earth, devoid of characteristics, incapable of being known, lacking a perceiver, and having transcended all such fitness [to be perceived]. (2.40)

Regarding an object that has been buried in the earth, which lacks connection with the senses, is not perceived as invariably concomitant [with its cause], and whose existence cannot otherwise be conceived except through its non-perception, and whose observer has vanished—there exist for it no grounds for cognition such as perception, inference, presumption, or scripture.
For analogy (*upamāna*) has similarity as its domain; thus, it is utterly remote from being a ground for such an object.
It transcends the capacity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), yet it is not non-existent.
But how can there even be existence (*sattva*) for this [subject]? Even so, there would be doubt.

In that case, if existence were defined as the fitness characterized by being the cause of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then since the absence of the cause of a means of valid cognition would be certain, there could be no doubt.

Alternatively, if existence were some specific nature that is fit for a means of valid cognition, it has been stated that this is unsatisfactory because it abandons the original subject matter (*prakṛtahāna*).
Alternatively, this [passage] refutes the view that the referent of the word "existent" (sat) is that which is qualified by being an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For it is not reasonable for there to be a doubt permeated by a word expressing a qualified entity when the absence of that qualifier has been ascertained.
Moreover, since even non-existence (abhāva) is an object of cognition (prameya), being fit for a means of valid cognition is not the defining characteristic of existence. For instance:
"In this way, he establishes that which is non-existent as an object of cognition."
For it is immeasurable; why then is it thus and not otherwise? // 2.41 //

Indeed, by one who desires the distinction between the categories of the existent and the non-existent, the non-existent must necessarily be established in some way; otherwise, there would be a confusion of linguistic and practical conventions (*vyavahāra*).
In that regard, whether it be the objectless state of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or the absence of all causal capacity, such is the object of the cognition of the non-existent.
In every respect, it is thus an object of knowledge (*prameya*).

For if it is undetermined by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being such, why should it be of that nature and not otherwise? If there is no operation of a means of valid cognition regarding its being thus or not thus, for what reason is there an attachment to one side?
Furthermore—

How can a foot be placed down without first ascertaining the absence of thorns? For its presence [would be known] either through another apprehension or by the consequence of its being already present before. (2.42)
If inquiry (*jijñāsā*) were not to proceed due to the absence of cognition,
how could one set foot upon a spot purified by inspection (*dṛṣṭipūtaṃ padaṃ nyaset*) when the absence of insects, thorns, and so forth has not been ascertained? For instance,

that [setting of the foot] would occur either through the determination of the ground and other objects distinct from the insects and thorns, or through the non-determination of the insects and so forth, or through the determination of their absence.
In this regard, it cannot be [the case] first through the determination of another object, because that would lead to the undesirable consequence [of perception] even when thorns and the like exist;

for even in those cases, there exists the determination of some other entity. Furthermore, it would follow [that perception occurs] even prior to the determination of the specific spot on the ground, since the determination of some other entity whatsoever is already present.
Furthermore, because [an object] such as an insect or a thorn cannot be definitively determined, there would be no desire to know its existence or non-existence.
Even through an effort preceded by such a desire to know, one obtains only the mere non-determination of it, for the non-existence of which [non-existence] is not an object of cognition (*prameya*).
And that [non-determination] existed even prior to that [effort].
However, an inquiry is appropriate for the sake of ascertaining non-existence only when there is an object of cognition that is non-existent;
nor is mere non-determination itself the object of inquiry, because it is established by its very nature. For it is by means of determination that such non-determination is removed.
And because it is immeasurable, that non-existence as well is indeed immeasurable.
Now, if it is thought:
Activity [occurs] because there is no determination of the object of a means of valid cognition even when the conditions for perception are present;
that is incorrect—for here, the status of being an object of a means of valid cognition is seen to be of no utility. (2.43)
For [the object] is indeed employed in the cognition of what is non-existent by way of being the non-other cause;

if activity occurs due to non-discrimination, then there is no utility in the object being the domain of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because non-discrimination is equally present in the other case as well, and from that [non-discrimination alone], activity arises.

For one whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the object of cognition, activity proceeds from the discrimination of that [nature]; thus, its status as the domain of a *pramāṇa* is useful by virtue of being the non-other cause for that [activity].
This non-apprehension is not caused by a deficiency in the reason while the object itself exists, because its causes are complete;
therefore, it is due to the absence of the object.
Now, wherever there might be activity, in that case [it belongs] to pure consciousness alone. // 2.44 //

If one does not desire absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) as the subtle object of consciousness, then that [isolation] is not accepted as the sole object, since it exists even when mixed with form. (2.45)
And for that which is already distinguished, there can be no further qualifier other than the absence of anything else.
If it is thought:

"In a particular location on the ground or elsewhere, activity characterized by the placing of feet and so forth occurs; that [activity] arises from knowledge regarding that [location] in its mere state."
In this regard, it must be deliberated:
is this "isolation" (*kaivalya*) intended for cognition—the restriction to a single object and non-connection with other objects—or rather for the object?

If it were for cognition, then even when a gross portion of the earth or the like has been cognized, there would be no investigation into the presence or absence of subtle things such as insects or thorns.
It would indeed proceed from the cognition that apprehends the bare ground alone.
Now, regarding the object itself, it must be considered there as well: is the isolation of the object by its own nature, or through its connection with a qualifier?
In this regard, it cannot be by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), because that [nature] exists even when [the object] is mixed with others.

Rather, activity characterized by placing a footstep and so forth occurs through the delimitation (*pariccheda*) qualified by the absence of insects, thorns, and the like, which is attained through connection with qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa-yoga*).
For no qualifier is observed to be of a different kind from the absence of other things, such that the thing qualified by it would become isolated (*kevala*).
[93,ii] To what object would the cognition and the conventional expression "it does not exist" refer? // 2.46 //
If the absence of the means of knowledge (*māna*) has been refuted, what then remains of the absence of the object of knowledge (*meyābhāva*)?
Furthermore, by this [absence], the object of the cognition and the word "it does not exist" must be expressed;
yet that cannot be in the form of a real entity (*vastusvarūpa*), because it would then follow [absurdly] even in the case of a mixture.
It has been stated that this is not only because there is no other qualifier, but also because of the absence [of such a thing].
Now, one might object: the meaning of "it does not exist" is "this is not cognized by valid means of knowledge," and not that non-existence itself is apprehended.
This is contradictory—

"It does not exist" and "it is cognized"—if this is so, then the absence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) would have been stated as the object of the cognition and the word "it does not exist. In that case, what fault would there be in the absence of the object of cognition (*prameyābhāva*), such that one should bypass it and state the absence of the means of valid cognition as the object? For there is no difference whatsoever between the two in terms of being indefinable (*nirupākhyatva*).
Now, it might be thought:
"In the absence of apprehension, the delusion of apprehending what is non-existent is the error consisting in the conventional usage of non-existence. (2.47)

And since conventional usage is not observed in the case of non-existence—just as one does not perceive darkness in the absence of light—the cognition and the linguistic convention "it does not exist" would simply not occur. How can these two, which are perceived by all people, be denied? It is said in reply:
This is an error consisting in the determination of the opposite in the absence of the cognition of existence;

likewise, it is an error consisting in the conventional usage of the opposite in the absence of the conventional usage of existence, just as there is the delusion "I see darkness" in the absence of the perception of light.
For there is no such thing as "darkness" that is actually visible.
This is not the essence:
in this way, there would be the delusion of perceiving the non-existence of the three worlds during deep sleep and so forth. (2.48)
For one who does not discern anything at all, an error is not possible;
for one who does not perceive the object of superimposition and the thing superimposed cannot experience the delusion that it is silver. (2.49)
That which is conventionally designated as "non-existence" is not distinct from existence; and that [non-existence] resides in the domain of cognition.
The perception of darkness is merely the shadow of the earth or the absence of light. (2.50)
An error of perception does not occur unless one has previously seen [the object].

Indeed, if an error consisting in the perception of something contrary could arise even in the absence of seeing, then there would be an error of perceiving the non-existence of the entire universe during states such as deep sleep, just as there is an error regarding the non-perception of light.
Furthermore, there can be no error for one who does not discern anything at all.

For instance— one who does not grasp through cognition both the object of superimposition (the thing present before one) and the thing to be superimposed (silver) does not become possessed of the error of silver.
[The causes of such error are] misapprehension, memory, or the apprehension of a common property.

Furthermore, the absence of cognition is not the object of knowledge, nor is the absence of linguistic usage; neither is there an awareness of absence, nor a linguistic usage of absence, because an absence, being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), cannot be an object of knowledge.
In that case, since neither of the two objects to be superimposed is apprehended, it is not a false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
Having accepted existence as fitness for being a means of valid cognition, the absence of defects is stated: "Or let existence be fitness for a means of knowledge, and let that be cognized. (2.51)
When that [scripture] is measured, the reality of the thing exists within the scope of the scripture;
nor is there dependence upon it, because there is no internal division of meaning therein. (2.52)
Even those who do not assert that existence (*sattā*) is something distinct [from the object] may maintain:
"Let existence be the fitness for being an instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatā*); let that very thing be the object of cognition (*prameya*)."
That object of cognition, which is the reality of the thing itself, is the meaning of the scripture.
Nor is there the fault of dependence on other means of valid cognition, because there is no admixture with other means of valid cognition;
for what is understood is merely that [the object] is "capable of being engaged by a means of valid cognition."
For instance—

even those who maintain that existence is the fitness for being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatā*), and not something distinct from it— they do not admit any contact with an internal object here.
For if there were such contact, another means of valid cognition would have to be sought.

How is it that [the object] need not be sought? When a statement culminates in the fitness for being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-yogyatā*) and does not itself bring about the awareness of the existence of a specific object, then whatever means of valid cognition is suitable for that specific object must necessarily be relied upon. For what purpose is it relied upon? For the sake of attaining the realization of the existence of the specific entity. But what is the existence of a specific entity? It is its fitness for being a means of valid cognition.

In that case, it is indeed already understood that it exists, because the word "is" (asti) culminates in the meaning of existence; for being capable of being apprehended by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-yogyatā) is the very meaning of "is.
He shows that even when the integration with another means of valid cognition is admitted, there is no fault of resulting in invalidity:
Our word is not a means of valid cognition whose object is distinct from the objects of other means of valid cognition.
In this context, however, this object has been cognized by me independently;
yet it is dependent upon the mere object [of cognition], because the comprehension of the object depends on something else. (2.54)

However, even if an object is not sublated, if there is a contradiction regarding the aspect of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it becomes non-authoritative in that regard—just as, for example, the words of the Buddha or an untrustworthy person [are non-authoritative] when they contradict the means of valid cognition. (2.55)

Furthermore, the word of a reliable person (āptavākya) is not sublated regarding its object nor regarding its status as a means of valid cognition; it is independent with respect to its status as a means of valid cognition. Otherwise, how could worldly practice proceed? (2.56)
Then, through the state of being the speaker, it is free from differentiation;
it is the self-awareness in which the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge has dissolved. (2.57)

Let the Vedāntas proclaim that which is not established by any other means of knowledge; for the object [of their teaching] will be established as already proven, just like the words of a human being. (2.58)

[96,i] Indeed, it is not the case that a statement whose object is already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not itself a means of valid cognition; for the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*) is indeed a means of valid cognition.
If it is asked, "How can a means of valid cognition be dependent? it is replied:
That [cognition] is indeed independent with respect to the sense that "this object has been cognized by me.

For, regarding the object alone, there is no cognition that "this object is thus," whereas there is the cognition that "this person knows it to be thus"; therefore, it depends upon the knowledge of the person.

In that regard, it attains the status of a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) due to its independence with respect to the apprehension; and subsequently, the object is established by way of that [apprehension].
How then is it said that certain human statements, even if their content is not contradicted, are non-authoritative due to being dependent (*sāpekṣatva*)? It is replied:

although there is no contradiction regarding the object itself, that upon which its authority regarding the object depends—that is, the means by which it establishes it—is contradicted in its authoritative aspect.

Because that [means] is unestablished, the object is not established through it; thus, it is non-authoritative with respect to the object, as in the case of the Buddha’s words concerning supersensible matters (*atīndriyārtha*), since it is impossible for an ordinary person to perceive such things.
As it has been said:
"In that case, the possibility of an exception arises from human incapacity."
And just as the speech of a deceiver is [invalid] because its speaker's habit of stating things not as they have been perceived is known through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),

the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), however, is not sublated either with respect to its object or with respect to its status as a part of a valid cognition— that is, it is not contradicted by the scope of a valid cognition. Furthermore, since it is independent regarding its own status as a valid cognition, and brings about the establishment of the object by means of that [validity], it cannot fail to be a valid means of knowledge.
Otherwise, linguistic usage based on words would not be possible.

And thus, even though the meanings of the Vedāntic statements coincide with those of other means of valid cognition, there is no contradiction of their authority, just as in the case of the speech of a reliable person. To explain:

Let those other means of knowledge (pramāṇas) indeed bring about the comprehension of that extraordinary, self-luminous nature which is devoid of the distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge; and through them, the establishment of the object may occur just as it does through the word of a reliable person (āpta).
However, this much would be the difference:
because of the absence of a speaker in the case of the Veda, there could be no such contact [with the cognition] as "by me."
[96,ii] Having concluded the argument based on concession, he summarizes the subject at hand:
"In this way, being an object of cognition is not existence."
[96,iii] But another opponent objects:
"Indeed, even the other [position] is not tenable."
For indeed, there can be no conceptualization of a universal without a prior recollection.

Just as the kind of reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) that arises in one who has seen a cow occurs in relation to another [cow], it does not occur in relation to something else that is not a cow. (2.60)
However, let it be accepted that the application of a single word [to multiple individuals] is like the case of "the man with the staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth.
The perception of a perceived form is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a universal (*sāmānya*).
For example:
Upon seeing a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), one thinks of a black-spotted cow (*bāhuleya*) as "this is that very same [cow].
Nor does that [recognition] occur in anything other than what has been grasped as existent.

Furthermore, the application of a single word—even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*)—is caused by connection with another object, just like words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) or "cook" (*pācaka*).
To this it is replied: What indeed is this prior reflection, which is the conformity of the cognition with its previous form? (2.61)
Even in the interval between [two individuals], that [universal] certainly exists to some degree;
however, a complete accompaniment in its entirety is not observed in the case of Khaṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
If it is not of such a nature, then its own negation cannot be known merely through difference;
for a jar and a bowl do not lack the genus "clay" merely because of their difference. (2.63)

For the nature of the cognition regarding water-jars is indeed such as it is for those made of precious gems; the cognition of an ordinary clay pot does not possess that same quality in a gemstone jar. (2.64)
What, then, is this "prior reflection"? Is it the appearance of a prior form within the cognition, or is it the subsequent synthesis of the former and the latter in the form "this is that"?
If the first alternative is taken, such [reflection] certainly exists, though only in a subtle degree, within the interval between two moments of existence.
For instance:
by virtue of their distinction from the indefinable (nirupākhya), the existence of real entities manifests as a common nature;
otherwise, like the indefinable, even existent things would manifest as being absolutely distinct [from one another].

Now, as for the "concomitance of all forms" (*sarvarūpānugama*), that does not exist even in the case of a common object (*sāmānyagocara*) intended [as the universal], because there is no concomitance between a hornless cow (*khaṇḍa*) and a horned cow (*muṇḍa*) in its entirety; for if such were the case, it would follow that they are one and the same, which would result in the non-existence of the universal. Nor is it the case that [the concomitance] is of such a kind as it is in the case of hornless cows and the like.
That is incorrect.

It is not tenable to deny the existence of a persisting form (*anvayirūpa*) that is cognized merely on the basis of particularity (*viśeṣa*), for such [mere particularity] would also be possible in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth.

For the kind of conformity of form (*rūpānugama*) that occurs when Devadatta is seen a second time does not exist for one who, having seen a broken-horned cow (*khaṇḍa*), sees a hornless one (*muṇḍa*).
Moreover, even within the scope of a commonality, it is not the same everywhere;
for the continuity of form (*rūpānvaya*) in a water-jar and a bowl differs from that in various other types of jars.
Yet, by that much, those two are not devoid of the genus "clay" (*mṛjjāti*), because they appear as having some degree of similarity.
Now, as for the second alternative, it is said here:
"That [notion] is a prior reflection"—even this claim that it is a manifestation does not hold up.
For one who has seen a water-jar (*maṇika*), that [reflection] does not arise in relation to a small bowl (*mallaka*). (2.65)

The claim that the cognition consisting of a synthesis of the prior and the posterior—which brings about the understanding of non-difference in the form "this is that"—is called *pūrvāvamarsa* (recollection of the prior) because it is the cause for the conceptualization of a universal even among distinct things—this too is not tenable.
For the establishment of non-difference does not result from synthesis alone;
it also results from the manifestation of a non-distinct form.
Otherwise, a single object could not exist in an identical place and time;

for in the absence of difference in place and time, there would be no synthesis [of cognition] as "that. Furthermore, for one who has seen a jar in a bowl, the synthesis as "that" does not occur immediately, just as it does not between a broken and a hornless [cow].
And yet, there is no deficiency in the genus "clay" in this case;
for upon reflection, the cognition that "this belongs to that same genus" is identical even when there is a difference in substance.
If the connection with the universal is equal [in both cases], why then does the reflective awareness "that" occur in one instance and not in another? It is said:
When the nature of the universal is predominant, its true essence shines forth; when it is deficient, its distinctness appears because that [essence] does not manifest. (2.66)
Because, even though a commonality exists between a jar and an arrow, the cognition "that" does not arise with respect to another jar,
even though it possesses a greater degree of commonality.
Therefore, because those things whose nature is general arise in abundance, there is the manifestation of reality as "that" (saḥ); but when they are few, it is not so, because they do not manifest.
And it is not the case that a single word applies [to both] as it does to "the one to be punished" (daṇḍya) and so forth; thus he says:
"The means of valid cognition is to be known through its effect, because there is a cognition that [the object] exists without being conjoined [with the cognition]. (2.67)

Therefore, it arises first; hence, there is no equality with [the cognition of] a staff-bearer and the like. A qualified cognition does not occur without the apprehension of the qualifier, nor is there an apprehension of the means of valid cognition prior to the qualified cognition, nor at that very time.
For it arises from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone;
and since the means of valid cognition is inferred from its effect, which is the act of cognizing, it is apprehended only after that cognition has occurred.
Therefore, because the means of valid cognition is not [yet] apprehended, that [cognition]—being devoid of the conjunction with it—is not caused by its connection with a means of valid cognition.
If, then, there is no application of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to the object denoted by "exists" (*asti*), how can there be an operation of time conforming to that [object]—

as in "the well exists," "the well existed," or "the well will exist"? This is because the distinction is conceptually constructed through its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as the existence of Devadatta is distinguished by the limiting adjunct of his conjunction with Pāṭaliputra.

And since there is no disagreement among those who know the principles of word-meaning that "there is no connection between word-meanings without an action," he says: "But other wise men [hold] that it is established by mere relation alone. (2.68)

They say that a king’s words may be devoid of action, as are fruit-bearing trees; for even in the absence of action, a relation is perceived in such expressions as "this man belongs to the king" and "these trees have borne fruit.
Nor is it appropriate here [in the case of "asti"] to claim that there is an "action of being" (*astikriyā*).
For it is understood that what is to be established here is not the existence of a man whose connection with a king is already known, nor the existence of fruit-bearing trees; indeed,
these two sentences do not culminate in mere existence,
but rather in the man's connection with the king and the trees' connection with the fruit.
“The man here belongs to the king,” “these trees have borne fruit”— but not [in the sense of] “the king’s man exists” or “those that have borne fruit exist.

Furthermore, as for the view held by some— that one considers the possession of an action through an injunction of the act of cognition, saying “let it be understood”— that too has already been refuted, because the cognition is established from the word itself.
[99,ii] Furthermore, even if there is no sentence devoid of action, and there is dependence upon an action, he says that even so there is no fault:
"And because it culminates in the act of production, the qualified [object] is capable of being understood. (2.69)
"The cause arises from such a cause as this.
Even from a sentence that culminates in the act of origination—such as "The world is born from such a cause"—the existence of that kind of cause can be understood.
For example:
"The existence of such a tree [is inferred] from the fact that 'this fruit was produced from such a tree.
Likewise, certain scriptural passages establish Brahman in this very manner:
'Indeed, all these beings arise from Ākāśa alone'; 'Just as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire, even so from this Self all the gods [proceed],' and so forth."
Likewise:
"As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its thread], as herbs arise upon the earth,
and as hair and body-hair grow from a living man, so does this entire universe arise from the Imperishable."
This is indeed true:
"Just as from a well-blazing fire thousands of sparks of the same nature emerge,"
"In this same way, my dear, various beings are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also merge."
Likewise:
"For the divine Person is formless; he is indeed without exterior or interior, and unborn."
For it is without breath, without mind, pure, higher than the high imperishable.
From this are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs;
as well as space, air, light, water, and the earth that sustains the universe.
Thus it is said.
Now, an objection is raised: an injunction must be resorted to precisely for the purpose of connecting the meanings of the words.
But surely, in the case of human utterances, the connection [of words with their meanings] is dependent upon other means of valid cognition. // 2.70 //
In other cases, however, the meanings of words are connected with one another by depending on an injunction;
in those [other] cases, the arrangement of words serves to fulfill the speaker’s intended meaning. (2.71)

In the case of an object cognizable through other means of knowledge, the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*) is established for the sake of accomplishing the meaning of an injunction in the Veda; for in its absence, [the injunction] would be incoherent. (2.72)
The apprehension of a qualified object is an error; it is a delusion of grasping where there is no [actual] grasping.
For in the world, the co-utterance of words is for the sake of accomplishing the intended meaning;
the intended meaning is not accomplished by a single word alone.
Furthermore, the object intended for expression is apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, in that case, the relation [of the word-meanings] depends upon that other means of valid cognition.
And thus, when there is a contradiction with that [other means of cognition], there is simply no relation among the word-meanings.

Regarding the [Vedic passage] "the old bull with the sandals and the blanket," since there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the Veda, this [understanding] is based on an injunction (*vidhi*).

However, in the absence of such an injunction, the comprehension of a specific meaning that arises— due to the impossibility [of otherwise accounting for it] and because of the syntactic proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*)— is called an error (*bhrānti*).
Thus, this is the delusion of apprehending a relation when there is no apprehension of distinction.
In this regard, the following must be investigated: how is it that in the world, a relation is dependent upon other means of valid cognition?
If it is argued that this is because it is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
that is incorrect, because even that which is unprecedented (*apūrva*) is cognized [by scripture];
otherwise, the statement would be purposeless.
For speech is employed to make known to a listener a meaning not yet understood.

Now, if it is argued that this [meaning] is already understood through another means of knowledge merely as being capable of association [with words], this is equally true in the case of the Veda. To explain:
In the statement "he buys with a reddish one," there is a connection [of the quality] with the act, not [a connection] of the reddish [cow] with the one-year-old cow.

Likewise, it is established solely by the capacity of suitability determined through other means of knowledge that the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) is the object of the injunction (niyoga), and not the meaning of words denoting substance or quality.
Now, the intention to express (vivakṣā) is not understood from a single word alone, because the mere intention to express its [single] meaning would be purposeless.
Therefore, the establishment of a specific intention to speak does not occur with respect to word-meanings that are unconnected; thus, they are combined when employed by such an intention.
And that [intention] is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Even so, it would be based on the speaker's intention, because there is a combination of those things employed by it.
It is not based on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because that [other means] is neither its establisher nor its motivator.
As for the claim that there is a desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) regarding what is established by another means of valid cognition—
Let it be so; however, its connection (*saṃsarga*) is not what is required [for verbal cognition]. For even in the case of the speech of a deceiver, there is a cognition of connection.
As for the claim that there is no connection when there is contradiction— let it be so;
however, even then, there is no connection from that [contradiction].

Even when there is contradiction, there is no non-connection [of the word with its object], because it is perceived. Yet, even though it is perceived, it is sublated by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Thus, some speech is false, while some is meaningless.
The example beginning with "ten pomegranates" contains a small degree of truth;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between the true, the false, and the meaningless.
Now, a person, having perceived an object through another means of valid cognition and desiring to speak of it, communicates it to another.
Therefore, the meaning of that statement is simply the apprehension [of the object] through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

That very apprehension is the motivator (*prayojikā*) for the connection of word-meanings (*padārthasaṃsarga*). Due to the absence of such a motivator, the connection of word-meanings is not established in the Veda.
Let it not be so;
rather, it is only a specific meaning that serves as the motivator.

Now, if it is argued that because the capacity of words is understood from worldly usage, there can be no connection [of meaning] due to the absence of a worldly motivator, then [this objection] would apply even in the case of a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

Now, in the world, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) applies only to the fact of association in general, not to its specific details; for both cognition and linguistic usage are established by that general fact alone. Thus, even without the perception of other means of knowledge, the comprehension of a qualified object is accomplished.
Now, in the world, the truth of a connection [of words] is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For even a connection previously unknown to the listener attains truth by way of inferring the speaker's [reliance on] a *pramāṇa*; for in the absence of that, it lacks truth, as seen in the statements of the Buddha and others.
Therefore, in common worldly usage, a connection is said to be based upon another *pramāṇa*.
Let it be so;

however, in the case of the Veda, because there is no admixture with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the comprehension of its meaning occurs independently, and thus it is based solely on the word itself.
Let this matter rest for now;
let it be as it is in the world.
However, this is what must be questioned:
How indeed could there be dependence on injunctions? For if it were otherwise, [the injunctions] would be in vain. // 2.73 //
The injunction would likewise be without an object; this is the same in the case of what is expressed by another word.
Since there is a comprehension of a qualified meaning, the meaning of another word is also employed [as the object]. (2.74)

If it is argued that because there is no evidence for its having a meaning, this [word] must be meaningless, then the injunction (vidhi) would likewise be so; for what reason? Or else, there would be another word [to provide the meaning]. (2.75)

When an object is already established by another means of valid cognition, an injunction is not applicable to it; for that object, being cognized as something not otherwise accessible, would necessarily imply [the injunction]. (2.76)
An object is not a thing established as it is [by its own nature] such that it would merely be a subject of restatement;
for if the knowledge of the relationship [between word and object] were denied, there would be no activity on the part of one who is unacquainted with it. (2.77)
Otherwise, one would overstep one's own duty (*svadharma*) for the sake of another’s accomplishment.
An injunction (*vidhi*) does not directly denote a relation in general or its specific instance;
rather, it implies it, for otherwise the mere mandate (*niyoga*), being devoid of an object, would be purposeless.
This is equally true for other word-meanings as well.
Even those [meanings], being isolated and failing to attain connection with other word-meanings, would be meaningless because they lack the comprehension of a new (synthetic) meaning.
Furthermore, in common usage, word-meanings are not understood by words as being restricted solely to their own individual forms.
Rather, they are prompted by the cognition of a qualified object,
because such linguistic usage is thus established;
and in this way, for each individual word-meaning, there is an implication of a relation.
It might be argued:

"In the world, let there be no futility for those [words] employed with conscious intent; therefore, they have the purpose of conveying a connection [of meaning]. But in the Veda, however, there is no evidence for their having such a purpose."
Therefore, let another category of entity be indeed purposeless.
This is not sound.
One cannot establish an unproven object on the grounds that it would otherwise be purposeless, for that would lead to the absurd consequence of establishing just anything whatsoever.

Therefore, from worldly usage, it is understood that words possess the capacity to convey their own meanings only as connected [to one another]. Consequently, even in the Veda, there is an implication of such connection.
If it is argued that other word-meanings are purposeless, why would that not apply to the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) itself? Now, if this is your view—
Other words are employed when an object is already established by another means of valid cognition;
they terminate in the restatement of that object as it has been understood.
For instance:
An object being restated (*anūdyamāna*) is incapable of implying a new meaning (*apūrvārtha*), because it merely follows what is already understood through restatement.

A prescriptive word (*vidhāyaka-śabda*), however, has as its domain a meaning not otherwise accessible; that meaning, being cognized, is capable of implying a new meaning when it could not otherwise be accounted for.
Therefore, in the Veda, the connection with a new meaning is based upon injunction (*vidhi*).
That is incorrect.

If the meaning of the injunction were not an object of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the knowledge of its relationship [to the word] would be impossible; thus, one would have to deny it.
And in that case, since it would not depend on the knowledge of such a relationship, even one who has not mastered the linguistic convention (*avyutpanna*) would engage in action.
Furthermore, the property of depending on the knowledge of a relationship, which belongs to words, would be set aside;
or else, the property of independence from that [relationship], which belongs to sentences, would have to be accepted.

If, however, its dependence on a relationship were not denied, it would necessarily result in the word having as its object something already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus there is no distinction. Even for one who maintains that the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] occurs from the word itself when [the object] is cognized: // 2.78 //

There is no fault of mutual dependence, for that [cognition] is not known by itself; rather, it is understood through another [means], namely, by the comprehension of the word and indicated by its subsequent activity. (2.79)
In that case, the apprehension of the relationship is as easy as it is for other categories;
this is also the view of one who thinks—
The knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning] does not pertain to an injunction whose object is established by another means of valid cognition;
rather, it pertains only to that which is established by the word itself.
Nor is there the fault of mutual dependence.
Since the establishment [of the object] from the word depends on the knowledge of the relationship, and the establishment from the word is preceded by the knowledge of the relationship,
it is not said that [the object] is cognized directly from the word itself;
rather, it is cognized by another elder from the word employed by an elder.

And from understanding that, one infers from the activity of that elder: "Surely some object that serves as a cause for activity has been apprehended by this elder from this word, since he acted upon hearing it. Just as, for example, from seeing the bringing of a cow—which possesses a dewlap and so forth—upon hearing the command "Bring the cow," one infers his comprehension and thereby grasps the relationship [between word and meaning].
If that [self] is thus inferable, how can it be the exclusive object of verbal testimony?
Since that [cognition] also has words as its precursor, it is the exclusive domain of inference;
why then is the cognition from words not also preceded by inference? (2.81)
It cannot be established that these two [the word and its object] have no beginning, like the seed and the sprout;
for everyone, prior to [perceiving] the word, there stands the inference of the cognizer. (2.82)
The word is merely reiterative of that [object] as possessing another property;
for one who understands it through inference does not understand from the word what has already been understood. (2.83)
In another cognizer, the cognition is not produced by a restatement of another's cognition;
furthermore, if the meaning of a word were merely the cause for activity, it would be something non-worldly (alaukika). (2.84)
It cannot be so conceptualized, even on the basis of its worldly establishment.

If the prescriptive meaning, established as a qualification of the cognition inferred from activity, were the object of the knowledge of the relationship [between word and meaning], then it would not have verbal testimony as its sole means of valid cognition.
Now, if it is argued that inference is preceded by verbal testimony, then verbal cognition would likewise be preceded by inference, and thus both would have inference as their sole object.
Indeed, it is impossible to establish a priority between these two, as in the case of a seed and a sprout;

for there is understanding through inference of what was previously apprehended by words, and there is understanding through words of what was inferred once the relationship [between sign and signified] was known.
Moreover, for all cognizers, comprehension from verbal testimony is preceded by inference; thus, for them, the word is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*). To explain:

every cognizer who understands from a word understands what has already been inferred and whose connection [with the meaning] is known; however, one who is currently inferring does not infer what has already been understood through a word.

But surely, it is only that which is understood through the word that is inferred. True; however, this is by means of this particular cognizer. And the cognition belonging to one person does not serve as a restatement for the cognition of another.
Furthermore, since the understanding of the relationship [between word and object] occurs merely through the cause of activity, the meaning of a word would have to be that alone.
Moreover, it is not possible even to postulate something non-worldly (alaukika), because activity is accomplished even by means of what is worldly.
It might be argued as follows:
In Vedic activities, because that [capacity] is impossible, there is the postulation of something non-worldly.
This is not so;
for a word whose capacity is understood from worldly usage is also a communicator in the Veda.
In that case, regarding worldly activities, as well as in the Veda whose connection is already known in the world, there would only be comprehension of that [meaning];
or, in the event of impossibility, there would be falsity.

Now, since the causes of activity are manifold and because of their variability, the meaning of a word cannot be a specific cause of activity; rather, the meaning of a word is the universal (sāmānya) that underlies these causes of activity.
In that regard, since worldly qualifications are impossible in the Veda, another non-worldly (alaukika) qualification is understood.

Even so, that which is the meaning of a word in the Veda—the universal—is established in the world; thus, its status as a restatement (anuvāda) does not cease, just as in the case of other word-meanings.

As for that specific distinction, it is the object of a *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference because [the alternatives] are otherwise impossible; thus, it is not the case that it is not the domain of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor is even a residual inference possible in the case of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*).
Now, if it is thought:
Just as worldly linguistic usage is beginningless, so too is Vedic linguistic usage.

In that regard, since there is no cause for activity other than worldly activity within Vedic activities, the knowledge of the relationship [of word and meaning] for Vedic injunctions pertains to a non-worldly cause of activity.
Nor is it something to be inferred, because the cognition of that [relationship] is itself inferred from the activity [it prompts].
Its establishment, however, occurs solely through the force of that very cognition;
and since that cognition arises from verbal testimony, it is not dependent on any other means of knowledge.
Furthermore, it is not correct to claim that only worldly [means] can possibly be the instruments for attaining the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).
For in the worldly context, the status of being a means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhanatā*) is cognizable through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In that regard, because the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is observed, and because the meaning of words is determined in accordance with that usage, the fact of being cognizable by other means of valid cognition also enters into the meaning of the word.
To this it is replied:

Let it be granted that the correspondence between word and meaning proceeds solely from Vedic usage; nevertheless, its status as an object of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is not thereby excluded. For instance:

At the time of knowing the capacity of a word for its cause of application regarding a non-worldly (alaukika) object, has that object been cognized by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it has been cognized, then since the relation of the word [to that object] is being known at that very moment, it must necessarily be said to have been known by another means of valid cognition. Now, if it has not been cognized, how can there be knowledge of the relation with respect to it? For a relation, which depends upon two relata, cannot be cognized when those two relata themselves have not been cognized.
Even he who thinks:
"For the relation of a word is its power (śakti); and that [power] does not reside in the object, because the object is already established [prior to the word]."
But its cause must be inferred; and that [cause] is inferred from activity.
It is precisely there that the relationship, characterized by causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*), is cognized.
He should be asked this:

is the capacity grasped in the mere condition (*pratyaya*) itself, or in a specific condition that is the cause of activity (*pravṛtti-hetu-pratyaya*)? If it were in the mere condition, then anything whatsoever might be understood from it.

If, however, it were in a specific condition that is the cause of activity distinct from worldly ones, then, because that [capacity] is inferred through the methods of presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it would follow that it falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
For there are two possible ways for a qualifier to function:
either it serves as an auxiliary factor drawn in by memory toward the cognition of the qualified object, as in "there is fire because of smoke";
or it is the object of a means of knowledge that apprehends the qualified whole, as in "the cow is white."
In both cases, it is the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the word has not yet apprehended its relationship [to the object].

If it were drawn forth by memory (*smārta*), another means of valid cognition would have to be sought. Even in the second alternative, it is because it is inferred from the inference of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*).
Now, the validity of inference consists solely in its being a cognition;
however, in that case, the qualifier is merely an object of cognition,
and it is by virtue of that alone that it serves as a factor for the cognition of the qualified entity.

The cognition of the qualifier, however, arises from an inferential cognition, just as when the validity of a qualified object is inferred from the words of a person, the establishment of the object follows from that very means of knowledge.
For in that case, the object is a qualifier of the speaker’s cognition merely by being apprehended.
This [position] is unsatisfactory, because apprehension is included within recollection, valid knowledge, doubt, error, and conceptual construction.
In that case, the cognition of a non-worldly qualifier is not memory, because it was not previously apprehended.

It is not doubt, because there is no contact with two alternatives. Nor is it conceptual construction, because it would follow that even the cognition which is the cause of purposeful activity would likewise be such.

Likewise, there is no error; for if it were to correspond to reality, how could that cognition apprehending such an object be devoid of an object? By process of elimination, it must be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And it is well said: "Another person is made to understand by means of another's cognition.
Now, suppose this view is held:
One person does not understand another through the other's cognition; rather, it is only through one's own cognition, by virtue of the capacity of that other's cognition.

Now, it must be stated what kind of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) constitutes that person's own cognition: it cannot be verbal testimony (*śabda*), because the definition [of verbal testimony] is "cognition of an object arising from the cognition of a word.
Nor can it be [verbal testimony] derived from the cognition of that [other person's] word.
From what, then, [is it established]? From the knowledge arising from the word, which has been inferred.
Now, if its validity is established, the existence of the cause for activity is proven.
And its validity arises from its being produced by a word free from defects.
Therefore, it is said that verbal testimony possesses authority (*prāmāṇya*) in that regard,
because the determination of the object therein depends upon it.
That too is incorrect, according to the definition that "verbal cognition is the knowledge of an object derived from words."
Even human speech is not a means of valid cognition with respect to the object itself;
rather, it is [a means of valid cognition] with respect to a qualification of the cognition.
And two possible ways for such a qualification have been stated.

In that case, because memory is impossible, it is only while being itself cognized that it serves as a factor for the cognition of the qualified object. Otherwise, one would have to seek another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the object.
Furthermore, the object is not established by the speaker's cognition alone; for it has been stated that one person does not apprehend another's cognition.
As for what was stated—

that the establishment of an object depends upon the speaker’s cognition— that is so because, if that [cognition] is false or impossible, the perception of the object is also sublated due to the sublation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and if that [cognition] is not sublated, the object is not sublated either.
But it is not the case that the meaning is not the object of speech;
otherwise, the very point that human speech is dependent on other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding its object and is thus contingent would not hold.
For that which is not the object of something cannot be either contingent or independent with respect to it.
And thus it has been said: "The establishment of validity, however, occurs because of the possibility of the speaker's cognition being the cause [of the sentence].
Establishment means non-sublation (*abādha*), not validity itself.
And that [establishment] belongs to the sentence due to the possibility of the speaker's cognition being its cause, but not to the speaker's cognition alone.
Furthermore, the relationship of a word is with its object, not with the cognition [of it];
for it has been stated thus:
"The relationship of a word with its object is innate (autpattika)."
The inclusion of the term "object" (*artha*) here is for the purpose of refuting those who hold the view that "a word does not touch its object; the connection of a word is with cognition alone.
Therefore, the relationship between a word and its object is simply their mutual fitness (*anyonyayogyatā*).
Nor can it be apprehended when the object is unmeasured;
for it has been stated that when an object is measured, it falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor does it apply to mere cognition, because a cognition that possesses an object must be included within either memory or a [valid] means of knowledge.

If [the sentence] were meaningless, with what would it have a connection? Furthermore, if that object were apprehended by a cognition other than verbal cognition—even one that is not of the nature of valid knowledge—then why would the suspicion of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) not arise, given that this object would become the domain of non-verbal knowledge as well? Moreover, the fact of being cognizable through another means of knowledge does not enter into the meaning of a word, because the meaning of a word is established neither by positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone nor by negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone.

For when another factor is the motivator for an action, it is understood that the absence of which prevents that action from occurring is also a motivator of that word; just as when other causes are present, that whose absence prevents the effect from arising is also understood to be a cause.

And here, since we observe the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth when there is an intention to express a cause of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*), and since we do not observe them even when [the fact] is cognizable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the absence of such an intention, the status of being a cause of the highest good is indeed the meaning of the word.

Although there is observation when [the object] is accessible through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and non-observation when that is absent, nevertheless, this is not due to the absence of accessibility through another means of valid cognition while it remains a cause of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).
In that case, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful; since there is no application [of the means] when both are absent, on what basis is the lack of application grounded?

In this regard, since it has been determined that the capacity to be a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatā*) is the motivator (*prayojaka*), it is understood that in its absence, [the action] is devoid of that basis. Since the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established by that alone, there is no evidence for anything else being the meaning of the word.
Otherwise, even properties such as existence (*sattva*) would enter into the meaning of the word "śiṃśapā," because they are present whenever those [trees] exist.
Because [the word] is employed when that [quality] is present and not employed when it is absent.

Now, if it is argued that since being a *śiṃśapā* (a type of tree) is the meaning of the word, its non-employment when existence (*sattā*) and so forth are absent is based solely on the absence of those [qualities], and its employment when they are present is thus justified—and therefore no causal capacity (*sāmarthya*) need be postulated for them—then this is equally applicable here as well.

Furthermore, if it is argued that because being a cause of the highest good (*śreyas-hetutva*) is the object of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and because that [causality] is impossible in the case of the Veda, the Veda lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
That is incorrect;
for that which is the object of a particular means of valid cognition in one place is not thereby rendered false in another.
For [an object] is within the range of the external sense-faculties when nearby, but it is accessible through scripture and inference when at a distance.

Likewise, in the case of sacrifices and the like, which yield results at a distant time, there will be the quality of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) as understood through the Veda. Nor is that which is accessible to one means of knowledge sublated by another means of knowledge simply because it is not perceived by that other means, since the operation of various means of knowledge occurs according to the distinct determination of their respective objects. Now, if [the sacrifice] were an object of another means of knowledge, its lack of authority would follow due to contradiction with that [other means], because no immediate result is perceived.
But since the meaning of the word does not fall within that domain, there is no contradiction with it;
this would be so if there were a contradiction, but there is none.

It has been stated that "the immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) is indeed not enjoined. Now, let there be no injunction of immediate sequence, and let the meaning of the word not be something cognizable through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If a category of reality is accepted as established by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in every respect, it must be accepted exactly as it is so established;
otherwise, it would not be established by that [means].
And its status as the cause of immediate spiritual welfare is established by that very [means].
That is not so.

First of all, it is not a rule that actions have their fruits immediately following them, for we observe otherwise in the cases of agriculture, medicinal herbs, drinking [medicine], and so forth; furthermore, even in the case of sacrifices and the like, an intermediate effect is established by the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Moreover, when a qualified entity is established, its qualification—namely, the mere fact of being a cause of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*)—is also established.
And the meaning of the word extends only that far;
nor is there any contradiction with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) within that limit.
Thus, since there is no defect even in a worldly cause for activity, the postulation of something non-worldly is useless.

And because this [consciousness] is inferable like pleasure and so forth; for instance, pleasure and the like, whose cognitions are inferred from the brightening of the face and other signs, are inferred along with that very [inference].
In this case, no separate means of valid cognition is required for the existence of the person;
even though this is the view that the meaning of a person's speech is simply the speaker's own cognition.
In that case, since cognition does not occur without an object, the existence of the object is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference (*anumāna*).

Even then, the cognition which is the cause of purposeful activity—being itself established by such activity—cannot exist without its object; thus, like the meaning of authoritative verbal testimony (*āptavacana*), its status as an object of inference does not cease.
Furthermore, because the cognition derived from inference is brought about by words, it is characterized by verbal testimony as its means of valid knowledge (*śabdapramāṇaka*).
That is incorrect;

for the knowledge of the meaning of the words of a reliable person (āpta) does not have the senses as its instrument, and thus that object becomes one whose means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the listener is direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Therefore, it is rightly said:
“If that [self] is thus inferable, how can it be the exclusive object of verbal testimony?
Likewise:
“It cannot be postulated, since its existence is established even through worldly [means].”
Thus [it is said].
[110,i] Now, in the form of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is manifested by its own word. // 2.85 //
It is said that [the means of knowledge] is both a sublater and independent with respect to another means of knowledge.
Now, it is argued:
We do not say that the injunction would otherwise be in vain, and thus the connection [of the result] depends upon it;
rather, that [connection] is conveyed by its own word through the very nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, because it is a means of valid cognition, it implies a previously unknown object of cognition (*prameya*), and it is independent of any other means of valid cognition.
For this [inference], unlike a word, does not depend upon a prior established state because it depends upon a relation.
Nevertheless, if it were unestablished, the two faults mentioned previously would apply; if it were established, it would be a mere restatement. (2.86)
Let its authority reside where that of the Veda does; in this regard, however, it is useless.

Even so, if that [Smṛti], though being of the nature of a means of knowledge, is not established by another means of knowledge regarding the commencement of activity for those who are unlearned and the transgression of dharma, then—should it be established—it would merely be a restatement of what is already known, and thus no new matter (apūrva-artha) would be implied.
Moreover, let it be that the word itself possesses authority in those cases where its authority is desired;

what is the use of this [inference]? But has it not been said—that because it depends on the knowledge of the connection between words [and their meanings], it is merely repetitive and is not capable of bringing about the understanding of a new (previously unknown) object?

This is not sound. If the word is merely reiterative, then how could the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) being reiterated—which itself is already known—convey a previously unknown object (*apūrvārtha*)? For there can be no comprehension of a means of knowledge that is devoid of contact with its object (*prameya*).

Therefore, that [object] is cognized exactly as it has been apprehended as the object of knowledge; and where is this means of valid cognition [effective] regarding that object, and not in the case of sacrifices and the like denoted by their own words? (2.87)

Even in the absence of an injunction, there exists for the listener a novel connection with worldly things; and if it concerns the capacity to be a means to a result, the word is not at fault therein. (2.88)

Since it is equivalent to other word-meanings, the connection of word-meanings is not based on the requirement of an injunction; for those meanings have already been manifested by their own respective words. (2.89)
Therefore, because it possesses a form capable of connection, it participates in the relation; for among people, co-utterance is employed for the sake of a qualified object. (2.90)
Therefore, a connection [of the injunction] with the non-existence of the act is not possible,

nor can the object of knowledge (*prameya*) of the injunction be determined. To begin with, sacrifices and the like are not the objects of knowledge, because they are the referents of words such as "he sacrifices" (*yajati*).
Nor is their relation beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For instance, even in worldly sentences that do not consist of injunctions, such as "A son is born to you, O Brāhmaṇa," a previously unknown relation is perceived by the listener.
Now, the object of knowledge (prameya) consisting in the capacity for the means to achieve the fruit is stated:
indeed, for one who possesses desire (*kāmin*), an injunction (*niyoga*) is not possible with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) when that is not a means to the desired end;
for if it were not a means, that [injunction] would not have been performed by the desirer.
That too is untenable;
for there is no fault whatsoever in the word such that it should be bypassed and another means of knowledge sought.
The dependence upon other means of knowledge has already been refuted.
However, the contradiction arising from the non-perception of an immediate result remains the same even if that [obligation] is understood through a *niyoga*.
Since immediacy is not an object of valid cognition (*apramāṇārthatva*), its absence is equally applicable to the word (*śabda*) as well.
Alternatively, the word is not defective in its capacity to bring about the result; rather, it is the *niyoga* itself that is indeed defective.
For from that [mere word], the comprehension of the means for achieving a human goal is not possible.
This must be understood through the *Vidhiviveka* and the *Bhāvanāviveka*.
Therefore, since the meaning of an injunction is identical to other word-meanings in its dependence upon the knowledge of a relationship, it cannot be stated as having a specific distinction.
The connection between word-meanings is based on that [sentence].

However, all word-meanings, having been understood from their respective words as being in states such as *kāraka* (grammatical participant) which are capable of relation, become connected through proximity (*sannikarṣa*), because the operation of words is understood from worldly usage.

And in the world, the presentation of word-meanings by means of words occurs through proximity for the sake of a qualified meaning, not for the sake of the mere comprehension of the individual word-meanings themselves.
And thus, connection (*saṃsarga*) is based solely on the mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of all word-meanings.
For all of them are revealed by the words in their mere essential forms (*svarūpa*), without their forms being fully completed.
In this way, because the injunction (*vidhi*) is equal to the other word-meanings, the connection is not based specifically upon it.
Furthermore, since connection depends upon all word-meanings, a connection is not possible in the absence of an injunction (*vidhi*).

Thus, an injunction need not even be resorted to for the sake of establishing a connection. How so? If it is argued that the knowledge of the connection among the meanings of words arises precisely through the focus on the mandate (*niyoga*), [we reply: for the capacity of that [mandate] toward that [connection] is understood by inferring its causal cognition through the observation of activity following other instigating statements.

This is not so, because even in a sentence that does not incite action but rests upon its own form, a relationship [between words] is grasped. For instance, when one who desires fire is told— while other implements for cooking are present— "There is fire in Caitra’s house," and he subsequently observes the bringing of it from there, it is understood [that the word "fire" denotes the object].

“Here, the existence of fire has been cognized by this person, and that [cognition] arises from this sentence. Yet it cannot be said that there is a comprehension [of an injunction] from such sentences as “Bring it from there” or “Go there,” because the accomplishment of activity through the sentence occurs merely by means of the cognition of the existence of fire; thus, one cannot postulate that the sentence possesses the capacity for enjoining action.
