Furthermore, since the application and comprehension of the word are established through connection with another meaning, there is no evidence for its connection with a specific meaning;
otherwise, as has been stated, the meaning of the Veda would be entirely without a basis of valid cognition.
Now, it is argued that [the Veda] would be purposeless without the knowledge of what ought to be done. (2.91)

There is no purpose for the employment of a sentence other than engagement or withdrawal; if it is argued that the injunction to understand is the same [as the former], then that alone is the purpose. (2.92)
And if this [scripture] were to surrender this very same purpose, which is required for the accomplishment of the qualification for wisdom, action, and worship; 2.93.
Well then, that statement does not terminate in its own form;
this is the same as [the case where] a sentence is completed by following another sentence. (2.94)
If there is an entry into an injunction for you now, it is otherwise in vain;
thus, the portion concerning the injunction for the realization of reality has been fully set forth. (2.95)
[113,i] Now, it might be thought:
knowledge that consists merely of the essential nature of an object, being devoid of the knowledge of what is to be done and lacking both engagement and withdrawal, is purposeless.
For the activity of speech is indeed prompted by engagement or withdrawal;
thus, [the Veda] must contain injunctions for the sake of purposefulness. Otherwise, it would be meaningless.
To this it is replied:
even in the case of an injunction for performance, the same pointlessness applies. For instance:
Even the statement, "It should be realized in this manner," does not imply any activity or cessation distinct from the knowledge of its own nature.

If it is argued that the knowledge of the nature itself is the purpose, then that is equally true even for [the Upanishads] which rest solely upon that nature. Furthermore, the injunction to realize is meaningful by providing the object for the wisdom and meditation required by the governing injunctions, such as "One should cultivate wisdom," "One should form a resolve," and "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self,'" for it is impossible to have wisdom regarding an object whose nature has not been understood.
Even a statement that rests upon its own form is meaningful in that way;
it possesses all the more capacity for conveying that [form].
But, one might object, if this is so, its status as resting upon its own form is lost, since it has entered into the sphere of the mandate (*niyoga*).
Even so, that [injunction] does not culminate in its own application, because it enters into another injunction.
Now, if it is thought:
"A sentence that has already reached completion in its own meaning enters into syntactic unity with another sentence."
Thus, this is stated as the contextual connection;
otherwise, it would merely be a definition of a sentence.
This too is the same.
Even upon entering into the sphere of an injunction (*niyoga*), its status as being grounded in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not lost.
Now, one might object: "Surely there is an entry into an injunction, for otherwise it would be purposeless. Let it be so.

First of all, the injunction for the realization of reality has already been refuted on the grounds of its pointlessness, since the comprehension of reality is established from that very word even without an injunction.
Now, one might object: "But the originative injunction (utpatti-vidhi) is established as being concerned with the comprehension of the nature of ritual action."
Just as there is a method for the knowledge of reality, so may one abide in awakening. // 2.96 //
And its engagement is considered to proceed from authority, like the authority for ritual action;
therefore, it consists of making known what was unknown and instigating that which has not yet begun. (2.97)
The wise declare that even this [injunction] is of the same nature;
for in that case, the comprehension of the nature of the action is not intended as the fruit of the injunction. (2.98)
However, for that which depends on a specific task, there is a connection with the sentence stating the result;
here, the connection to the qualification (*adhikāra*) belongs to that which is not enjoined [as a primary action]. (2.99)
The reality [of the object] does not constitute an entry into the qualification for the awakening to that reality;
for perception directed toward rice and the like does not partake in such qualification. (2.100)
Furthermore, as for the objection that the purpose of an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) is merely the performance of the ritual action (*karma-rūpa-pratipatti-mātra*):

Regarding the statement, “An offering on eight potsherds for Agni,” there is no initiation [of action] from that alone, because such initiation is dependent upon an injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*).

Likewise, for an injunction regarding the realization of reality, the purpose is merely the realization of reality; whereas for an injunction regarding engagement, such as "one should cultivate wisdom," the purpose is engagement.
Since there is thus a difference in the purpose of the injunction between engagement and comprehension, they state that it has two characteristics.
"The making known of what was unknown" and "the instigation of one who has not yet acted"—

this too is without substance, because it is not accepted that the fruit [of an injunction] is merely the comprehension of the essential nature of the prescriptive element as it pertains to its production.
Rather, there is a connection with the sentence of qualification (*adhikāra-vākya*). For instance,
when it is understood that an injunction is a means to a human goal in general, and there arises an expectancy for its specific nature, the connection with qualification is obtained.
Nor is that same result [liberation] the fruit of the injunction for the realization of reality;
for the true nature of the Self, which is the subject of meditation and so forth, is not the object of an injunction because it is non-actional (*akriyātman*).
As for the knowledge of reality that has that [Self] as its object, it has no connection with an [agentive] qualification (*adhikāra*), just like the perception of rice and other such things.
For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the essential nature of rice and so forth does not partake in being a constituent part of the performance (*prayoga*),
because those things already cognized are connected to the qualification (*adhikāra*), just like garments made of wool and the like which have been completed.
For the actions such as weaving or carving do not enter into the qualification.
[115,i] Now, the procedure for the domain of the third realization is set forth, because it is connected by virtue of being the object of the awakening to reality (*tattvāvabodha*).
For the object of the second realization is not the object of the awakening to reality, but rather the object of its cultivation (*abhyāsa*).
[115,ii] Therefore, this other knowledge arising from words is prescribed as being accompanied by a means;
it is non-dual, having transcended the grasping of the distinction between the grasper and the grasped. (2.101)

For the statement, "The reality of the Self is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) and is not an object for the cognition of a sentence-meaning consisting of the connection of distinct referents"—this too is fragile. 2.102

This manifestation of the non-dual self, free from the delusion of limitation, is the abiding in one's own nature, perfectly tranquil; that is the fruit, and it is not the domain of ritual injunction.

For it is held that the activity of the prescriber consists in making known the means to achieve that [result]; indeed, the wise maintain that an injunction is simply the state of being a required means. (2.104)
For that reason, determination and so forth do not arise without cause, nor from verbal expression.
We do not say—
It is taught that the awakening to reality arises from words;
however, it is the apprehension of the cessation of the distinction between the intellect and its objects of cognition.

Therefore, it is non-dual—either because of the absence of a second cognition of that same kind, or because of the absence of the duality of knower and known—and thus it is other than that [dualistic state].

And because that supramundane [reality], which is the means for its arising, cannot be understood through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is prescribed together with the means such as tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), reflection (*manana*), meditation (*dhyāna*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and so forth;
for the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is not an object of verbal knowledge.
Indeed, the means of valid cognition consisting of words is characterized by the sentence (*vākya*).
Furthermore, its object consists of the synthesis of various categories of entities, since it is perceived as following after them.

And how could the true nature of that cognition—which appears as a blending of merely diverse objects—be the sphere of the non-proliferated (*niṣprapañca*) reality of the self, which is untouched even by a trace of duality?
This too is without substance.

Since that realization of the reality of the Self— which is non-dual and devoid of even a trace of contact with duality— is its abiding in its own essential nature due to the absence of the delusion of limitation;
for it is through the turbidity of limitation that it appears in the form of the non-Self,
but there is no realization of reality other than that.
Because of the Vedic revelation, "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite";
and because the reality of the Self is free from all inauspiciousness such as sorrow, according to the revelation that it is "free from evil" and so forth;

and because it is self-luminous and unsurpassed bliss, according to the revelations: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," and "This is its supreme bliss; other beings live on only a fraction of this very bliss."

And thus, the abiding in that very nature—due to the cessation of all inauspiciousness and the attainment of unsurpassed bliss—is the fruit, the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha) which is perfectly tranquil.
And it has been said:
"There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self."
Nor is it correct to say that one does not engage even in a human goal (puruṣārtha) if the means (upāya) are unknown, because desire is the precursor to engagement.
Thus, instruction regarding engagement occurs through that [desire] in certain cases, such as:
"Now, therefore, the inquiry into dharma" (athāto dharmajijñāsā).
Likewise, it has been said: "For whatever one desires, that one does.
Moreover, if one does not engage in an action because the means are unknown, one must necessarily be prompted toward it by the communication of the means, with the result in view.
Since the engagement in that [action] is thereby established, one need not assume the operation of an injunction (*vidhi*) in that regard.
As it has been said:
"The desire for that [result] is indicated by the purpose.
Therefore, the operation of the injunction pertains solely to the means of accomplishing the result.
But surely, activity characterized by a purpose occurs even when there is a result; where, then, does the operation of the injunction (vidhi) reside? In the "manner of being" (itthaṃbhāva).
This is not sound, because just as activity occurs by implication regarding the general means (*sādhana*), so too it occurs regarding the general manner of being.

For a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) that does not provide benefit is incapable [of inducing action]. If it is argued that one should be prompted toward a specific instance of that [benefit], then let it be the same for a specific instance of the means as well. Furthermore, an injunction (*vidhi*) is simply the state of being a sought-after means, because its defining characteristic is the impelling of one who has not yet acted; and because the property that is the cause of action is what is denoted by the word "impelling" (*pravartanā*), since there is no other cause for action than the fact of being desired (*iṣṭatā*) and the fact of being a means to that [desired end]; and because the fact of being desired is determined by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one acts spontaneously, knowing indeed: "This must be done by me. Thus, the state of impelling one who has not yet acted does not apply to the fact of being desired itself.

However, since there is no cognition of "being the means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) through any other means of knowledge, and it is cognizable solely through verbal testimony, it cannot serve as the cause for the engagement of a person who has not yet engaged without that verbal testimony.
Therefore, being established by the authority of verbal testimony, it is designated as an "injunction" (*vidhi*).
And for one who performs [the action], the means to be performed is the cause of engagement.
It is not established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, for one who performs it, there is the injunction of its being a means (*sādhana*).
Consequently, from the injunctive word, it is understood that the performance has as its object precisely that which is the means.

[117,i] But surely those who know the injunction (vidhi) explain the injunction as being: determination, intention, the initial impulse, mere activity devoid of the three times, and the relation between an unknown action and its agent.
This is not sound.
For it is precisely determination (*adhyavasāya*) and the other factors that are sought here as the cause;
and that [cause] is none other than the state of being a required means (*apekṣitopāyatā*).
Nor are those [factors] devoid of causes.
It might be argued:
"The naming of these [categories] is their cause. But that is incorrect.
For these [entities] would arise from verbal designation (*abhidhāna*), not from actual production.
Indeed, it has been explained in the *Vidhiviveka* that things such as jars are not causes for purposeful action (*pravṛtti*) by mere cognition alone.
Alternatively—

Not by way of denotation; nor does determination and so forth arise from the word, because [the word] is a communicator [of meaning], which would entail the consequence of activity even in one who has not learned the linguistic convention, and so forth—this has been stated in that very same place.
Alternatively: "He who thinks—"

"That from which there arises the determination ‘this must be done by me,’ and from which there arises the cognition ‘I am enjoined’—that is an injunction (niyoga), a synonym for the word ‘prescription’ (vidhi). To this, it is replied:
It is precisely because [the action] is a means to a desired end that there arises the determination “this must be done.
For instance:

In the world, the cognition that "this must be done" arises regarding a means to what is desired by the agent; however, in the absence of such a means, the cognition is "this must not be done. These two [cognitions] are understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with respect to that object.
Likewise, the cognition "I am enjoined" or "I am impelled" is the perception of a cause for one's own activity;
and that [cause] is nothing other than the state of being a desired means (*iṣṭābhyupāyatā*).
Indeed, it is not logical to claim that something which has been observed to possess efficacy is causeless—that is, a non-cause—without a reason.
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for conceiving the extraordinary (*alaukika*) by abandoning the worldly (*laukika*).
Why? Not from verbal designation (*abhidhāna*).
Indeed, the designation of something extraordinary is not possible, because—as has been stated—the relationship [between word and object] cannot be apprehended.
Alternatively, it is because determination, initiation, performance, and completion [of action] proceed from that very [source], since it is the means required [for the result];
for it is only when that exists that the activity of one who has been enjoined occurs, whereas there is no activity from the injunction of anything else.
This might be the case:
one engages in action because of the cognition that "it ought to be done";
otherwise, what ought to be done would not have been performed.
And that is not so; for the cognition of an obligation does not arise without a cause.
Indeed, it has as its motive the attainment of one's own purpose.
It might be argued as follows:
The cognition that something ought to be done arises from the word alone.
To this it is replied: not from the denotation [of the word].
The cognition of what is to be done does not arise from the word alone;
for the mandate (niyoga) is the meaning of the word. That mandate must be either an attribute of the commander or something independent.
But "duty-to-be-done" (kartavyatā) is a property of the object.

Now, if one were to say that the mandate (niyoga) is a property of the object, then the status of being a sought-after means would already be established. Or else, the duty-to-be-done would arise from the mandate itself.
Even so, the word is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [obligation], because it directly denotes the injunction (*niyoga*).
Nor is it so by implication (*artha*), since we observe the injunctions of untrustworthy persons even concerning what ought not to be done.
Now, if it is argued that the status of being an action (*kāryatā*) is understood from the injunction;

The claim that "the understanding of what is to be done regarding an object depends upon its accomplishment" is incorrect, because in common worldly experience, the status of an object as something to be accomplished (kāryatā) is perceived independently.

For instance, when there is an injunction such as "The cow should be milked by you," if it has already been milked by another person, one does not begin to milk it again; this is because the object is perceived as having already been accomplished, and thus its status as something to be accomplished no longer applies.
Nor has the injunction been accomplished by another person, because that other person was not enjoined.
In that case, for the sake of fulfilling the injunction, there would have to be a commencement of milking once again.
This matter has been examined in detail in the *Vidhiviveka*; therefore, enough of this digression.
It might be argued:
this knowledge is enjoined because it is the means for attaining liberation.

For liberation is heard to be accomplished through knowledge: "By means of knowledge they ascend to that," "Through knowledge one attains immortality," and "He who, having known that Self, understands it, [attains] all desires"; likewise, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him," and so forth.
Nor is there any finitude even in that which is to be accomplished, because it is accessible through scripture and involves no return—thus it is said:
"And he does not return again."
For this is not accessible through reasoning— that reasoning by which its true nature might be established. However,
that which is accessible through scripture has its true nature established by scripture alone.
Alternatively, its infinity [is established] because it is to be accomplished through infinite knowledge;
and even though consciousness is momentary, it possesses infinity by way of its continuum.
Regarding this, they say:
And liberation is not its fruit to be accomplished, nor is there any other liberation.
The cessation of ignorance is liberation; that [ignorance] is declared to be saṃsāra.
Non-dual, peaceful knowledge itself is said to be its cessation. (2.106)

What, then, is this liberation (*mokṣa*)? If it is the non-arising of future bodies, senses, and cognitions—based on the scriptural vision that "neither pleasure nor pain touches one who dwells bodiless"—then that is a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and cannot be something to be accomplished.

Or, if it is the attainment of Brahman, would that be like [the meeting] of Caitra and the village, as suggested by the scriptural texts concerning a path for the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman?
“There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Moving upward through that, one attains immortality. And:
“In as little time as it takes to cast the mind, he goes to the sun; this indeed is the door to the world. Likewise: “He reaches the light, from the light to the day,” and so forth.

Or rather, it may be like the attainment of the juices of various flowers in honey, or of rivers in the ocean, characterized by non-distinction; for as it is seen in the world that "the honey-makers produce honey," and as it is said, "Just as, my dear, these rivers... Or else, it is the effect's attaining the state of the cause, according to the Śruti: "Thus the knower, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains the supreme equality."

Alternatively, it is characterized by a transformation into that very form, like a tiger in yoga, as seen in the scriptural statement: "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and "he attains Brahman.

Or, it is characterized by the recovery of one's own nature through the removal of coloration, like a crystal, because of the Vedic revelation: "Having reached the highest light, he manifests in his own true form.
In this regard, the first alternative is not tenable because [Brahman] is omnipresent, as stated in the passages, "Of all that is within it," and "Eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent.

Furthermore, it is because of non-difference, since there is the teaching that through the knowledge of That, everything is known; because of the direct declaration, "That thou art"; because of the use of the word "Self" everywhere with reference to the inner self; and because of the denial of the perception of difference in the passage, "But he who [sees] another [deity]."

For this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable; nor is it possible due to [the Self's] partlessness (*niravayavatva*), because—as stated in the scripture, "partless and actionless"—an undivided state characterized by the mutual interpenetration of parts is impossible.
Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because an effect is always [potentially] a cause.
If, on the other hand, there were the destruction of the form of the effect, it would follow that liberation consists in annihilation.

In this regard, there is a contradiction in the statement "by knowledge he attains immortality," because [if that were so] it would follow that liberation is the destruction [of the self] by means of knowledge alone;
and since the destruction of the self is undesirable, [liberation] would be fruitless.

Furthermore, the primary relationship of cause and effect has been refuted in the passage concerning the "Imperishable" (akṣara) by the Śruti itself, through the teaching that modifications are unreal, namely: "A modification is a mere name, a verbal handle."

Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable, precisely because there is no difference [between them], since consciousness, which is the very nature of Brahman, is without distinction. If it is argued that the absence of sorrow, delusion, and so forth is what distinguishes the individual cognizing selves (*vijñānātman*), then in that case, if sorrow and the rest were the very selves of the cognizing selves, they could never be destroyed. If, however, they are merely attributes (*guṇa*)—distinct entities that arise and pass away and are momentary—then, by virtue of their very momentariness, they are already destroyed; thus, no further effort toward their destruction would be required.
And it has been stated that [liberation] is not required for the non-arising of those who have attained the state of a Non-returner.
Now, if it is argued that there is a specific sovereignty within Brahman,
and that liberation is the attainment of that [state] through transformation into its nature— on the basis of the Vedic scripture, "He becomes his own lord"— [we reply:]

That is incorrect, because multiple lords are untenable. Would the sovereignty of the individual conscious selves (vijñānātman) be inferior to or equal to that of Brahman? If it were inferior, there would be no attainment of the nature of Brahman, nor the state of self-sovereignty (svārājya).
For instance:
The Supreme Lord, denoted by the word "Brahman," would be their ruler;
and thus there would be the state of being ruled by another.
And in that case, finitude is heard [in scripture].

“But those who know otherwise than this, having other kings, belong to worlds that are subject to decay. And it is observed in the world that by the will of the Supreme Lord, there is a falling away from sovereignty for those whose sovereignty is inferior.
However, equality [of all souls] is simply impossible simultaneously.

If one [of them] is the sovereign lord of all and the ruler of everything, what could the other do to be a lord? Furthermore, there is contradiction. Indeed, there is no reason for these two to possess a single mind. In that case, regarding a single object, if one follows the intention of the other—despite having a contrary intention—then the latter would not be a lord.
There is no conformity with both [principles], because of contradiction.
If there is no conformity with either, both would lack sovereignty.

If it is argued that the cause for unanimity is the accomplishment of the task, as in the case of an assembly, since otherwise such [unanimity] would not be established—[we reply: then each individual lacks sovereignty.
Now, if it is argued that sovereignty is spoken of in a figurative sense to avoid contradiction, [we reply: there would be finitude.
Furthermore, because the creation of the world is impossible [if it were merely figurative], sovereignty cannot be equal to that of Brahman;
for it is heard in scripture that the Supreme alone is the creator of the world.
Through the worship of that [Brahman], liberation occurs after the period of creation.

Therefore, just as with a crystal, the manifestation of one's own nature through the removal of passion (*rāga*) and other afflictions is the attainment of Brahman; for the individual self (*vijñānātman*) has the very nature of Brahman.
And thus it is said: "Having reached the highest light, he manifests in his own form. For if another form were produced, the use of the word "own" (*svena*) would be untenable.

If it is argued that [the expression] is justified because of the non-difference or the connection with that which is being produced, we say no; for the qualification would be meaningless, since everything that is being produced belongs to the self.

In this regard, just as a cloth that is already white is said to have "become white" upon the removal of dirt, so too, when the veil of delusion is removed and its own nature is manifested, it is said that "it manifests itself in its own form."
Likewise, [it is said]: "Being Brahman, he attains Brahman.
Thus, because delusion is characterized by abiding in one's own nature (*svarūpa*), it is not an effect, since the nature exists even prior [to delusion];
for that which is adventitious is not the true nature.
Nor is there any difference [between them], because liberation is simply the removal of ignorance in the manner already described.
Ignorance is saṃsāra;
and knowledge itself is the cessation of ignorance, provided that ignorance is non-apprehension, since the very existence of a thing is the exclusion of its non-existence.
Now, as for error (*viparyāsa*), even so, its cessation occurs only with the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) which is its opposite.

Indeed, the cessation of the cognition of silver is neither something other than the production of the cognition of mother-of-pearl, nor is it something to be accomplished by that [cognition] or by another effort; for the two are simultaneous and do not depend on any further effort.
And thus, the simultaneity of knowledge (*vidyā*) and the attainment of Brahman is heard in scripture:
“Knowing Brahman, one becomes Brahman indeed”; likewise, “knowing the bliss of Brahman, he does not fear”; “He knew Himself alone, thinking ‘I am Brahman’;

therefore, He became all that exists”; and “What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness?”—here, [the words] “knows,” “becomes,” “knowing,” “does not fear,” and “what delusion” correspond to “perceives,” because they are heard in that sequence. As for the occasional occurrence of a different sequence, it is like the expression, “he sleeps having opened his mouth.”
But surely, if there is identity, simultaneity is also untenable.
No; for even a single entity is designated in the form of both existence and non-existence, as in:
"When the jar perishes, at that time the shards are born."
How then are the scriptural texts concerning the paths, the non-differentiation [of the soul], its emergence, and its lordship to be understood? To this they reply:
The scriptural texts concerning the paths do not have as their object the knowledge of Brahman that is pure and free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

For where Brahman—purified of all adjuncts and characterized by being "not coarse" and so forth—is the object of meditation, there it is said, "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman," and "From him the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) do not depart; they are merged right here. Thus, by means of the non-departure of the vital breaths, the attainment of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*) alone is declared.
For as long as that [state] has not been reached, the nature of that Brahman as the conscious self (*vijñānātmatva*) does not exist apart from its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

However, where it is said, "Consisting of mind, having breath for its body, whose form is light," there the object of worship is that which possesses adjuncts; those [scriptural passages] have that as their subject matter.
Where this is heard—

“Indeed, there are two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here; there is the lake Airammadīya, the Aśvattha tree Soma-savana, the city Aparājitā, and the golden hall built by the Lord for Brahman.
Likewise, there is the scriptural statement regarding those who do not know Brahman attaining that same goal: “And those who, in the forest, worship faith, truth, and austerity.”
But the attainment of the Supreme Brahman is not possible for those who do not know Brahman, as it is said: "By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where all desires have vanished;
neither those who give sacrificial gifts nor the ignorant ascetics go there."

Thus, it is because of such statements as, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death. If so, how is the scriptural teaching on non-returning to be understood? On this point, some hold the view that by resorting to gradual liberation (*kramamukti*), having reached that [intermediate state] and there attained knowledge of reality free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhitattvajñāna*), they attain the supreme state.
As it has been said:
"Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of the Vedanta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation and are pure in being—
they all, having attained the supreme immortality at the time of the final end, are liberated in the worlds of Brahman."

"In the worlds of Brahmā" is a reference to the *kārya-brahmaloka* (the effected world of Brahmā), for its plurality is established there by way of its constituent parts, as indicated by the use of the plural number.

"The time of the ultimate end" refers to the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), which is the conclusion of Brahmā’s own term of office. At that time, being immortalized in the form of the Supreme Brahman, they become immortal through the yoga of renunciation—that is, through the yoga consisting of the renunciation of their own performed actions and their fruits, and through the meditation that "all this, including the agent and so forth, is Brahman."
And thus says the Smṛti: "When the time of universal dissolution has arrived, at the end of the Supreme, all those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state along with Brahmā."
Others, however, think as follows:

just as in the world of the Moon, having dwelt there for as long as their merit lasts, those who have experienced their enjoyments return while that world itself still persists; it is not so in the case of the world of Brahman, from which there is no return while it persists.
Rather, their stay there lasts until the dissolution of that [world].
For at that dissolution, one does not return from there;
and thus non-return is heard in scripture.
Accordingly, the qualification "they do not return to this human whirl" and "to this [world] here" implies that the immortality mentioned in "he attains immortality" is relative, as for example—
“‘The gods are immortal’—
and likewise there is a traditional recollection from the Purāṇas:
‘For immortality is said to be that state which lasts until the dissolution of all beings.’”
As for what is thought—
that although Brahman is all-pervading, there is a distinction between its modified and unmodified states,
and consequently, a distinction of location— [that is not so].
Furthermore, a distinction of location is heard in scripture regarding the unmodified Brahman: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven.
Therefore, a specific path is appropriate for the attainment of Brahman, which is unmodified and has a fixed location.
This must be carefully considered:

first of all, this path does not belong to one who has not yet produced non-dual, pure knowledge (*vidyā*), because [the scripture] speaks of it for the knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*); nor does it belong to one who already possesses such knowledge.
"Because all distinctions are destroyed upon the arising of knowledge.

Even the scriptural statement regarding non-distinction, illustrated by the example of the river of honey, refers to the absence of discriminative knowledge, and not to a literal non-distinction of that kind.
Even the scriptural accounts of creation are not primarily concerned with creation;
what then? They have as their main purpose the realization of the single reality of the Self.
Therefore, the determination of their meaning must be established solely in accordance with that [realization], and not in contradiction to it.
For instance:

"O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known? Because it begins with the state of unity—“In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second”—and concludes with the realization of the reality of the single Self through unity—“All this has that as its essence;
That is the Truth; That is the Self; That art thou”—this entire passage is understood to be devoted solely to the comprehension of the reality of the oneness of the Self.
In this regard, if the subsequent creation of the principles (tattvas), such as fire and the rest, were enjoined as being real, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).

Therefore, just as in the case of the Upāṃśuyāja injunction, where the statements beginning with "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper" do not attain the status of separate injunctions due to the defect of syntactical split—instead remaining as praises for the sake of that [injunction] by conforming to its purpose through the introduction and conclusion concerning "freedom from redundancy"—so too the scriptural texts regarding creation exist as means to [realize] oneness.
Nor can the opposite be asserted.
The scriptural mention of oneness itself is for the purpose of understanding difference, because there is an introduction through oneness and a conclusion through it in all cases;
that by which a passage begins and that by which it concludes constitutes its meaning.
Furthermore, the understanding of difference results in no fruit.

However, from the realization of oneness, there is seen and heard a fruit, namely the cessation of grief and so forth, because that [cessation] is understood through the vision of the pure, unitary Self, as it is heard in scripture: "What delusion, what grief can there be for one who perceives oneness? Furthermore, that which lacks a fruit of its own serves as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) to that which possesses a fruit;
thus, it functions as a means.
And this world does not have non-existence as its root.
What then? It has non-dual, singular Existence as its root.
Furthermore, because the effect is non-different from its cause, this world is indeed one with Existence, just like a jar or other such objects.
For jars and other such objects do not transcend oneness with clay in its form as clay.
[Objection: But in this way, would not the primary relation of cause and effect be asserted?
[Reply: This is not so, because it is merely a means for entering into the realization of oneness.
Indeed, it is not the relationship of cause and effect alone that is to be established here, such that it would be taken as primary according to the literal meaning of the words.
It has been stated that [the goal] is attained through the means of unity;
and by this means, the person is led into unity.
And that [position] is primarily contradictory to the principal [teaching],

because the scripture, through its repeated declarations such as "one only, without a second," is intent upon the negation of all difference; therefore, it cannot be said that there is unity in the form of the cause and plurality in the form of the effect.

Because it is established that only the cause is real in the statement, “That is the Truth, that is the Self,” and because elsewhere there is the scriptural teaching that difference is accessible through illusion in the words, “Indra [appears] through māyās,” and because the absence of difference is heard directly.

“For here there is no diversity whatsoever. Since it has already been explained that difference and non-difference are contradictory and thus untenable prior [to such realization], their lack of contradiction is now described: the conceptualization of difference exists merely as its (the Reality’s) material cause, like the reflection of an image, or like letters, words, sentences, and so forth.

For just as there is no production of reflections of various forms from the original object (*bimba*), because the conceptual differentiation of the various reflections consists merely in the original object being their material cause;

for indeed, there are no entities that are reflections distinct from the original object or from one another. Rather, the original object is the mere appearance of that multiplicity, having it as its material cause.

Likewise, there are no such entities as words, sentences, or contexts apart from the phonemes, because the conceptualization of them consists merely of those [phonemes]. It is said that "words are produced from phonemes" and "sentences from words.
Furthermore, even in a dream, creation is heard of in scripture:

"There are no chariots there, no yoked horses, and no roads; yet he creates chariots, yoked horses, and roads. This [creation of words and sentences] might be similar to that, since its purpose is something else.
The Lord himself has stated that it is not ultimately real because of the unreality of modifications, saying: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name.
[126,i] Even in the scriptures concerning divine sovereignty, this is heard to be the ripening of one's own knowledge of qualities—

“He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold,” “he obtains all desires,” and “he becomes a self-ruler”—this refers to [the state of] *sāmrājya*, not liberation (*mokṣa*), for the latter has as its sole cause the knowledge of Brahman free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi-brahmavidyā*). As for the scriptural mention in some places of "non-return" (*apunarāvṛtti*), two interpretations have been explained for that as well; such is one view.
Others, however, think as follows:

because Brahman is the self of all and the lord of all, and because he is the enjoyer of all enjoyments, and because the joys of the gods and others consist solely of his own bliss, the scriptural declarations such as "He attains all worlds and all desires" and "He becomes his own ruler" are intended to praise liberation, which is characterized by the manifestation of the nature of Brahman. This is for the sake of extolling that state in which the manifestation of the form of Brahman occurs.
Objection: If all desires are attained through being the Self of all, would there not also be the attainment of all sorrow, delusion, and so forth?
Reply: No, because those [sorrow and delusion] are not of the nature of Brahman, being superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Knowledge, sovereignty, bliss, and enjoyment, however, are the very form of Brahman, according to such scriptural passages as: “Brahman is consciousness and bliss” (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*); “There is no other seer but He” (*nānyo ’to ’sti draṣṭā*); “Other beings live on but a fraction of this very bliss” (*etasyaivānandasyānyāni bhūtāni mātrām upajīvanti*); “He is the Lord of all” (*sarvasyeśānaḥ*); and “Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī” (*etasya vā akṣarasya praśāsane gārgi*), and others.
And thus, whatever lordship, whatever consciousness, and whatever bliss exist in beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects—all these belong to Brahman;
it is logical that he, whose own nature as Brahman has become manifest, partakes of them.
However, the worlds and so forth are superimposed by ignorance and are not the form of Brahman.

How could they possibly assail that which has manifested as the very nature of Brahman? But surely, since non-dual Brahman is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), there is an absence of any object of knowledge and an absence of anything to be ruled; therefore, both consciousness and sovereignty are untenable.
In that case, even the scriptural statements "the All-Knowing" and "the Lord of All" would have to be explained away.
This is not sound.
For His status as Lord is not produced by that which is to be ruled, nor is His status as Knower produced by that which is to be known.

Rather, by means of His established nature as knowledge and His established power of ruling, He attains the object to be known and directs and governs that which is to be ruled, just like light and heat.
For indeed, by means of His established nature as light, the sun illuminates that which is to be illuminated.
However, its nature as light does not depend upon that which is illuminated, nor is the burning power of fire dependent upon the fuel to be burned.

And thus, because the entire phenomenal world is manifested by that very consciousness, its omniscience is established by such scriptural passages as, "By its light all this shines," and "There is no other seer but He.
Its status as the Lord of All is likewise established by its sovereignty, since through its lordship, the various lords exercise their rule over those who are to be ruled.
And thus, by saying "He is the Lord of Beings" and "He is the Guardian of the World," the sovereignty of Brahmā, Indra, Yama, and the others is declared.
Furthermore, the attainment of all desires [is attributed to Him] because the bliss of the gods and so forth belongs to Him;
through the attainment of bliss within desires, the desires are attained, but not in their own essential form.

Thus, it should be described as: "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and delighting with women," because he experiences the enjoyment of bliss pertaining to those objects, but not because of actual union with women and the like. This is just as in the expression, "delighting in the Self, playing with the Self, having the Self as his companion"; for literal play with the Self or companionship with the Self is indeed impossible.

Since the very same [attributes] such as knowledge belonging to Him, though limited by conceptual construction, exist in all beings without being delimited [in their essence], therefore, wherever there is no absolute limitation due to their excellence, the Lord— having designated those respective beings as His own self on account of proximity,
saying "Among sages I am Vyāsa," and so forth— concluded with the words, "Whatever being is possessed of glory."
Likewise, there are such statements as "the unseen seer, the unheard hearer," and so forth, because the seeing and other functions of all beings are dependent upon that consciousness.
Others, however, say:
Whatever designation there may be regarding the Supreme that relies upon name and form, all of it is for the purpose of meditation.
For example: "The person who is in the sun," "He has golden hair and beard," and so forth.

For the Supreme, who is established in His own majesty, there can be no confinement to a specific location, nor can there be any connection with specific forms for Him who transcends all distinctions.
Furthermore, this [Self] is distinct from the body, because of the scriptural statement regarding the rising above all evils:
"He has risen above all evils. Moreover, such meditation is enjoined;
likewise, it should be understood from His omniscience as well.
Thus, the manifestation of that very nature of Brahman as the Self is its attainment; that is liberation. And that [attainment] is indeed knowledge itself.
Therefore, liberation is not something to be produced, nor is it something other than knowledge—this is sufficient.
[128,ii] Now, it might be thought: let liberation not be something to be accomplished.
However, the destruction of the causes of bondage is what is to be accomplished;
the means for that accomplishment would be the vision of the Self.
And its fruit is heard to be the destruction of the karmas that are the causes of bondage.
“And his karmas are exhausted when He, the higher and the lower, is seen.

Likewise: “Just as a tuft of reed-stalks thrown into a fire is consumed, even so all his evils are consumed. By the word “evil” (pāpman), merit (puṇya) is also included, because it has a faulty result; for elsewhere, beginning with, “Day and night do not cross this bridge, nor old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor good deeds, nor evil deeds,” and concluding with, “all evils turn back from there.”
And without the destruction of that [karma], there is no attainment of security;

therefore, it must necessarily be performed. Nor is there no destruction of karma whose fruit has not yet been experienced, because expiations (prāyaścitta), when enjoined in connection with a fault, have the destruction of that [fault] as their result.
Therefore, just as by means of expiatory rites, the destruction of the causes of bondage is accomplished through knowledge;
and that itself is liberation, because the root *muc* signifies the loosening of bonds.
And thus, there is no fault of being finite, since even the effect, which is a total destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), is imperishable.
To this it is replied:
Even the destruction of the cause of bondage does not result from that [knowledge] by way of expiation and the like;
for when all ignorance has dissolved, nothing remains to be destroyed. (2.107)
Ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of bondage, has reached its end within knowledge (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, the destruction of the cause of bondage is not something to be accomplished by the vision of the Self;
rather, it arises precisely while that [knowledge] brings about the dissolution of the entire empirical functioning of ignorance.
Furthermore, the differentiation of the enjoyment of the fruits of karma has ignorance as its substrate.
In that regard, when ignorance is uprooted without remainder, there is nothing further to be severed;
for actions are superimposed by ignorance, and upon the destruction of that [ignorance], they are indeed destroyed along with it by means of knowledge.
For one who perceives non-duality as the reality of the Self, there is no room at all for the ripening of karma, since that ripening depends upon the perception of duality.
And because the cessation of karma occurs only through the eradication of ignorance,
therefore, karmas are considered by those who practice *prasaṃkhyāna* to be equal to doubt and error.
“The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when He, who is both the high and the low, is seen.”

[129,i] But if liberation is accepted as occurring through the exhaustion of karma in this way, then liberation would occur immediately upon the vision of reality, without waiting for the fall of the body. The scriptural passage that speaks of waiting for the fall of the body—“For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged”—would be contradicted.

However, for one from whom it is understood through scripture that knowledge is the means for the destruction of [karma], according to that [scriptural authority], the destruction of some [karma] occurs through knowledge, while the destruction of others occurs through experience.

In this regard, although the statement "and his karmas are exhausted" suggests the exhaustion of all [karma] without distinction, because of the scriptural declaration that "for him there is delay only so long [as the body lasts]," it is understood that there is no exhaustion of those actions whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*) and whose experiences have already commenced; their exhaustion occurs only through experience.
For if all [karma] were exhausted, the waiting for the fall of the body would not be logical.
As it has been said:
“But only those previous [karmas] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], for that is their limit”; and “But having exhausted the others by experience, one attains [Brahman].

For if ignorance were destroyed by knowledge alone, there would be no distinction regarding the cessation of the worldly process of the ripening of karma; since all [karma] would be destroyed, one would be liberated immediately.
There is no fault at all.
For this scriptural passage does not state that liberation has death as its limit qualified by a long duration; rather, it expresses its swiftness.
Just as someone, wishing to convey that something is very quick, says with regard to some task: [and so forth].
"It has been so long for me since I bathed and ate"—this [statement] is likewise [an example].
Otherwise, one would not have said "only that long" (*tāvadeva*);
rather, one would have simply said "for a long time" (*ciram*).
However, from the expression "just then" (*tāvadeva*), it is understood that the intent is swiftness. Therefore, liberation occurs immediately; there is nothing to be awaited.
Nevertheless, waiting for the fall of the body does indeed occur there as a necessary consequence.
Alternatively, having restated the quality of being "long," the fact that it has the falling off of the body as its limit is stated here;
otherwise, if both the length and the specific limit were being stated, there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda).
In this regard, the meaning is as follows: if for someone it is long, it lasts only until he is liberated.

Now, in the first position, since the fall of the body occurs immediately after the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the description of the characteristics of one whose wisdom is established (*sthitaprajña*)—beginning with "What is the speech of one whose wisdom is established? and so forth—is not tenable.
In the second position as well, because the destruction of all [karmas] would take a long time, it is untenable to prescribe a specific limit for that state.
It is said:

first of all, the one of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña) is not yet a perfected being (siddha) whose ignorance has entirely vanished; rather, he must be a practitioner (sādhaka) who has merely attained a particular stage.
Nor do we say—
The separation from the body occurs immediately after the realization of Brahman;
however, one must wait for the exhaustion of the karma that has already begun to bear fruit through experience.
In that regard, for some, liberation occurs at that very time.
For some, there is a certain degree of delay.

For example, when the fear arising from the superimposition of a snake upon a rope ceases upon the perception of reality, the trembling and other such symptoms may cease for some at that very moment, while for others they persist for some time due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) thereof.

In the same way, even when all karma has been exhausted, the maintenance of the body persists, being dependent on the persistence of the latent impressions of the fruition currently being experienced.
It is like the continued spinning of a potter’s wheel even after the potter’s activity has ceased.

[131,i] But if, in this way, the perception of distinctions such as the enjoyer and so forth persists for one who knows Brahman, then it would persist even after the fall of the body; in that case, liberation would not be certain even for the knower.

And thus, there is a contradiction with the Śruti text: "Only for so long is it delayed. Now, if it is argued that because ignorance has been eradicated, it cannot persist, then it would not exist even for a moment; this is the very same contradiction. This is a rope with a noose at both ends. It is replied:

Just as, even when fear has vanished and one has regained composure, trembling and other such symptoms may persist due to mere residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), yet this persistence does not mean that the fear itself continues for a long time;
nor is the impression equal in effect to its primary cause;
nor is it stable.
Otherwise, there would be no cessation of trembling and the like at all.
Nor does one require another cause for their cessation once the vision of reality—which is the cause for the removal of fear—has occurred;
for it ceases gradually from that very vision itself, or spontaneously, like the momentum of the spinning of a potter’s wheel.

Thus, when ignorance has ceased and all karmas—both those whose effects have already begun and those whose effects have not yet begun—have ceased, even the wise person, though he perceives this Self as an experiencer within the body due to the residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the fruition that has already commenced, does so merely as a reflection; he does not, like the ignorant, possess a firmly established attachment.

And this one whose wisdom is steady has been described as such: free from desire, satisfied in the nature of the Self, his mind undisturbed by sufferings—which, though appearing merely as shadows, are clung to because of a lack of insight into reality, like artificial tigers and the like—and devoid of longing for pleasures, which are like artificial delights.

Just as for the ignorant person there is a perception of objects such as women fashioned from clay or wood that is merely shadow-like and devoid of attachment, so too for the wise man, whose karma and ignorance have perished, there is a perception of objects through mere impressions, appearing only as shadows.
And thus, [the scripture] shows the wise man’s lack of attachment to the body: "Just as a snake's slough might lie dead and cast away upon an anthill, even so is this body.
For the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) does not yield a result equal to that of the primary cause, like the trembling and so forth;
nor does it persist for a long time, because the residual impression endures only for a short duration.

And in that very same way, no other cause is required for its cessation, because it too ceases either gradually through the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) or by itself. This state is celebrated as "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*). Furthermore, the exhaustion of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of karma whose effects have already begun is understood to occur only with the falling away of the body.
If that [karma] were to continue, the fall of the body would not occur at all; thus, it is impossible for even a mere shadow of its fruition to be seen after the fall of the body.
For the residue of the fruition of whatever karma has initiated a particular body manifests only within that very body.
As for those karmas whose effects have not yet begun—that is, those whose operation has not been attained—they have already ceased, and therefore no latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of them remains.
For the persistence of a mere trace of an effect follows from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) whose activity has been obtained;
indeed, when fear has not attained its activity and trembling and so forth have not yet arisen, there is no persistence of trembling and so forth from that impression.

Therefore, since those whose effects have not begun have not attained their activity, and since the exhaustion of the impressions of effects already begun is understood to occur upon the fall of the body, liberation (*kaivalya*) is inevitable for the knower once this body has fallen.

And in this case, the persistence of trembling and so forth occurs either from the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the cause that has already produced its effect, or from the residual impression of the effect itself, or likewise from the residual impressions of both;
or else, fear arises from the residual impression of fear, and from that, trembling and so forth;
or trembling and so forth persist from the residual impression of trembling and so forth.
In every case, even when the cause has ceased, there persists a remainder of the effect due to residual impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, the maintenance of the body for the knower (*vidvas*) occurs either from the residual impression of karma that has attained its manifestation or from its ripening (*vipāka*).
As it is said in another treatise (*tantra*):
“Maintaining its body, it persists by the force of its formative impulses (saṃskāra), like the whirling of a potter’s wheel.
As for those, however, who think—

It is argued that for those karmas whose fruition has already begun, just as it is impossible to stop an arrow in flight or a wheel in motion, there can be no obstruction; therefore, one must await their exhaustion through experience.
This is incorrect, for an arrow can indeed be obstructed by walls and the like, and destroyed by cutting and other means.

Furthermore, there are propitiatory rites (*śāntika-karmāṇi*) intended for the destruction of such karma whose ripening is imminent, as indicated by dreams and other signs, and which is to be experienced in the present body.
Therefore, stability arises from conditioning alone.
[133,i] But is it not the case that ignorance itself is simply the remainder of the effects of conditioning?
In this regard, how does the dissolution of all ignorance occur, or how is it that nothing remains to be severed? It is said:

those two [ignorance and its effects], once swallowed by the counteragent—the vision of the pure, unitary Self—are already dissolved; for, being incapable of action and devoid of binding power, they require no other cause for their cessation.
Indeed, for one who directly experiences the pure Self, the appearance of karmic fruition—which does not touch that Self—is rendered ineffective as a bond and is utterly dissolved.

Just as for one who perceives the true nature of a painting or the like, the appearance of a woman or other such forms does not serve as a cause for passion and the like; so too, for one who knows the Self to be pure—or even if a contrary appearance, such as blackness, arises in relation to a sword or similar object—that appearance, failing to find any foothold due to the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), simply dissolves away.
Consequently, the Self does not grieve because of the impurity caused by that appearance, nor does it rejoice because of its brilliance.
This is because, although both appear, their manifestation within the Self is obstructed by the vision of reality.

And thus, as for what is said—that the maintenance of the body must proceed either from karma or from residual impressions (saṃskāra)—what is the distinction? And how can there be an exhaustion of karma while its effects continue? For its exhaustion is understood only through the cessation of those effects.
Therefore, it is only logical that "having exhausted the others by experience, one attains [liberation]."
That too has been refuted.

For the ripening of karma (karmavipāka) touches the self and involves grief or rejoicing for the ignorant; but for the knower, because it does not touch the self, it is a mere appearance, like the specific reflections produced by a jewel, a sword, a mirror, or other such objects.
It is not a true ripening, because it is neither rejoiced in nor hated.
And thus it has been shown: "Having encountered this or that, whether auspicious or inauspicious, one neither rejoices nor feels aversion.
Likewise—

“That which is the waking state for beings is night for the sage who sees. For one who sees, the phenomenal expansion of the body and so forth is night; because he does not touch it, it is equal to that which is not being seen.

Objection: If the appearance of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca*), even when it has arisen, does not touch the Self because it is obstructed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and if it is thus ineffective and not bondage—since that [knowledge] arises from verbal testimony alone—then what is the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*) and the like? Reply: It is said: Verbal knowledge is of the nature of indirect cognition (*parokṣa*), whereas the appearance of phenomenal diversity is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, because there is no contradiction between the two, the appearance of phenomenal diversity does not fail to touch the Self, is not ineffective, and is not non-bondage; just as in the case of a substance whose sweetness is determined through another means of knowledge, yet its sweetness remains directly perceived.

The appearance of bitterness at the door of the sense-organ does not persist as a mere appearance without contact with a substance; and thus that substance, like something ultimately bitter, results in suffering for one who has not realized its sweetness.

However, for one who has directly realized the reality of the Self through meditation and other means, even though the appearance of the phenomenal world exists, it does not touch the Self due to its opposition [to that realization], just as the appearance of a lion in Devadatta [does not touch him].
In the superimposition "Devadatta is a lion," although the appearance manifests, it does not touch him; it is ineffective and not a cause of fear.

The manifestation of the reality of the Self is eternal; therein, there is no further possibility for error. Verbal cognition, however, is dependent on a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is momentary, and therein there is again the possibility of error.
For it is observed that when one does not investigate the means of knowledge, one may again experience fear of a rope due to the delusion that it is a snake.
Therefore, even in this case, one should constantly maintain verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*).

What else could there be that constitutes meditation (*upāsana*) other than this? Consequently, the destruction of the cause of bondage is itself knowledge (*vidyā*), and it is not something to be accomplished by means of that [knowledge].

The same should be said regarding the non-clinging of future demerit (*uttarāghāśleṣa*): "Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus," because the distinction between agent and action has been dissolved through knowledge.
Thus, there will be no assumption of multiple fruits for knowledge, nor will there be a transformation of statements describing the present state into injunctions regarding results.
As for what was said— that Brahman is not the object of verbal cognition— it is replied to as follows:
Brahman is not accessible through the cognition of words, for the operation of cognition is impossible [with respect to it].

A subject that is unestablished is not fit for the demonstration of a specific cognition; nor is a positive affirmation possible when its locus has not been delineated, for mere cognition itself is not what is being affirmed. (2.109)
Indeed, it is not mere knowledge that is enjoined, but rather a specific object of knowledge.
Furthermore, there can be no injunction regarding something that is unestablished and undefined;
for one cannot be enjoined toward an object that is unknown.
Furthermore, the distinction of cognition is mediated by its object;
and an object that is not already established is incapable of defining the distinctions of that cognition.
Nor can the nature of the self be established through anything other than words.

If there is no establishment [of the object] even from the word, then, since the specific cognition mediated by that [word] is not established, the object is untenable, and consequently the injunction is untenable.
Furthermore, he demonstrates that for one who maintains that the injunction concerns a specific cognition, the very authority regarding the reality of the self is lost: [135,i]

Whether the ritual procedure is aimed at its own accomplishment or is intent upon the accomplishment of an action, the realization of the non-dual reality of Brahman is independent of such causes. (2.110)
The understanding of this [mantra] derived from its application consists in its purpose being knowledge or ritual action;
that which is not intent upon that [purpose] is not authoritative, like the cognition arising from an explanatory passage (arthavāda). (2.111)
Since an injunction pertains to action, it is incapable of operating upon a substance;
on the contrary, the accomplishment of that [substance] results from its connection with existence (sattā), and thus the [injunction] fails. (2.112)

The cognition of the qualified object is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but not [the cognition] of the qualifier; for even though the cognition is qualified, it is necessarily determined by its object. (2.113)
It does not indeed establish the existence [of the object], because it occurs through superimposition (*samāropa*).

If, first of all, the state of being an action (*kāryatā*) were understood as belonging to the injunction (*niyoga*) itself, then that [injunction], having culminated in its own accomplishment, would cease together with the word.

Alternatively, if the understanding of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) arises regarding the object (*viṣaya*) by virtue of the application (*viniyoga*), even so, [the injunction] culminates in the establishment of that object.
In either case, it does not touch upon the reality of things;
therein, the realization of the non-dual nature of the self would be devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*).
It might be argued:
"The reality of the thing is understood through the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words 'the Self which is free from evil, ageless,' or otherwise.
But that is not so, because [those words] have another purpose.

For that [cognition] does not terminate in the thought "this is thus," but rather culminates in a sense of duty in the form "this is to be understood as such"; it is not a means of valid cognition regarding the true nature of things, because—like the knowledge arising from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding historical narratives—it is intent upon something else.

Nor is the reality of the Self itself the object of an injunction, because an injunction has as its object that which is to be performed, and action is of that nature; for if a substance were presented by its own word as an already established fact, it would be impossible to apply an operation toward that which is not to be performed.
On the contrary, the establishment of the essential nature of a substance occurs through the accompaniment of existence touched by one of the three times, which is not subject to an injunction.
“Such a thing existed, exists, or will exist.
Therefore, it is defective when its own nature (*svarūpa*) is being established;
for there is no comprehension of the existence of that which is to be enjoined even across the three periods of time.
For when it is said, "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the existence of the sacrifice as belonging to the past, the present, or the future is not understood.
But is it not the case that the future time is understood, since an injunction has the future as its object?
This is not so.
For that which is enjoined will not necessarily be performed, because it would follow that there is no fault in failing to perform what has been enjoined.
But surely, the expression of a qualified action is accepted as being authoritative even with respect to its qualification— as in the case of "one should sacrifice with soma."
Likewise, in the statement, "The son of Devadatta, adorned with armlets and earrings, broad-chested, is studying," the entire collection of qualifiers is perceived along with the act of studying.
True;
the means of knowledge that establishes a qualified action is also a means of knowledge for the qualifier, since the cognition [of the whole] occurs elsewhere [than through the parts alone].

For a cognition, when being cognized as qualified by a particular object, does not necessarily establish the actual existence of that particular object, because it can also occur through the superimposition of such an appearance upon something else that is otherwise; just as in the case of the statement, "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire," where there is no perception of fire in the sky and so forth.
Here, he says:
Surely our cognition does not have a contrary object, because that would contradict direct experience.
Furthermore, the cognition of silver is a memory of silver because it lacks reliability.
Indeed, it is not logical that one thing should be perceived as another, for that would contradict actual experience.
How could one thing be the object when something else appears in consciousness? Moreover, this is due to a lack of reliability.
If cognition were to deviate from the form of the object, there could be no ascertainment of that object through it.
Furthermore, a cognition that does not conform to the form of the object would be without an object and without a support, and thus it would be ungraspable;
for the mere cause of cognition cannot be its support, just as the eye and other sense organs are not.
Thus, since it is not a means of cognition (*avedaka*), the object is not established through that [perception] even by depending on something else.
What then is this "silver" when the eye is in contact with mother-of-pearl? It is memory, arising from the apprehension of a common feature.
If so, how is it an error? It is due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between what is being perceived and what is being remembered.

Thus, this is merely the conceit of those devoid of discrimination who perceive non-difference when the difference is not grasped—just as, from a distance, one has the conceit of perceiving contact among trees when the intervening space is not perceived.
Therefore, the thought "I remember" is simply a recollection of silver that lacks discrimination.
To this, it is replied:
For this [cognition] would not have arisen with respect to a fragment of mother-of-pearl at that time. // 2.115 //

If it is argued that the activity toward silver occurs because of its proximity, [we reply] no, because of its non-proximity; if it is argued that this is due to the non-cognition of its non-proximity, then from what source comes the restriction of activity? (2.116)
Whatever occurs there is caused by the proximity of those very [elements], because elsewhere there is no apprehension of difference and likewise no apprehension of distinction. (2.117)

If the difference in activity arises from the non-apprehension of distinction due to similarity, then one would act toward unseen objects such as clods of earth because of that lack of discrimination. (2.118)

If that cognition does not arise there [in the shell], then it would not arise even with respect to a fragment of mother-of-pearl; if, on the other hand, it exists as having a contrary object, how can its nature as a misapprehension be denied? (2.119)
Because it is not seen, there is no engagement with it, just as with a fragment of mother-of-pearl;
for that form by which it is seen is not the cause of such engagement. (2.120)
If it is argued that this [error] arises from the non-discrimination between what is seen and memory, then let this be examined here:
does the cognition of silver arise from the awakening to reality, or from the non-awakening to reality? (2.121)

In the former case, activity occurs toward what is seen, while the cognition is held to have a contrary object; in the latter case, there is no distinction between the seen and the unseen, and [the cognition] is not useful. (2.122)
For those two are indeed employed for superimposition in one's own perception of yoga;
otherwise, there could be no visual error regarding what is unseen or unconnected [to the senses]. (2.123)

If a piece of mother-of-pearl in contact with the eye were perceived as "not silver," or if silver were perceived in that same way, a person desiring silver would not proceed toward the piece of mother-of-pearl with the intention of grasping it, because for him there would be no cognition of it as "silver," just as in the case of a clod of earth or similar objects.
Nor does that activity occur with respect to the remembered silver, because of its absence from that location;
for even when an object has been cognized, one who desires it does not proceed toward a place where it is not present.
It might be argued:
"Activity occurs there because silver is perceived while its non-proximity is not perceived.
That is not so, because the activity occurs with respect to the fragment of mother-of-pearl itself.
However, activity occurs precisely there because it is based on the proximity of that object.

Since the cognition is merely of silver and lacks the discrimination [of memory], activity would occur elsewhere as well, because the non-apprehension of non-proximity is no different in that case too.
Now, it might be thought:

in the case of objects in other places, there is no activity because one perceives their distinction from silver through a specific perception; however, in the case of a fragment of mother-of-pearl, there is activity because one fails to grasp its distinction from the silver revolving in memory, due to the cognition of only the common white and lustrous form and the absence of a cognition of its specific qualities.
Even so, in the case of the worlds and so forth which have not been seen, there would be activity because their difference from that [silver] has not been ascertained.

Now, if there is no cognition of silver in those [other things], then there is none in the other case either. Or, if such a cognition were present, one would have to admit that it is a misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).
If, on the other hand, it is argued that one does not act toward unperceived things simply because they are unperceived, then one would likewise not act toward the mother-of-pearl.
Now, it may be argued: "That which has the form of silver is not cognized by that [means of knowledge].
Just as there is no cognition for one whose eye is not in contact [with the object], so too there is none for the mother-of-pearl, even though it is in contact.
If this is what you think—
Due to the distinction between what is being seen and what is being remembered, the [cognition] operates only when there is contact with the eye, and not in any other case.
Even in that instance, this must be examined:

does the activity arise from a cognition of non-difference based on the perception of proximity—since there is no actual agent of distinction (viveka-kṛt) for the apprehension of distinction—or rather, from the mere absence of the cognition of difference? In the former case, there is error; in the latter case, there is no distinction between the visible and the invisible, or between that which is in contact and that which is not, because the non-apprehension of difference is equal in both.
For there is no utility whatsoever for the non-apprehension of either the sensory contact or the perception; however, it does exist in the case of the superimposition of what is unreal.
Indeed, a sensory superimposition is not possible in any way with respect to that which is unapprehended or not in contact [with the senses].
If it is argued that memory is distinct from perception precisely because of its own cognition, then how could there be non-discrimination?
Otherwise, there would always be non-discrimination whenever a universal is perceived. (2.124)
Error does not arise from remembering something else, nor from the observation of doubt;
for if you consider doubt to be produced by the non-discrimination between two remembered objects, [then that is not the case]. (2.125)
Therefore, this [objection] applies to neither of the two, because a reversal is observed in both cases within traditional memory (smṛti):
[the reversal] regarding direct perception (adhyakṣa) occurs through specific cognition, whereas [the reversal] regarding memory occurs if it is analyzed with discrimination. (2.126)
If this self-cognition does not exist, how could there be a single cognition when there is forgetfulness?
For one who remembers the very oneness of the previous form clearly in the moon, [how could it be otherwise]? (2.127)

How can there be for you the delusion of duality caused by defects such as cataracts, or the perception of water for one who longs for water but whose mind is fixed upon a mother-of-pearl shell? (2.128)
For there would either be no error at all, or it would have to exist in the water itself.
Furthermore, you must explain this:
is that which is being remembered distinguished from that which is being perceived by its own cognition alone, or not?

The very nature of recollective cognition (*smṛti-jñāna*) is such that it either manifests [the object] as distinct from the object of valid cognition (*pramātavya*), or it rests solely upon its own nature.

In the former case, how could there be a non-discrimination (*aviveka*) between the object remembered and the object of perception, since they are already distinguished by their own respective cognitions? In the latter case as well, there would always be error in recollection, because when one perceives a general feature (*sāmānya*), there is non-discrimination due to the memory of another [particular].
But that is not so, for doubt (*saṃśaya*) is also observed.
Now, it might be thought:
when there is a single recollection, there is error due to non-discrimination;
but when there are multiple recollections, there is doubt.
"It is not due to a lack of discrimination regarding a single [object];
that is incorrect, for even when there is recollection of many [objects], error is observed."
