If, in the case of a perceptible object, that which is being remembered is distinguished from it by means of a cognition of its specific qualities (*viśeṣajñāna*)— and not by means of a cognition of itself— then, in the absence of such a cognition of specific qualities, there would be only doubt when both are remembered, rather than the appearance of one thing being an error (*viparyaya*). However,
if that which is being remembered is distinguished from it by means of a cognition of itself, then the distinction between memory and error is admitted.
In that case, even when there is recollection of multiple [alternatives], error is possible due to specific defects of the sense organs;
and this has been demonstrated:
even when there is perception of a common property, if one recalls only one alternative at a certain time, there is neither doubt nor error, because the defects have not been nourished.
Therefore, at that time, it is from one's own cognition alone that the remembered object is discriminated, not from the determination of a specific perceived object.
If this is so, how can there be a non-discrimination between the presently perceived and the remembered?

Moreover, the unity [perceived] in the moon while one is recollecting its previous form is a different matter entirely; it is an illusion of duality, not born from a failure to discriminate between two things being recollected.
Nor is it due to a failure to discriminate between the distinct functions of the cognitive faculties, because those two [faculties] are neither perceptible nor objects of recollection.
Furthermore, for one whose mind is fixed on mother-of-pearl, there would be no error of perceiving water when they are thirsty.
Or it may have the appearance of water, due to the distinction between the remembered object and its own cognition. Furthermore, not every error is necessarily bound up with similarity. (2.129)
An illusion of yellow is seen in what is white, and an illusion of bitterness in what is sweet;
for due to some slight resemblance, there would be no one who does not experience error in that regard. (2.130)

Therefore, due to the specific distribution of the capacities of the defects of the sense organs, there is a restriction [of error] to particular errors; however, when there is no apprehension due to a defect, there is no restriction to error. (2.131)

If error arises from the recollection of a similar object upon seeing a similar one, how could there be an illusion of yellow in what is white, or a delusion of bitterness in what is sweet? [Furthermore,] such an internal bile would be perceived even by one who does not employ the external sense organs, because—like collyrium applied to the eye—it would be invisible due to its location within the organ, just like the blackness inherent in it.
Moreover, if there were error based on any slight similarity, there would be the undesirable consequence of all types of errors occurring everywhere.
Therefore, the production of specific erroneous cognitions is determined by the particular capacities of the defects of the sense organs.
If, however, the operation of the defect consisted merely in non-apprehension, there would be no restriction regarding error due to defects such as jaundice (kāmalā) and the like;
for error is not caused by similarity, since error is observed even in the case of what is dissimilar.

Nor is there a failure to grasp that [object] even in memory due to the recollection of specific details; furthermore, because of the particularities of place and time, what was remembered is not clearly distinguished. (2.132)
Cognition that has apprehended various locations and is distinct from them is also called "memory"; thus, cognition is stated to be something other than memory. (2.133)
Nor is that [recognition] established by a fruit distinct from the fruit of memory; for when there is a distinction between memory and [perception], recognition is an error. (2.134)
Furthermore, that which is not present would be known as being present;
thus, because the memory is undiscriminated, it would possess a contrary object. (2.135)
And because the mind is not impaired, there is no lack of presence or non-appropriation;
for it has been stated that a defect is the cause for the non-grasping by the sense organs. (2.136)
It has also been stated here that there would be no restriction on the operation [of cognition], and in this hypothesis, it follows as a consequence that all cognitions would be false. (2.137)

For no object is ever grasped by any cognition in its entirety; for one who has not known the distinction [between subject and object] in that way, there occurs error such as the appearance of two moons. (2.138)
Seeing that which possesses continuity, whose own self would he deny?
Now, it may be thought:
Recollection is distinguished precisely by its own cognition.
However, at times, because there is no apprehension of the specific features (viśeṣa) therein—as occurs in the case of perception—there is non-discrimination (aviveka).

But when there is apprehension of the specific features, even if only the universal (sāmānya) is seen in relation to the object conjoined with the sense organ, there is no non-discrimination; consequently, when both alternatives are recollected, doubt does not arise, and when only one is recollected, there is neither doubt nor error.
Even so, there would be no error even when two things are remembered;
nor is there a grasping of distinctions in memory, because it is the distinction itself that is being remembered.

If it is argued that the object being remembered is distinguished by its specific place and time, then [the answer is] that there is no grasping of a difference in place and time [at the moment of memory].

That is not so; for that which is perceived as being in a particular place is understood to be distinct from the object currently being seen, based on the cognition of its difference in space and time—even if it is infinite in number.

Nor can there be non-distinction simply because the difference in space and time is not grasped, since it is impossible to remember an infinite number of instances, and because there is no difference in space for that which is already perceived in a specific location.

If it is argued that there is no distinction because the object is not grasped as being "remembered," whereas there is a distinction when there is the knowledge that it is being remembered—therefore, cognitions of silver and the like, which lack the awareness "I am remembering," are the causes of error.
In that case, memory is indeed complete; nothing of its own object has not been grasped by it.
It is memory itself that distinguishes its own object from the perceptible; thus, there is no lack of distinction between the perceived and the remembered.
For the cognition "I remember" is something distinct from memory, serving to differentiate perception from recollection.
In this regard, the following must be considered:
does memory distinguish its own object or not? If it distinguishes it, then there is an absence of error.

On the other hand, if memory does not distinguish its own object, then it has been stated that error would occur even upon the perception of a common feature when another [object] is being remembered.

If it is argued that [the distinction] is due to the discrimination [of the cognition] "I remember," that very [discrimination] would itself lack self-discrimination; for the difference in a cognition known through its effect must be inferred from a specific difference in that effect. If the effect of remembrance were not distinct from the effect of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), by what could that [remembrance] be understood as distinct? Even when there is a discrimination of remembrance, the error of recognition—"That is the very same"—is observed; yet there is no non-discrimination of perception. Since both [perception and remembrance] undergo modification through the discrimination of one [from the other], and because of the non-discrimination from remembrance, there would be an error of remembrance, not an error of perception.

Therefore, it is not the case that "I do not remember" constitutes non-discrimination due to a lapse of memory. Alternatively, if non-discrimination is defined as the cognition of something absent as being present, this would result in the undesirable consequence that memory itself has a distorted object. Or, if it is argued that it is so because the absence [of the object] is not apprehended, let that be the case for dream-cognition; however, it cannot apply to error arising from the sense organs.
Because the non-apprehension [of an object] is caused by the impairment of the mind,
and because there would be no restriction on the occurrence [of cognition] in this way— as has already been stated—
if an entity were apprehended, then due to the non-apprehension of some part of it, all cognitions would be erroneous in cases of delusion.
For no cognition whatsoever has an object in its entirety.

Moreover, even when there is a cognition of distinction, it is observed that one may still follow after errors such as the double moon or confusion regarding directions due to other means of knowledge; thus, error is not merely non-apprehension.
Cognition, which consists in the negation of what has been presupposed, occurs when there is an attainment [of the object]. // 2.139 //
Non-apprehension does not bring about attainment, nor does contrary cognition;
rather, it is the two appearances of silver and of the object conjoined with the eye [that do so]. (2.140)
This is not understood as a negation of the object presented by that [cognition]; nor does this cognition subvert mere non-apprehension. (2.141)
For indeed, such a birth would not exist if it were afflicted by all-grasping;
this is a cognition of discernment, not a cognition that functions through the negation of what has been clung to. (2.142)
Speaking thus out of impudence, he denies his own conviction;
for such a discerning intellect does not exist regarding either succession or simultaneity.
When there is the attainment of a cognition of identity, there can be no determination of difference; for one who remembers silver while perceiving an object in contact with the eye. (2.144)

Having first perceived silver through a general perception and not yet discerned its distinctness, one later realizes it by discriminating; such is not the case in the initial perception of the universal.

In the absence of the recollection of both alternatives, doubt does not necessarily arise, because there is no perception of their distinction due to the lack of awareness of their temporal proximity. (2.146)

Because it appears as that [object], the apprehension would be of what is desired; otherwise, there would be a non-apprehension. In that case, the cause would be either non-apprehension or the apprehension of proximity. (2.147)
Free from the denial of the apprehension of difference by virtue of its positive nature, error—when no contrary [apprehension] is admitted—is based on non-apprehension. (2.148)
It has been stated that [error] is to be known solely through verbal testimony; however, non-apprehension (agraha) is not the bondage of non-apprehension.

The cognition in the form of a negation of what was expected—“This is not silver”—is not possible if there is only non-apprehension, because in the case of mere non-apprehension, there is no possibility of such an expectation (prasaṅga). Indeed, non-apprehension does not cause the expectation of anything.
For that [silver] is indeed non-existent.
However, erroneous manifestation (khyāti), by presenting the non-existent silverness of the present object, or the presentness of the silver, brings about the consequence [of error].
But surely, there are two manifestations: one of the silver and one of the object consisting of the eye?
That is true;
however, this comprehension of negation does not pertain to those two things as they are presented [in the cognition].
For we do not understand that it is "this is not silver" as negating merely the silver, or merely the object in contact with the eye;
rather, [it negates] either the silverness of that which is in contact with the eye, or the contact with the eye belonging to the silver.
And the non-apprehension of these two cannot be the cause of attainment, precisely because it is a non-apprehension.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the object to be negated, the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) must necessarily be accepted.
Nor is it the case that only the non-apprehension expressed as "this is not [that]" is being excluded, for that would entail such a state [of non-apprehension] in all cognitions.

Furthermore, if all cognitions were produced by the sublation of non-apprehension, this would be merely a cognition of distinction (*vivekajñāna*), and not a cognition in the form of the negation of what was previously presumed; thus, our position is consistent with the nature of actual experience.
For indeed, when silver and a fragment of mother-of-pearl are perceived simultaneously as distinct, such a cognition does not occur; it does not occur when they are perceived sequentially.

If it is argued that such a cognition would occur when they are perceived as non-distinct, this is correct, because when two things are perceived as distinct, there is the negation of their non-distinction.
[The objection that there is] no possibility [of such a cognition] because it involves the apprehension of two distinct things is refuted.
Moreover, it sometimes happens as follows:

one who remembers silver, perceives only the general features of an object in contact with the eye, does not grasp its distinction from silver, and then, through the clarity of his vision, realizes [the truth].
And at that time, there is no such cognition, because there is an absence of grasping without discrimination.
Now, if there is no error upon seeing a commonality, there would have to be doubt;
and the determinative knowledge that dispels that [doubt] is exactly of this same nature.
This is not sound.
For indeed, when there is no recollection of two alternatives, even upon the perception of a common feature, neither doubt nor error occurs.
Indeed, there is the cognition of mere radiant form present before one, and the recollection of silver.
Nor is their difference apprehended, nor their identity.
In that case, discriminative knowledge is not of such a nature, because identity is not apprehended.
Now, if it is thought—

Due to the non-apprehension of the distinction and the perception of temporal proximity, either the silver appears as if in contact with the eye, or the object in contact with the eye appears as if it were silver.
Therefore, since there is a "reaching" [of the object], the negation is logically justified. But in that case, you have admitted the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*).
For that [error] is not something else, because it appears as such despite not having that nature;
it may well be caused by ignorance of reality (*tattva*).
Indeed, it does not arise when there is knowledge of reality, because of their contradiction.
In that case as well, the sole basis is the manifestation of proximity;
however, the apprehension of distinction is its exception. When there is no such apprehension, that very manifestation—being free from exception—is the cause, not non-existence.

Furthermore, if one does not accept the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), then error would be caused by non-apprehension; thus, it would be quite a contradiction to say that "non-apprehension is caused by non-apprehension. Moreover, since there is no second object in a dream, how could there be a lack of discrimination? If there were a lack of discrimination due to being remembered, then when a substratum is perceived as undiscriminated, the perception of another attribute would contradict the previous perception, and the former would have to be considered an error.
But that which is a contradiction with common experience is cited as a fault of one's own.
This silver is cognized as having the same form through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Because there is a cognition through coreferentiality such as "this is white silver," the fault of contradicting one's own experience is attributed to the opponent; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a difference between two cognitions, which would result in a contradiction with experience.
When it is being cognized, the lack of confidence is sublated by that very cognition.
Incapacity [to prove the point] does not follow from deviation, because the effect is nonetheless obtained;
however, if [the reason] were merely "knowable" (*prameyatva*), then due to deviation, the effect itself would not be obtained. (2.151)

For when there is a lack of confidence regarding an object being known— namely, the thought that it might otherwise be so— that lack of confidence is blocked by the very production of that same cognition which determines its true nature.
For instance,
it is precisely such a cognition that is required for the cessation of that lack of confidence.
And that [cognition] certainly exists.

Nor is it logical to claim that a cognition is an ineffective means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because the function of a means of valid knowledge—ascertainment—is established by the very nature of cognition itself. For validity consists precisely in ascertainment.

However, there is no dependence on whether deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or non-deviation exists; for in its absence, even the non-deviation of smoke and the like would lack validity, whereas the eye possesses validity even when it deviates with respect to white, black, and other objects. Furthermore, deviation is never observed to be a cause of sublation that destroys validity, as is the case with defects, since the eye and other senses remain valid despite their deviation.
[Objection: But surely deviation is seen to destroy validity in cases such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and "verticality" (*ūrdhvatva*).
This is not the core point.
It is not that [the cognition] lacks authority because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case, but rather because of the absence of the function of determination (*pariccheda*).
And that absence [of the function] is due to the absence of the cause.
For the determination of the possessor of a mark (liṅgin) occurs through a mark (liṅga) that is non-deviant;
however, where non-deviance is not the cause, there is no dispute regarding the validity of the determination even when deviance exists.
And in the case of the sense organs, knowledge is the cause of determination in exactly that same way, and not like a mark.

Nor does the arising of doubt undermine validity through deviation, because when an object is correctly determined, the state of being twofold [i.e., the presence of alternatives] cannot be the cause of doubt. People do not entertain doubt regarding a post that has been ascertained by its verticality.
Knowledge determines its object at the very moment of its arising.
However, that which is non-determinative is not at all the subject under discussion here. And thus, it is a contradiction to say that from very determination itself there is non-determination.
For one who seeks the non-deviation of cognition for the sake of confidence, there is precisely no confidence, because there is no confidence even regarding the knowledge of non-deviation.
For that [non-deviation], being unestablished, cannot be a cause for confidence regarding itself or other cognitions;
if it were established by another cognition, there would be an infinite regress.

Moreover, if there is no confidence in the object based on the nature of the cognition, then while that [cognition] remains unestablished, with what could the non-deviation of the cognition be grasped? Furthermore, even non-deviation is said to consist solely in the nature of the cognition, because in the case of "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*), it is contradicted.
That being the case, that alone would be the means of establishing the object; the non-deviation (avyabhicāra) would be redundant.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that deviation does not undermine validity.
Moreover, even when there is no apprehension [of the object], that basis for discrimination which is desired is not set aside by punishments upon seeing its opposite. (2.152)

Defects that do not cause an increase [in the intensity of the cognition] do not destroy the capacity of the effect; therefore, the distinction between grasping and non-grasping depends on the presence or absence of those defects. (2.153)
For in the case of the opposite, an extreme impairment is established, both by the obstruction of the desired effect and by the arising of the contrary. (2.154)
Therefore, even here, a distinction between existence and non-existence is postulated; otherwise, how could the suspicion of non-apprehension when a defect is absent be dispelled? (2.155)
For the existence of the effect is not necessarily tied to the presence of the cause;
thus, the effect would have to be perceived directly, or else it would have to be inferred by means of a logical reason. (2.156)

In the opposite case, the absence of the fruit is logical because of the absence of the cause. Furthermore, the means for discernment and the presence or absence of defects are not barred by force regarding what is grasped or not grasped.
In the case of error, the causes of error are harmful; they certainly obstruct the desired effect and result in its opposite arising.

Furthermore, even when the sense organs and other factors are not defective, there is no cessation of the suspicion that perception might fail to occur; for even when the cause is present, the effect does not necessarily follow, and the opposite may happen.
The non-cognition of perception would have to be inferred by means of a logical reason (*hetu*), whereas from the result one infers the causal capacity of the cause.

However, due to the absence of defects, the non-existence of an effect that would result from error is a valid inference, because an effect does not arise in the absence of its cause. [146,i] The consequence of being without an object-support (anālambanatā) occurs when there is the imposition of another form. // 2.157 //
In this way, even in the case of non-apprehension, it would follow for you that there is no transfer of its own nature;
yet, if the transfer of some [nature] were equal [in both cases], then in that instance it would not be so. (2.158)
For if that [object] were likewise situated there for another person as well, then it would exist in that same way everywhere; and the same would apply to your apprehension of it. (2.159)

Just as in that case, because it is signless, the state of being signless is present in right knowledge, so too, even though there is apprehension, the absence of apprehension is determined in this way. (2.160)
The status of other [factors] as causes is not distinguished from that of cognition alone;

furthermore, there is a loss of their status as objects (*ālambanatva*), just as in the case of the appearance of another form, even when something conjoined with the eye is apprehended, because the failure to impart its own nature (*svarūpānarpaṇa*) is equal.
Or, if it is argued that some universal form possesses its own form—

Now, as for the claim that some objects conjoined with the eye are apprehended in their own form, such that there is no lack of a common objective support (*ālambana*) even when some [of those forms] are not apprehended— this is the same [for our position],
because even when other forms appear, certain of its own forms do indeed appear.
Now, if it is not accepted that what is conjoined with the eye can be an object of perception, then the opponent likewise does not accept the contrary.
For it has been said:
"Therefore, when one perceives something as being otherwise than it actually exists..."
That knowledge is without an object, and it has non-existence as its object.

[147,i] Now, if there is a suspicion that even in other cases there might be a lack of an object (*anālambanatā*) because the object of a distorted cognition is not actually conjoined with the eye, that same [suspicion] applies equally to non-apprehension as well.

For just as in a distorted cognition it is observed that there is independence from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the thing conjoined with the eye, so too in a correct cognition this is suspected due to the commonality of being a cognition. Likewise, even a thing conjoined with the eye is not apprehended in its complete form; therefore, it becomes a non-object (*anālambana*), yet it serves as a cause for a similar recollection.

If it is argued that the absence of an object [is established] because of non-apprehension, why is it not suspected that there is likewise no object even in cases of apprehension? If you say "because of the absence of defects," that is equally true in the opposite case as well; moreover, being without an object does not mean having a different object.
For the eye is not taken as an object in any other way.

And the meaning of "having an object" in the case of mother-of-pearl is its fitness for the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of silver; for it is precisely because of this that one who seeks silver takes hold of it.

For even in the case of a jar, its status as the objective support (*ālambana*) of its own cognition is nothing other than its fitness for conventional usage (*vyavahārayogyatā*); this is because cognition does not possess the form of the object.

In that regard, the mother-of-pearl is not apprehended in its own true nature by the cognition of silver, because the conventional usage based upon it does not occur. However, it is apprehended in the form of silver, because the practical usage of taking it up (*upādāna-vyavahāra*), which is based upon that [form], does occur there.
[147,ii] Even regarding an injunction whose culmination lies in action, someone says that for the sake of establishing the nature of the thing itself:
"Just as the purpose of threshing, sprinkling, and so forth is established as being for the sake of the substance. (2.161)
Knowledge, by its very nature, has substance as its object, and likewise for the self because it is an agent;
even if this were so, how can the establishment of the desired form [of the self] be considered possible? (2.162)
The word is established as the effect of that cognition which has its object;
for what other purpose could there be for the object of cognition than the manifestation of its own form? (2.163)
The postulation of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) is not logical when the seen is possible;
therefore, just as [the capacity for purification] is understood in the case of rice grains from the injunction regarding sprinkling and so forth, [so it is here]. (2.164)

The unseen refinement (*adṛṣṭasaṃskṛti*) is the form of the injunction for knowledge, as it is of the self. Just as threshing, sprinkling, and so forth, by their very nature, have the substance as their purpose—since the substance is indicated as the object (*karman*) by the accusative case—so too knowledge has another as its purpose by its very nature; and since the self is indicated as the object, it is for the sake of that [self].

Therefore, even when an injunction has cognition as its object, it touches upon the nature of the self; it does not terminate in mere cognition, because the cognition is understood as something to be performed since its purpose is the nature of the self, and thus the nature of the self is implied by the very injunction of cognition.
This might be argued:
let it be that the intended purpose of the cognition is the self.
However, a means of valid cognition must be stated for the realization of the Self characterized by the removal of evil and so forth.
The scripture, for its part, culminates in the necessity of performing the knowledge of such a Self—
namely, "one should produce knowledge directed toward a Self of this kind"— but not in the form "the Self is of this kind."
To this it is replied:

for it is not logical that something which accomplishes nothing should be performed for the sake of another. Furthermore, there is no other fruit of knowledge regarding ritual action than the cognition of its nature; for when that [cognition] is perceived, one does not postulate another unperceived result.

In this regard, just as from the injunction itself—"He sprinkles the rice"—there is the understanding of an invisible refinement (*adṛṣṭasaṃskāra*) in the rice, even though it is the sprinkling that is the object [of the injunction];
otherwise, the necessity of performing the sprinkling for the sake of the rice would not be logical.

For in that case, the sprinkling would not have been performed for the sake of that [rice] if it were not producing some effect there. Thus, the existence of the invisible refinement is established by the injunction alone, just as in the case of "One desiring heaven should sacrifice."
Otherwise, it would not be logical for one who desires heaven to understand that the sacrifice is something to be performed if the sacrifice were not a means to heaven.
If one were enjoined toward what is not a means, then the one desiring heaven would not be truly enjoined;

and even if it were performed, it would not have been performed by one desiring heaven. Therefore, even from an injunction whose object is an action, the understanding of the relationship between the end and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is verbal (*śābda*).
Likewise, from the injunction regarding the object of knowledge, there arises the realization of the nature of the self.
For it is not logical to enjoin a cognition directed toward a self that is not of such a nature; rather, if the self is not of such a nature, it is nevertheless apprehended by that cognition.
This has already been answered, because [consciousness] is an illuminator even in its formless state. // 2.165 //
Otherwise, the fruit of that discipline would not be the manifestation of knowledge;
for while dissolution is to be warded off, distraction is not so, since it is as pleasant [as the former]. (2.166)
Furthermore, there would be no distinction between the distraction of one in a state of absorption and mere non-apprehension.
But surely, if there were an appearance of a form that does not exist, one would have to postulate an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa-phala*). (2.167)

The visible fruit seen in the manifestation of form is the characteristic of its accomplishment; it is not merely from what is seen that the purpose is realized, for that [accomplishment] follows after the goals of human endeavor. (2.168)
And that nature is not divided between the appearances of form and the formless, just as it is not divided in reality—emptiness of conceptual proliferation—as it is manifested by knowledge. (2.169)
The abandonment of suffering, karma, and afflictions would likewise occur even with respect to what is not real;
and this would be logical here, because it does not contradict perception and other means of valid cognition. (2.170)
Furthermore, these [terms] would not be used in a figurative sense, since they pertain to the domain of action.
From the rule regarding the knowledge of the self's nature, this much is understood:
that it is illuminated by knowledge, is apprehended as an object, and attains a state of being fit for conventional usage.
And that manifestation is seen both in its own form and in the form of another;
for example, mother-of-pearl in the form of silver.
This has already been established.
This is not merely a case of non-apprehension; rather, it is the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).

Since both possibilities are equally plausible there, on what basis can it be asserted that the realization of reality must necessarily be accepted, and not the appearance of one thing as another? Otherwise, the injunction for the knowledge of the Self would not bear fruit.
That [negation] indeed has the purpose of dissolving what is not the Self. For it is observed that the comprehension of a reality occurs through the dissolution of what is not that reality.
And if the Self were not manifesting in the form of the manifold of name and form (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*), what would there be to dissolve? Now, if this is your view—
This ignorance is of two kinds: that which veils the light and that which causes distraction.
In the states of dream and waking, it is the cause of distraction; in deep sleep, it is the cause of concealment, characterized by dissolution.
Among these, the cessation of the concealing ignorance is the fruit of the injunction for knowledge.
And that is incorrect;
for the cessation of obscuring ignorance is not sought by the person in the same way as the cessation of distraction,
since the latter consists of manifold suffering.

Furthermore, worldly existence (*laya*), being described in the Śruti as repeatedly characterized by bliss due to the cessation of various sufferings, would instead have to be sought after [as a goal].

Moreover, for one who does not accept error (*viparyāsa*), there could be no distinction within ignorance (*avidyā*), because it would be nothing more than mere non-apprehension (*agrahaṇa*) throughout all three states.
Therefore, there are two types of ignorance—non-apprehension and erroneous apprehension—which exist in a relationship of cause and effect.

Both dream and waking states are characterized by the non-apprehension of the causal [state]; thus, the classification of deep sleep as being characterized by non-apprehension is logically established.
As it has been said:
"Viśva and Taijasa are considered to be bound by both effect and cause."
But the wise one is bound by the cause; however, these two do not succeed in the fourth state.
But surely this distinction is otherwise— namely, by way of non-apprehension and correct apprehension:
the concealer in deep sleep is characterized by non-apprehension, while in the other two states it is incorrect apprehension.
For instance: [the opponent claims that] because an undivided, partless entity is apprehended while its state of being such [as manifold] is not apprehended, there is an appearance of it as distinct.
This is not sound.
If, first of all, that [state] is merely an incorrect apprehension, or a lack of clarity in cognition, or an apprehension of an object in some particular form rather than in its entirety—
then, in that case, a cognition that is unclear regarding something distant or subtle is a cognition of a general characteristic (*sāmānyajñāna*),
and it is not ignorance (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, since no cognition grasps an object in its entirety, it would follow that all cognitions are false.
Even if non-difference is not grasped, and even if difference does not cease, there is nothing to be removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), because difference is not perceived.
Indeed, the non-grasping of non-difference is not what must be removed.
For that [unity] does not commit any fault;
rather, difference is the locus of manifold suffering.

Now, if the apprehension of what is not distinct as having a distinct appearance belongs to that which is non-distinct in essence, then you have accepted the theory of erroneous cognition (*viparyayakhyāti*).
"It appears as both non-distinct and distinct.
Now, it might be argued: "We do not say that it appears as distinct, but rather that it appears as if it were distinct."

What is the meaning of "as if"? It is this: if, just as a separate entity that is not manifesting its oneness manifests, so too the single reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) manifests while its oneness is not being grasped;
thus, it is said that there is apprehension in some respect and non-apprehension in its entirety. And regarding that, it has been said:
"It manifests, as it were, but it does not manifest."
What is the purpose of the comparison in the case of illumination? It is the engagement in conventional usage based upon that [illumination].
If conventional usage is based upon that, then illumination is established.
An effect does not arise in the absence of a cause.

Now, if it is argued that the very non-apprehension of non-difference is what is mistakenly taken to be the apprehension of distinctness, that is incorrect; for it is not admitted that non-apprehension—which is a negation—can be apprehended either in its own form or in the form of another.

And if difference (*pṛthaktva*) is not manifesting, how can there be its apprehension? Furthermore, if one abandons the conceit of difference regarding what is non-different, yet adopts the conceit of apprehending difference while failing to apprehend non-difference, what would have been resolved? Therefore, it is well said:
"In mere non-apprehension, there would be no distinction between dissolution and distraction.
Indeed, no fruit whatsoever is observed from a realization in the form of the non-self;
in that case, there would have to be an assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). But for the realization of the nature of the self, the observed fruit is the establishment of its own true nature.
It is said:
it is not from the mere observation of anything whatsoever that something is considered to have a visible purpose; rather, it is from that which touches upon human goals.
For by that, the injunction regarding it becomes free of further expectancy.
Furthermore, there is no difference in the human capacity for realizing what is real and what is unreal.
For just as one who realizes the pure, non-dual Self is not touched by sorrow because there is nothing left to grieve over,
so too he does not accumulate a store of karma because there is no duty to be performed.
He does not desire anything nor does he hate anything, because of the absence of objects.
Thus, even while living, the wise man becomes liberated;
likewise, although things are not as they appear, he realizes them as if they were directly present through the prior cultivation of their true nature.
Even an unreal object becomes a cause for the conventional usage of "real" due to the intensity of its cultivation.

And this alone is logical here, because it does not contradict perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and because ritual injunctions regarding action have real objects as their referents.
For if ultimate reality were the emptiness of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-śūnyatā*), then perception and the other means of valid cognition would be sublated.
Furthermore, ritual injunctions would have as their object things established through conventional usage based on the appropriation of unreal conceptual constructions.
Therefore, it is only from the standpoint of the non-ultimate truth that the injunction for the knowledge of the non-dual Self is appropriate.
If it is argued that the verb "to know" (jānāti) refers to the awakening to reality, we say no, because of the qualifying term "false" (mithyā) and so forth. // 2.171 //
If it were the case that the self is not known [by perception], it would not be so because its nature is not established [thereby];
it is even less so if it were established by another means of valid cognition, or otherwise. (2.172)
The cognition of that [object] is produced by means of a form imparted by the word; even though that form is not the reality itself, the cognition of it is thereby made possible. (2.173)
If it is thought:
"In the statement 'That is to be desired to be known' (*sa vijijñāsitavyaḥ*), the root *jñā* (to know) refers exclusively to the determination of reality;
therefore, there can be no injunction of knowledge based on the superimposition of what is unreal."
That is not so; for knowledge is qualified by falsity and so forth—
as in "false knowledge," "correct knowledge," and "doubtful knowledge"—
which would not be tenable if that [term] were restricted to a single [meaning], due to both redundancy and contradiction.
This might be the case:
if there is a cognition of something in a form other than its own nature, that is not knowledge of its self, but rather merely knowledge of another thing;
yet it is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) that is enjoined.
Therefore, it is said that "the establishment of reality [occurs through this]";
but that is not so.
Indeed, it is not merely this much.
“‘The self is to be known’—
if this were an injunction for the cognition of its form,
that would not be the case, because it is untenable in either way.”
If the nature of the self were established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then that knowledge would not be something to be enjoined.
On the other hand, if it is not so established, it is simply impossible [to know].
This might be argued:

“[The Self is] free from evil, free from old age, free from death,” and “All this is what this Self is”—the knowledge of that whose form is thus presented by these words is enjoined; and that [knowledge] can occur both through its actual reality and through superimposition. Therefore, because there is an injunction for knowledge of such a nature, its existence as being exactly so is not necessarily understood [from the injunction alone].
Furthermore, if knowledge has a perceptible object, it is obtained through perception itself.
For one who desires to know the nature of the self, or for one who does not desire to know it, that [scriptural study] is indeed in vain. (2.174)
If the means for that [attainment] is not known, then let there be a rule for that very [means]; for injunctions such as threshing are never devoid of a contact with the unseen (adṛṣṭa). (2.175)
If this knowledge is established as being supramundane, then it cannot be brought about by a ritual injunction; for an injunction functions only to bring about that which is to be performed. (2.176)

And the sense of "what ought to be done" regarding a perceptible object is established from that very perception; however, in the case of a non-worldly object whose nature is not [directly] perceived, it is established once that object has been communicated by the word. (2.177)
Since knowledge is the means for attaining the object of knowledge, a person is naturally inclined toward it;
however, regarding the means to that [knowledge], if it is not understood, he should be impelled toward it by an injunction. (2.178)
Therefore, the entry into an injunction necessarily destroys its status as a means of valid cognition;
thus, that which has an already established object should not be cultivated by one who desires to understand the nature of reality. (2.179)
[152,ii] Moreover, if the result of knowledge is already perceived, then since the engagement [with the object] is established by that very fact, an injunction is useless.
For one who desires to experience the nature of the self exerts effort toward the knowledge of it quite spontaneously.
But for one who is not thus [inclined], that [incentive] is useless; therefore, even by a hundred injunctions, he cannot be impelled.
Now, if it is argued that he does not engage in even an activity with visible results because of ignorance of the means, and for that reason an injunction is prescribed—this is trivial.
Therefore, let that very means be prescribed by which this person has not previously engaged due to ignorance;
for once there is knowledge, he will certainly engage because the result is perceptible.
It might be argued that even in the case of threshing and other such acts with perceptible results, an injunction is observed.
True; however, it is not devoid of contact with the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
For even in that case, there is necessarily an unseen result in the rice grains, or rather, through that medium, the accomplishment of the primary apūrva is itself unseen.
Now, if it is thought—
"The knowledge of the non-dual Self has never been seen before and is extraordinary;
therefore, it is enjoined even as having an immediate result.
To this, it is replied:
For what purpose is it enjoined?

Is it for the sake of realizing its own nature, which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or rather for the sake of performance? In that regard, it is not for the sake of establishing its own nature; for an injunction has performance as its fruit, not performance itself, since that [realization of nature] is established precisely through its having a perceptible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*).

Therefore, when the reality of the Self—whose nature is free from evil and so forth—is understood through the word (*śabda*) as something transcendent (*alaukika*), a person’s own inclination toward its direct knowledge arises spontaneously because that [word] serves as the means for its experience; thus, an injunction regarding it is useless. Just as when some wondrous object is understood through scripture, one’s own inclination toward its direct realization arises spontaneously.
However, an injunction is appropriate in the case of the means to that [realization], provided those means are unknown, in order to make known their status as means.

Thus, since an injunction (*niyoga*) is untenable with respect to knowledge, and since validity is impossible when an injunction is understood as having the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), one who desires the realization of the established nature of the self must not accept that it enters into an injunction through verbal testimony.
Now, in order to refute the second type of injunction regarding realization, he says:
For this very reason, there is no establishment of a continuum of consciousness;
even in that case, as before, there would be no valid cognition of its own nature. (2.180)

However, from a word established in its own essential nature, there arises an injunction for meditation based on what is cognized through another statement; or else, even that [injunction] would be in vain. (2.181)

Because the excellence of the cognition is observed through repeated practice, therefore the Vedāntas possess the status of a valid means of knowledge regarding that which is not an object of action. (2.182)

[153,ii] As for the view that one should perform sacrifice (*kratu*), one should cultivate wisdom (*prajñā*), and one should meditate deeply (*nididhyāsitavya*); and even where the state of resting in the essential nature itself is indicated, as in "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there too [the sense is] "I am Being" (*sad-asmi*).

Because it is intended that one should "hold the mind thus," meditation (*dhyāna*)—which consists of reflection other than hearing—is enjoined as a continuous flow of cognition (*pratyaya-pravāha*), with immortality as its fruit, just like ritual action (*karman*).

That too is not tenable for this very reason: because of the previously mentioned consequence of the absence of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the realization of reality, or because the sentence would then be focused on something else.

However, if it is maintained that the injunction of a continuous flow of cognitions regarding that [reality] is desired once that reality has been understood from another sentence which is itself focused on reality; [then we reply:]...
Let it be so; there is no fault whatsoever.
And thus, by saying "having understood, one should exercise wisdom," he demonstrates that the knowledge of the reality of the self is already established.
Or rather, that [meditation] would be entirely useless, because its purpose has already been attained.
For such reflection, which results in direct realization, has a visible purpose; no other fruit is required beyond that.
Indeed, it was explained previously that immortality is nothing other than the manifestation of one's own true nature.
In the world, it is observed that the practice of knowledge is the cause for the clarity of right knowledge.
For through a particular kind of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one comes to experience even what is non-existent; how much more so, then, what is real?

As for the injunction, "He should perform the sacrifice" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*), it does not enjoin the contemplation of the reality of the Self—which transcends all specific attributes—as having that [Self] as its fruit; rather, it enjoins the meditation on forms such as the mind-made (*manomaya*) or the vital-body (*prāṇaśarīra*), which are conditioned by name and form (*nāmarūpa-upādhi*), with sovereignty as their fruit, or else, gradually, with direct realization as their fruit.
The phrase “the wise one, having realized that very [Self]” (*tameva dhīro vijñāya*) is not an injunction for the production of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇavidhi*).

Because of the exclusion of anything else (*anyanivṛtti*) expressed by the word “that very” (*tameva*), the intention is understood to lie in exclusion; just as in the sentence “the cloth becomes red,” the purport of the statement lies in the quality of being red.

Here, non-differentiation was established following the differentiation of the principles (*tattva*) such as space (*ākāśa*); in that context, when the occasion for producing wisdom arises, it is enjoined by the words “that very.”
And likewise, in the first half [of that verse]:
"The stainless, supreme, unborn Self is greater than space, vast and eternal"—
thus the reality of the Self is shown to be superior to space and the other elements.
Since there is a possibility that he might act in that very same way regarding the application of wisdom (*prajñākaraṇa*), the word "that very" (*tameva*) is stated in order to prevent that.
Otherwise, the word "only" (*eva*) would have no purpose, nor would the thing to be excluded be understood.
And thus, this is elaborated upon by what follows in the single syntactical unit: "One should not meditate on many words. (*nānudhyāyādbahūñchabdān*).
Otherwise, the sentence would be split.

Furthermore, since there is no possibility of meditation upon the mere word—because that [meditation] is preceded by the word—it follows that this [injunction] has as its object only the meaning of the word.
Thus, in the passage "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'the Self' alone," the force of the particle *eva* (alone) indicates an injunction regarding that meaning.

The statement “it is to be meditated upon” (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*) also constitutes a single sentence whose sole purport is the nature of the Self, because it begins with “But for the sake of the Self” (*ātmanastu kāmāya*) and concludes with “All this is what this Self is” (*idaṃ sarvaṃ yadayamātmā*). Therefore, the phrases contained within it—“it is to be seen,” “it is to be heard,” and “it is to be meditated upon”—are not separate injunctions, even though they employ gerundive suffixes (*kṛtyapratyaya*). This is because the gerundive suffix is recorded as having other meanings besides injunction, such as fitness (*arha*) and so forth; thus, these words serve the purpose of praise, just like the statements “Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to silently” (*viṣṇurupāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*) and others found within the passage concerning the Upāṃśu sacrifice.
“This whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; thou art That”—this sentence culminates in the reality itself.
In this regard, the notion “I am Being” is merely a mental construction.

Therefore, since even the threefold knowledge cannot be an object of injunction, and since the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence occurs without an injunction, the authority of the Vedāntas regarding even an already existing reality (*bhūtārtha*) is established by virtue of their being independent due to their non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*). Accordingly, in the sūtra "But that [is known] through the harmony [of the texts]" (*tattu samanvayāt*), the word "but" (*tu*) distinguishes Brahman from dharma—which is characterized by injunction—and states that Brahman is to be understood through "harmony" (*samanvaya*). For "harmony" is the connection or application of the meanings of words; thus, Brahman is understood from this, not from an injunction.
[155,i] But surely, the authority of the Veda with respect to matters that are to be accomplished has been described without distinction:
"Dharma is a matter characterized by an injunction."
The meaning is that the subject matter of the Veda is characterized by injunction (*codanā*).
This is not sound.
For, in this case, this would be an investigation into the subject matter of the Veda whose authority is already established, just like the subsequent definitions [of the other means of knowledge].
In that case, it would not be appropriate to establish its authority immediately thereafter, nor [would it fit] the statement, "The definition of the means of valid cognition has been completed.
Furthermore, there would be no disagreement regarding the fact that the *mantras* and *arthavādas* have action as their purpose.
That [objection] will be refuted later on; moreover, much more could be said on this matter, so enough of this digression.

Just as cognition, when free from the interference of other human minds, attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its object, so too does that which is born from a scripture not of human origin, because it remains independent regarding what is already established (*siddha*). (2.183)
Thus ends the third section, the Section on Commissioning (niyogakāṇḍa).
[The Section on Accomplishment (siddhikāṇḍa)] [156,i]

Thus far, an effort has been made to refute those who, under the guise of discussing the authority of the duty of practice (*pratipatti-kartavyatā*), have asserted its lack of authority; now, however, an effort is being made to inform those who assert that it is indeed lacking in authority.
Regarding this, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:
"But since the meaning of a sentence consists of word-meanings related to one another, [it must] possess the nature of a word-meaning."
If the meaning of a word were [the sentence-meaning], the sentence-meaning could not exist without reaching [other words], as it would require another means of knowledge. (4.1)

[156,ii] First of all, words such as "Brahman" or "Antaryāmin" are not themselves the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because they function as causes for a subsequent cognition only when their relationship [to an object] is already established.

Nor is it the sentence [itself that is the means of knowledge]; for that does not directly denote [the meaning]. Rather, the comprehension of that [meaning] occurs through the mediation of word-meanings (*padārtha*), since there is no cognition of what is not a word-meaning.
For these [words], through their association in a relationship of primary and subordinate, convey a single word-meaning as qualified by other word-meanings.
In that case, the sentence-meaning is simply the word-meaning itself as thus qualified.

Nor can there be the status of a word-meaning for things not yet apprehended by other means of knowledge, because—as has been stated—it depends upon the cognition of the relationship [between word and meaning].

In that case, if it is not the meaning of a word (*apadārtha*), it cannot be the object of a sentence; for those [proponents], the sentence would be non-informative. If it is the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), then because it is already apprehended through another means of knowledge, the sentence would be merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*).
Therefore, regarding those sentences accepted as authoritative which have objects such as Brahman that are absolutely unperceived, do they contain words denoting those [objects], or not?
If they do not exist, they could neither be conjoined with nor distinguished from other things, and thus they would not be objects of cognition, like clods of earth and the like.

But if they do exist, nevertheless, they could not be conveyed by words with which they have no established relationship, and being uncomprehended, they cannot serve as causes for the comprehension of a specific sentence-meaning. In this regard, just as the phrase "Let the cuckoo be brought from the forest" possesses communicative power only when the referent of the word "cuckoo" is known, so too it is with those [words].

Therefore, there is no comprehension of a novel category of entity (*apūrva*) from the injunction (*codanā*); for that [injunction] indeed authorizes a person toward actions through prescriptions and prohibitions. As for the acceptance by the elders of the threefold [Veda], it is due to its utility in recitation (*japa*); and the *upaniṣads* are the *vedāntas*—this is because of their application therein.
To this, it is replied:

Once the status of being a category (padārtha) has been established in a general sense, it is possible—just as in common worldly usage—to communicate a specific, unprecedented [instance] by means of its unique qualities. 4.2.

Just as in the world, when one has already apprehended through another means of knowledge the general nature of birds—such as those found in a particular island described as "birds with feet made of emerald, beaks made of ruby, and wings made of gold and silver"—this general nature, when conjoined with a unique set of attributes not shared by others, acquires a specific form not previously apprehended by that other means of knowledge; and it is this specific form, not yet apprehended by another means of knowledge, that is established by the sentence.

For in every sentence whatsoever, it is precisely the unapprehended particularity that constitutes the object of knowledge (*prameya*). Thus, whether it be the generality of the cause or the generality of Being—as in the passages, "From which indeed these beings are born," and "Neither gross, nor subtle, nor short"—it acquires a specific form through its connection with and distinction from the meanings of such words, which is not apprehended by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and thereby becomes the object of knowledge for the sentence. Consequently, since the understanding of a novel matter (*apūrva-artha*) occurs precisely through the connection of word-meanings established in common worldly usage, there is neither a lack of informative power nor the status of a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*).
Or rather, when the form of Brahman—which is cognizable through all means of knowledge—is established, the dissolution of the phenomenal world is demonstrated by means of words. (4.3)

It is held that [Brahman], having dissolved all manifold conceptual proliferation, is not an object of any other means of knowledge in its true nature; thus, it has the sacred tradition (āmnāya) as its sole basis. 4.4.

Alternatively, Brahman is not entirely unknown in the world, because it is known through all cognitions; because there is nothing to be cognized apart from Brahman; because particular cognitions conform to the nature of the universal; and because it has been established that Brahman is the Truth remaining when all differences are withdrawn, as illustrated by the example: "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth."
What, then, is conveyed by the word? It is the absence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).

In that regard, both the referent of the term "phenomenal proliferation" is established and its negation is established; from the connection between these two, there arises the comprehension of that absence.

Its being based solely on the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) is stated because perception and the other means of knowledge are permeated by ignorance (*avidyā*); for it cannot be made an object in its form where all distinctions have completely subsided, since the subsidence of distinctions is to be understood through the sacred tradition alone.
The opponent, however, objects:
"But surely, if [the self] were restricted to the elements, it would follow that it is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha)."

Indeed, that statement which does not incite a person toward the accomplishment of any benefit nor turn him away from the accomplishment of harm, but merely recounts an already established fact, is devoid of human purpose (*apuruṣārtha*). Because it lacks human purpose, it is invalid (*apramāṇa*), like the ravings of a madman; and such is generally the case with the Vedāntas.
It is said:
"The means of valid cognition does not have as its sole purpose the attainment of human goals. (4.5)

"For they declare even equanimity to be the fruit of valid cognition" (*upekṣāmapi hi phalaṃ pramāṇasya pracakṣate*); it is inferred that this half-verse must have been present here, yet it is not seen in the manuscripts. Furthermore:
"Moreover, due to ignorance, the living being appears as one who grieves and suffers. (4.6)
And the cessation of that [cognition] is itself considered the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), when some object has been known by men who possess curiosity. (4.7)
The arising of knowledge for those who are distressed is accepted as a human goal;
and just as in the case of the sense organs and so forth, which are established in their respective forms, there is no lack of being a human goal.
And why should its being devoted to active engagement be prevented in this case?
If it is argued that the knowable object possesses human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) there [in the Vedas], then that is the same here as well. (4.9)
The goal of human endeavor is itself Brahman—tranquil and free from old age and the like;
therefore, it is taught to the disciple by means of the instruction, "That thou art. (4.10)

If it is held that perception and the other means of knowledge are auxiliary to the activity of another, then in this case as well, let them be accepted as auxiliaries to the activity of direct realization. (4.11)
It is not necessarily the case that the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

Indeed, the acquisition of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful are not the only fruits of a means of valid cognition; for those who know the nature of valid cognition declare even indifference (*upekṣā*) to be a fruit of a means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, being a human goal is not the definition of a means of valid cognition; rather, it is being the cause of valid knowledge.

Therefore, it is not the case that [the Upanishads] lack authority because they do not serve a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, such notions as "I am a mourner," "I am suffering," or "my wealth and so forth have been lost" are false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*) belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*), whose true nature is pure Brahman. The knowledge of the reality of the self as Brahman—which is pure consciousness and bliss—consists precisely in the cessation of these [false cognitions]. That [knowledge] is a human purpose in its very essence, because it consists in the cessation of the undesirable and the manifestation of the desirable.

And although its persistence continues due to past impressions (*saṃskāra*), nevertheless, for the wise person who maintains the continuity of verbal knowledge, it does not occur as before; rather, it ceases once and for all.
Furthermore, the fulfillment of human purpose is seen to reside in the very arising of knowledge, as in the case of those agitated by curiosity regarding an unknown object;
for nothing further is sought beyond that knowledge.

Nor is there a rule that only that which has activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*) as its object constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*); for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception and the rest, do not have activity and cessation as their sole purpose, since they have established entities (*siddhavastu*) as their objects, yet they do not forfeit their status as human goals.

If it is thought that the established entity known through perception and the rest—such as water—is the human goal because it is beneficial, then even those [means of knowledge] that are grounded in existing things possess the status of being human goals.

And here too, Brahman itself—the object of knowledge through scripture—is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), because it is the cessation of various misfortunes such as old age and because it is the manifestation of supreme bliss, being perfectly serene.

For this very reason, it is taught by the Śruti through the mouth of Śvetaketu as non-different from the person to be instructed, using the words "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*); for that [Brahman] is indeed non-different from the one to be instructed.
And that which is perceived as different is not the human goal.

Because of the state of being thus in reality and in the knowledge of identity with it, through the pacification of all inauspiciousness and by attaining the state of Supreme Śiva, the supreme human goal is fully attained.
If it is thought that even perception and the other means of knowledge are merely auxiliary to purposeful activity—
For activity characterized by avoidance, acquisition, and so forth, is rooted in an object already known through valid cognition;
such a status as a factor for activity exists here as well, because it is desired that one should engage in the effort toward direct realization once Brahman has been known through verbal testimony.

This *Brahmasiddhi*, with the radiance of its logic flashing forth through its skill in discerning the reality of the Vedānta, blocks the path to liberation for those who obstruct it, while tearing asunder even the dense, beginningless darkness; it instantly washes away the thick mire of the fallacious reasoning of worldly sects, having uprooted them all through its exposition, for the sake of the unsurpassed bliss of Śiva. 4.12.
Thus ends the *Brahmasiddhi*, the work of Maṇḍanamiśra.
